This is emphasized by the fact that they had established that those other than the *Ḥums* (al-Ḥums, a group of Quraysh and their descendants who claimed special status) circumambulated the House naked.

When He commanded clothing the outer body with garments, because the validity of prayer depends upon them, He commanded clothing the inner body with food and drink, because the capacity is customarily dependent upon them. So He said: ﴿And eat and drink﴾. What made this fitting is that some of them used to pious-ly restrict themselves in this regard during the pilgrimage.

When He commanded regarding clothing and food, He forbade transgression in both, so He said: ﴿And do not be wasteful﴾, by placing any of that in what is not the most deserving place for it, even by excess beyond the stomach. [Among that is that one should follow the Sunnah in drinking; it is easy, because the sediment settles in the vessel, and perhaps one may be harmed by drinking it. For this reason he forbade breathing into the vessel, because it may become foul-smelling and the soul will loathe it. As for food, one should make good use of the vessel and the fingers to gain blessing, and it is cleaner.] Then he gave the reason for this by saying: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the wasteful﴾, (p-388) that is, He does not honor them. There is no doubt that whoever is not loved by Him does not obtain any good, so every evil surrounds him. Among the forms of wastefulness is eating until the whole belly is filled, while moderation is restricting oneself to a third, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "A few morsels suffice the son of Adam to keep his back upright. If he must, then a third for food, a third for drink, and a third for breath." And: "The son of Adam has never filled a vessel worse than his belly." And: "The disbeliever eats in seven intestines, and the believer eats in one intestine." Narrated by al-Bukhārī from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both. The physicians said the intestines are seven, so the meaning then is that the disbeliever eats to satiety, filling the seven intestines, while the believer eats for sustenance, eating in one intestine, which is a seventh of his belly. To this refers "morsels." If not, then in two intestines and a portion, which is a third, and Allah knows best.

The occasion of the revelation was that they used to take off their garments when they wished to circumambulate, saying: "We do not circumambulate in garments in which we have sinned," and they would strip themselves of them so as to be stripped of sins, except the *Ḥums*, who are Quraysh and those born of them. They would not eat any food except the bare minimum and would not eat fat. The Muslims said: "O Messenger of Allah! We have more right to do that," so it was revealed.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 32:

Since it is well known that those people had become accustomed to what they had taken as religion, and they considered abandoning it a great matter, because Satan whispers to them that the expansion [of worldly life, and the expansion] (p-389) in it is among the things one should renounce, as many verses call for, He, glory be to Him, emphasized the permission in this matter by rebuking those who had forbidden it. He said, rebuking them, to make known that the praiseworthy renunciation (zuhd) is that which accompanies correct belief concerning the lawful and the unlawful; but renunciation that comes with altering some part of the religion by declaring the unlawful lawful, or the reverse, is blameworthy. ﴿Say﴾, rebuking and reproaching: ﴿Who has forbidden the adornment of Allah﴾, that is, the King to whom no one has any command, ﴿which He has brought forth for His servants﴾, that is, so that they may enjoy them, of garments, metals and other things.

When He mentioned the garments, which are a condition for the validity of worship, in a general way that included other things such as conveyances and so on, He followed them with food and drink, and said: ﴿and the good things﴾, that is, the lawful and pleasant ones, ﴿of provision﴾, such as the baheerah and the saa'ibah and the like. Since the meaning of the rebuke is: no one whose prohibition is considered binding has forbidden them, but rather has made them lawful, and since some extremist in religion may have gone to excess, holding fast to verses that repel one from the world and belittle its status entirely, let alone the adornment and good provision, He said, resuming in answer to one who asks, "For whom?": ﴿Say: they are﴾, that is, the adornment and the good things, ﴿for those who believe﴾. He expressed it with this phrase and did not say "and for others," to draw attention to the fact that they belong to them by right, ﴿in the life of this world﴾. As for the disbelievers, they follow them in enjoying these things, even though they have more of them; so they are not exclusively theirs, while they are for those who believe, ﴿purely﴾, that is, no one shares them with them. This is according to the reading of Nafi' with the nominative, and the implied construction in the reading of others is: in a state of being purely theirs, ﴿on the Day of Resurrection﴾. In this there is an emphasis on what has preceded regarding their being made lawful, after the emphasis and the removal of doubts, and a call to reflect on the distinction between the two situations, to clarify that the renunciation that is commanded (p-390) is only of the heart, in the sense that the world has no value in his sight, he has no inclination toward it, and it is not the greatest of his concerns. As for benefiting from it in what God has permitted, while regarding it as insignificant and not preoccupied with it, that is among the excellences.

Since this meaning is among the subtleties of meanings and the precious structures of expression, He, exalted is He, followed it with His saying, in answer to one who says: "Is this distinction so superior that other things are distinguished in this way?": ﴿Thus﴾, that is, like this wondrous distinction, ﴿We detail the verses﴾, that is, We clarify their rulings and distinguish some ambiguous matters from others, ﴿for a people who know﴾, that is, who possess the capacity and readiness for knowledge, so that they may thereby arrive at correct belief and righteous action.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 33:

When he had made clear that what they had forbidden is not forbidden, and that this was firmly established, he removed from souls what they had become accustomed to in opposition to it, and erased from hearts what they had been steeped in of its opposite. It was as if it were said: "Then what has God forbidden, when forbidding belongs to none but Him?" So the Exalted commanded him to answer them concerning that and to add that He has forbidden nothing other than it. He said: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden the indecencies﴾, i.e., the One who is good to me by making my religion the best of religions, ﴿the indecencies﴾, i.e., every single instance of them, which are those whose ugliness increases. Since indecency is that whose ugliness increases, and one might perhaps think that concealing it is not intended by the prohibition, he said: ﴿what is apparent of them﴾ among people ﴿and what is hidden﴾.

Since this applies specifically to what is greatly abominable in its foulness, he said: ﴿and sin﴾, i.e., (p-391) sin in general, which entails a requirement of recompense, for "sin" (ithm) is wrongdoing and its consequence. Since transgression (baghy) is of increased ugliness, specified in being among the swiftest of sins in punishment, he singled it out by mention, saying: ﴿and transgression﴾, which is exalting oneself over others unjustly. But since it may be applied to mere seeking, he confirmed its customary, legal meaning, saying: ﴿without right﴾, i.e., the complete right in which there is no admixture of falsehood; whenever there is in it an admixture of falsehood, it is transgression. Perhaps this excludes exalting oneself by right through victory over the transgressor, for that is a right of complete rightness, and calling it "transgression" is by way of mutual resemblance (mushakalah), to repel from engaging in it by placing it under the name of transgression, and to encourage pardon, as a similar usage was mentioned before in ﴿God does not love the public utterance of evil speech, except by one who has been wronged﴾ [an-Nisa: 148]. It is also possible that its restriction is an emphasis on its prohibition, in that it is not conceivable except as described as being without right, as He said, specifying and stating explicitly, as an alert to the severity of the abominableness: ﴿and that you associate with God﴾, i.e., the One who is singled out with the attributes of perfection, ﴿what He has not sent down any authority for﴾. For there is not found anything that anyone names as a partner except that it is something for which God has sent down no authority; indeed, there is in reality no proof for it and no evidence. Perhaps He restricted it by this only as a guidance that the foundations of religion may not be relied upon except with a decisive proof, so how then regarding the greatest of them, which is monotheism! For this reason He followed it with His saying: ﴿and that you say about God﴾, i.e., He forbade that you say about God, the One than whom there is none greater and to whom there is no equal, ﴿what you do not know﴾, i.e., what you have no knowledge of in particular, nor is it grounded in a knowledge more general, whether it be of the foundations or not.

(p-392) Since it had been established that people are of two kinds, the guided and the astray, and the blame of the astray was repeated for their audacity against God, by doing what He forbade them and leaving what He commanded them, and since the constant custom of kings is that they do not give respite to one whose opposition to them is repeated, it was as if it were said: "Why does He destroy the one who opposes Him?" So it was said, as admonition and warning: "They do not harm by that except themselves, and they do nothing of it except by His will. So their survival and their destruction are equal to Him. Only one who fears missing out or fears harm hastens; and for them there is a term that must be fulfilled. This is not specific to them, but ﴿For every nation is a term﴾, and it is coordinated with ﴿therein you shall live, and therein you shall die﴾ [al-A'raf: 25], ﴿so when their term comes﴾."

Since their outlook was on the respite within the term, and since cutting off their hope was part of their punishment, He placed it first and said: ﴿they cannot delay it by an hour﴾, i.e., from the term, "an hour," which is used figuratively, and the intended meaning is the least possible, because it is the smallest unit of time in common usage. Then He coordinated with the whole conditional sentence, not with its apodosis, the phrase: ﴿nor can they advance it﴾, i.e., beyond the appointed term; because the One who set it for them set it only while knowing everything that would happen in their affairs, and no new knowledge arises for Him, nor does anything of their circumstances newly occur. It is also possible that it is coordinated with His saying: ﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place and enjoyment for a time﴾ [al-A'raf: 24], and the verse would be informing that they will multiply and increase until they become nations, and they are not restricted as a whole, but each nation has a time.

(p-393) When the soul's eagerness to ask about what will happen after the appointed time of settling and enjoyment was stronger than its eagerness for this, because that is more hidden and so further from occurring to the mind, He placed first His saying: ﴿He said: "Therein you will live"﴾ [al-A'raf: 25]. And since mention of the remedy for the disease of exposing the private parts was more important, He placed first ﴿We have sent down to you clothing﴾ [al-A'raf: 26], and then what follows it, until this place became the most fitting for this verse, so it was arranged here.

When the indication had preceded toward urging the following of the Messengers, through the verses of the first aim of this surah's aims, such as His saying ﴿A Book has been sent down to you﴾ [al-A'raf: 2], and ﴿that you may warn﴾ [al-A'raf: 2], and ﴿Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 3], and His saying ﴿We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent﴾ [al-A'raf: 6], and His saying ﴿Say: My Lord has commanded justice﴾ [al-A'raf: 29], ﴿My Lord has only forbidden the shameful deeds﴾ [al-A'raf: 33], and the warning against the devils through His saying ﴿And do not follow other than Him as protectors﴾ [al-A'raf: 3], and through His saying ﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾ [al-A'raf: 16], ﴿Let not Satan tempt you﴾ [al-A'raf: 27], and other than these, it became clear that there is no way to salvation except through the Messengers. He concluded that with the term (appointed time), urging action during the days of respite. He followed that, urging attachment to the means of salvation by following the guiding callers before the escape is lost to the event of death, by explaining the recompense for whoever follows best in both abodes, with ﴿O children of Adam﴾.

Since it was within His right, glory be to Him, to punish whoever opposes the call of reason without sending a Messenger, and since sending Messengers was permissible for Him and a bounty from Him, glory be to Him, since it is not obligatory upon Him, (p-394) He indicated this with the particle of doubt, saying: ﴿Immā﴾, which is "in" (the conditional), joined to it "mā" for emphasis, ﴿there come to you messengers﴾. And since increased acquaintance with the Messenger is more decisive for removing excuse and stronger in proof, He said: ﴿from among you﴾, meaning: of your own kind, from your Lord.

[Since the predominant concern of this surah is knowledge, as has preceded in ﴿Then We will surely relate to them with knowledge, and We were not absent﴾ [al-A'raf: 7], and will come in ﴿And We had certainly brought them a Book which We detailed with knowledge﴾ [al-A'raf: 52], and others, the expression with qasas, which is the tracing of traces as preceded in al-An'am, was more fitting, so He said]: ﴿who relate to you My verses﴾, meaning: they follow up their mention to you in a definite manner, and some of them follow the traces of others in them, not differing in any one of the foundational principles.

Since meeting the Messengers is decisive and migrating to them is obligatory, because deeds are not accepted except by relying upon them, whenever a way to that is found, He linked the recompense with fa' (then), saying: ﴿So whoever fears Allah﴾, meaning: fears My station and fears My threat, by means of affirming the Messengers and receiving from them, ﴿and reforms﴾, meaning: does righteous deeds by following their traces, ﴿then no fear﴾, meaning: prevailing, ﴿shall be upon them﴾, meaning: because of that, from anything they anticipate, ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾, meaning: in their hearts, a grief over something that has passed them will recur for them at some time; because Allah gives them what gladdens their eyes. This seems to be an extreme in expression, because their veneration of Allah and their awe of Him may be described by fear.

(p-٣٩٥) When He mentioned those who affirm, He followed it with those who deny, saying: ﴿And those who denied Our signs﴾, i.e., despite the greatness they possess through their being attributed to Us. Since denial may arise from a doubt or some kind of excuse, He negated that by saying: ﴿and were arrogant toward them﴾, i.e., they brought about arrogance, in the manner of one who greatly desires it, transgressing beyond them to the opposites of what they were called to.

Since that is not a true cause of punishment, but rather an indicator of the one whom God created for Hell in order to establish the proof against him, the phrase ﴿Those﴾ was stripped of the fa' (the connecting particle fa'), i.e., the remote and the hateful, ﴿are the companions of the Fire﴾. Since the companion of a thing is the one who is constantly with it and known for it, he stated this explicitly: ﴿they﴾, i.e., exclusively, so as to exclude the disobedient who is without denial or arrogance, ﴿therein﴾, i.e., in the Fire exclusively, though it encompasses each of its tiers, ﴿abiding forever﴾. It has thus become clear that the affirmation of the fa' at first is for encouragement to follow, and its omission the second time is for warning against harshness of disposition. The situation in both places is one of danger. Perhaps among its benefits is an indication that when a messenger is sent, it is obligatory upon everyone who hears of him to seek him out to examine his matter; then if his truthfulness becomes clear to him, he follows him, and if he holds back from that, he is a denier. And God is the Granter of success.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 37:

Since the denial of the messengers sometimes takes the form of legislating something they did not legislate, and sometimes the form of rejecting what they legislated, in word or in deed, and since he informed that the deniers are the people of the Fire, he gave the reason for that with his saying: ﴿Who is more wrong﴾, meaning more outrageous in wrongdoing, ﴿than one who fabricates﴾, meaning deliberately attributes, ﴿against Allah﴾, meaning the Supreme King, ﴿a lie﴾, meaning like one who legislates regarding foods and clothing other than what He legislated, or claims that revelation came to him and so rules that something exists which does not exist, ﴿or denies His signs﴾, meaning by rejecting what the messengers reported, so that he rules to deny what exists.

Since the answer is: no one is more wrong than this, rather he is the most wrong of people, and since it is known that the wrongdoer deserves punishment, how then the most wrong? He said: ﴿Those﴾, meaning the distant ones from the divine presences, ﴿their portion from the Book will reach them﴾, meaning what was written at the breathing of the spirit, or the terms He appointed for them and the provisions He apportioned, as an emphasis in rejecting the objection of one who says: if we have opposed, why does He not destroy us? Then he limited the reaching of the portion with his saying: ﴿until, when Our messengers come to them﴾, meaning those whom We have allotted from Our greatness what We willed, while they are ﴿taking them﴾, meaning seizing their spirits completely from all their bodies. ﴿They say: Where is what you used to call upon﴾, meaning calling in worship, ﴿besides Allah?﴾, meaning you claimed that they were intermediaries for you with the Supreme King, and you called upon them while you were turning away from Allah. Call upon them now, that they may protect you from the torment of humiliation which We make you taste. ﴿They say: They have strayed﴾, meaning they have vanished, ﴿from us﴾, so there is no helper for us.

Since the God does not vanish, they knew their straying by their absence from them, so he said, translating that: ﴿And they will bear witness against themselves﴾, meaning they exaggerated in acknowledging ﴿that they were disbelievers﴾, meaning concealers, out of obstinacy, of what the light of reason had revealed to them, so nothing prevents it except the desires of the souls and the adherence to misery.

The commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 38:

Since it was as if it were said: "They have indeed confessed, and confession, as it is said, is an act of fairness. Will it benefit them?" It is said: "Far-fetched! Its place has passed with the passing of the abode of action. Undoubtedly!" ﴿He said﴾, meaning: the one to whom God has entrusted their affair, ﴿"Enter"﴾, being ﴿"among nations"﴾, meaning: among a totality of communities and groups, some of which preceded others. Then He described them, using the feminine ending (tā' al-ta'nīth) to indicate the weakness of their intellects, saying: ﴿"that have passed away before you"﴾. Since in past time there were those who believed, He introduced the preposition, saying ﴿"before you"﴾. Since the jinn were the origin of misguidance, He placed them first, saying: ﴿"of jinn and humankind"﴾. Then He mentioned the place of entry, saying: ﴿"into the Fire"﴾.

Since it is the customary practice of companions that they speak to one another, and at the time of gathering they greet one another, the listener became eager to know their state in that regard, and so He answered him, saying: ﴿"Every time a nation enters"﴾, meaning: from among them, into the Fire, ﴿"it curses its sister"﴾, meaning: the one nearest to it in religion and creed, whose traces have passed and whose beacon it has followed. The Jews curse the Jews, and the Christians curse the Christians, and so on, and this continued among them ﴿"until, when they have all overtaken one another therein"﴾, meaning: they followed and caught up with one another, one riding upon another, as the idgham (assimilation of letters) indicates, ﴿"all together"﴾, no nation remained among them, nor any individual from a nation, ﴿"the last of them will say of the first of them"﴾, meaning: in time and rank, namely the followers and the lowly, ﴿"Our Lord, these have misled us"﴾, meaning: on their behalf, addressing God with the address of the sincere, ﴿"Our Lord"﴾, meaning: the One who did not cut off His kindness from us in the world, despite what we did in returning His kindness with disobedience, ﴿"these"﴾, meaning: the first ones, ﴿"have misled us"﴾, meaning: because they were the first to establish misguidance, ﴿"so give them a double punishment"﴾, meaning: make them taste, because of that, a punishment equal to the punishment of others twice over, because they went astray and led others astray, and because they established misguidance. ("Whoever establishes a good practice in Islam will have its reward and the reward of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection; and whoever establishes an evil practice will bear its burden and the burden of whoever acts upon it until the Day of Resurrection.") From this is the saying: ("No soul is killed unjustly except that the first son of Adam bears a share of its blood") because he was the first to establish killing. Then they emphasized the severity of the punishment by saying: ﴿"from the Fire"﴾.

Since it was as if it were said: "They have indeed said something that has a basis, so how were they answered?" It is said: ﴿"He said"﴾, meaning: in answer to them, ﴿"for each"﴾, meaning: of the preceding and the following, the one followed and the follower, ﴿"is double"﴾, even though the two doublings are not equal, because the one followed, although he was a cause of the misguidance of the follower, the follower was also a cause of the one followed persisting in his misguidance and the severity of his obstinacy in it, by strengthening him through following and supporting him through defending and protecting him. Since they were ignorant of their deserving of the doubling because of this subtle point, He said: ﴿"but you do not know"﴾, meaning: of that.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 39:

When He mentioned the blame of the latter ones upon the former ones, He followed it with the reply of the former ones, saying: ﴿And the first of them will say to the last of them﴾, i.e., the first of the groups and nations, ﴿[causing them to be the cause] of their [own] (p-399) founding of misguidance for them and their calling of them to it﴾, ﴿So you had no superiority over us﴾, i.e., because of your submission to us and your following us in misguidance, ﴿so that we would bear for you some of the punishment because of it﴾, because our misguidance no longer benefits us, and you have shared with us in disbelief. ﴿So taste the punishment﴾, i.e., because of that, ﴿in Sijjin﴾, ﴿for what﴾, i.e., because of what ﴿you used to earn﴾, not because of your following us in disbelief.

When the custom had been established that people in dire straits expect deliverance, He informed that these were not like that, because they are impure and so are not fit for the abodes of holiness. He said, resuming in answer to one who seems to have said: "Is there no deliverance for these?" He manifested the place of the pronoun, for generality and for attaching the ruling to the description: ﴿Indeed, those who denied Our signs﴾, that is, which are known for their greatness in relation to Us, ﴿and waxed arrogant against them﴾, that is, they produced arrogance, transgressing beyond following them. ﴿The gates of heaven will not be opened for them﴾, that is, for the ascent of their deeds, nor their supplications, nor their spirits, nor for the descent of blessings upon them, ﴿the gates of heaven﴾, because it is pure from sensible and spiritual impurities. So when their wicked spirits ascend after death with the angels of punishment, the gates are closed before them, and then they are cast down from there into Sijjin. ﴿Nor will they enter the Garden﴾, that is, which is the purest and most noble of abodes, ﴿until﴾ what cannot be occurs, namely that ﴿the camel﴾ ﴿passes through the eye of the needle﴾, that is, enters and passes through, ﴿the camel﴾ despite its largeness, ﴿in the eye﴾, that is, in the hole, ﴿of the needle﴾, that is, the eye of the needle, meaning until what cannot be occurs. Thus it is a suspension upon an impossibility, for the camel is a proverb for the magnitude of body among the Arabs, and the eye of the needle is a proverb for narrowness of passage; it is said: "narrower than the eye of a needle," and from it comes al-mahir al-khirrit (the skilled guide), the guide who finds his way through narrow passages likened to the eyes of needles. And it is related from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he was asked about the camel, and he said: "The mate of the she-camel," mocking the questioner, and indicating that seeking another meaning beyond this apparent one is affectation.

Since this was for the deniers and the arrogant, he informed that it applies also to those who sever ties in general, saying: ﴿And thus﴾, that is, and like that recompense with this punishment, namely that their entering the Garden is impossible by custom, ﴿We recompense the criminals﴾, that is, those who sever what Allah commanded to be joined, even if they are mere followers imitating the arrogant deniers;

Then He explained the recompense of all of them, saying: ﴿For them there will be a bed of Hell beneath them﴾, i.e., a spreading beneath them; it is the plural of mihad (bed). Perhaps He did not mention it [the first time] because mihad is, in this context, like the explicit word (al-sarih) for it. ﴿And above them there will be coverings﴾, i.e., coverings, the plural of ghashiyah, that envelop them from Hell. He explicitly stated "above" here because the ghashiyah might be from the right or the left, or it may mean merely reaching and encompassing. Perhaps He omitted the first [mention of direction, i.e., "above"] because the verse is of the type of ihtibak (interlocking ellipsis): He mentioned Hell first as an indication of its being intended the second time, and He mentioned "above" second as an indication of "beneath" being intended the first time. (p-401) And since some of them may not have the capacity for either severing or connecting, He said in general terms, covering all kinds of misguidance: ﴿Thus﴾, i.e., and like that recompense, ﴿We recompense the wrongdoers﴾, so that it is known that the basis is the attribute. The mujrim is the sinner, and its root returns to severing (qat'). The zalim is one who places a thing in other than its place, like the act of one who walks in darkness. It is possible that by the variation of attributes, He, glorified is He, drew attention to their mutual entailment, so that whoever is a wrongdoer is necessarily also a sinner and a denier and arrogant, and vice versa.

When he had told of their conditions as a warning (tarhib), he followed it with an account of the conditions of the believers as an encouragement (targhib), and said, ﴿And those who believed﴾, in contrast to "those who denied."

When he said ﴿and did﴾, meaning: as confirmation of their faith, in contrast to "those who were arrogant," ﴿righteous deeds﴾. Since this could give rise to the assumption that doing all the righteous deeds, because it is a plural definite (jam' muhalla bi-l-alif wa-l-lam), is a condition for entering Paradise, he removed that assumption with a parenthetical clause (jumlah i'tiradiyyah) indicating ease, saying: ﴿We do not burden any soul except according to its capacity﴾, and as encouragement to acquire what is indescribable of bliss through what is within one's capacity. ﴿Those﴾, meaning: the high-ranking, ﴿are the companions of the Garden﴾. And since companionship (suhbah) indicates permanence, he stated it explicitly, saying: ﴿They will abide therein forever﴾.

[p. 402] Since a dwelling is not pleasant except with good neighbourliness, He said: ﴿And We shall remove﴾, meaning, by the greatness We possess, which nothing can overcome, ﴿whatever﴾ was in the world ﴿of rancour in their breasts﴾, meaning, enmity, hatred and deceit one of them harbours toward another. *Ghill* (rancour) comes from *yaghullu*, meaning it penetrates subtly into the core of the heart, and from *al-ghulul* (embezzlement), which is reaching sins that are hidden through cunning. It is said: "he *ghalla* in the thing and *taghalghala* in it," when he entered it gently, like love that enters the core of the heart, so much so that the one of lower rank does not envy the one of higher rank.

Since good neighbourliness is not enjoyed except with the tranquillity of settling and the solidity of the dwelling, and since water is the cause of prosperity and the pleasantness of homes, and since flowing water is more widely beneficial and more effective in bringing joy, He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Flowing from beneath﴾, and He indicated their elevated state by His saying: ﴿beneath them the rivers﴾. When their blessing was complete through water, by which every living thing lives, and it was known that from it come gardens, trees and everything that beautifies the dwelling, He informed about their practice of thanking God and His Messenger, which attracts increase, by His saying: ﴿And they will say: "All praise﴾, meaning, the comprehensive ascription of all the attributes of perfection, ﴿belongs to God﴾, meaning, the One who encompasses everything in knowledge and power, by His very essence and not by anything else. Then they described Him with what befits that, by His attributes as well, saying, informing that they had no means of reaching this bliss other than His bounty, both in this world ([p. 403]) and the next: ﴿Who has guided us﴾, meaning, with clarification and success. They attributed the guidance to what they had reached, using the effect for the cause: ﴿to this﴾, meaning, to the deed that brought us to it. ﴿And we would not have been guided﴾, meaning, and the state is that we were not at all capable of being guided, since our natures were formed contrary to that, ﴿had God not guided us﴾, meaning, He to whom all command belongs. The reading of Ibn 'Amir (Ibn 'Amir, one of the canonical Qur'an reciters) is without the conjunction *wa*, so that the clause clarifies what precedes it. Both readings refute the Qadariyya (Qadariyya, a theological school that affirms human free will in a way that denies divine predestination).

Since their acceptance of the messengers in the world was faith in the unseen, belonging to the category of knowledge of certainty, they were informed in the Hereafter of what they had reached of the certainty of sight, with joy and exultation, not as worship, and as praise of the messengers and of the One who sent them, by their saying, beginning with the particle of expectation because that is its proper place: ﴿Indeed, the messengers of our Lord have come﴾, meaning, the One who has done good to us, ﴿with the truth﴾, meaning, the established reality to which actuality corresponds, which has no cessation.

When they envied themselves, belittled them, and affirmed the favour to its people, He followed their saying with His saying, bestowing favour upon them by accepting their deeds. Since what is significant is the report of the inheritance and not who causes it, the verb was put in the passive form: His saying ﴿And they will be called﴾, meaning, to complete their bliss, ﴿that﴾ (the word here is the lightened form of the heavy *anna*, or it is the explanatory *an*), ﴿This is the Garden﴾, the elevated one, ﴿which you have been made to inherit﴾, meaning, it has come to you without toil or any contender, ﴿for what﴾, meaning, because of what, ﴿you used to do﴾. This is because He, glorified be He, made it a apparent cause through His generosity, whereas the true cause is what they themselves mentioned of His granting success.

(p-405) When they had settled in their abodes, and it was proclaimed to them that their settled state would endure, Allah, glory be to Him, informed that they turned, boastfully, toward the people of the Fire, gloating over them for their having been lodged in the abode of destruction. This was to delight their own souls with bliss and to vex the wretched, as stated in His words: ﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out to the companions of the Fire﴾, meaning after each of the two groups had entered its own abode. They inform them of the blessings that were bestowed upon them, and they remind them of what they used to threaten them with, namely the descent of retribution.

Then He explained what the call consisted of, with His words: ﴿that﴾. Here it is either the light form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy (thaqilah) [an-], and He mentioned the particle of expectation (harf al-tawaqquf) because that is its proper place, so He said: ﴿We have indeed found﴾, meaning by direct witnessing, just as we used to be certain of it through faith, ﴿what our Lord promised us﴾, meaning the One who showed us kindness in both abodes, of reward, ﴿as truth﴾, meaning we have found all that our Lord promised us, for us and for others, to be true, just as we used to believe. ﴿Have you then found﴾, meaning likewise, ﴿what He promised﴾. He mentioned the first object for the sake of delight, and omitted it here to belittle those addressed, and so that it would encompass what belongs to both groups, such that "found" carries the sense of knowing and also the sense of encountering. The use of "promise" rather than "threat" in this context also carries a mockery of them. ﴿Your Lord﴾, meaning the One who showed kindness to you, and you met His kindness with disbelief, of punishment, ﴿as truth﴾, because you have found that what your Lord threatened you with is true. ﴿They say: Yes﴾, meaning: indeed we have found all of that to be true. (p-405) Sibawayh said: "Na'am" is a promise, that is, in answer to "Will you give me such-and-such?", and an affirmation in the sense of "Such-and-such has indeed happened." [This verse is an instance of ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which two complementary elements are mentioned in each half and the counterpart of each is omitted from the other): He mentioned the second object first, as a sign that its counterpart is omitted in the second place, and He omitted it in the second place, as a sign that its counterpart is mentioned in the first place. And Allah knows best.]

When they had been granted blessings as described above, and among them was a good neighbour, and since life would not be wholesome with that except by removing the bad neighbour, they were informed of his removal, and their joy was increased by his humiliation, in His words: ﴿Then a caller will call out between them﴾, meaning because of what the people of the Fire had acknowledged against themselves, ﴿between them﴾, meaning between the two groups. ﴿That﴾ is the light form or the explanatory form in the recitation of Nafi', Abu 'Amr and 'Asim, while the rest read it with a doubled letter and put ﴿the curse of Allah﴾ in the accusative, meaning the expulsion and distancing of the Greatest King, in a manner of wrath, ﴿upon the wrongdoers﴾, meaning those who, despite the clear evidence, placed things in other than their proper places, like one who has never seen any light at all.

﴿Those who bar﴾, i.e., they have the act of barring (*al-sadd*) toward those who wish to believe, toward those who have believed, and toward others, through misguidance by means of enticement and intimidation, deceit and trickery. ﴿from the path of God﴾, i.e., the path of the religion of the King, who has no equal, the clear and broad path. ﴿and seek to make it crooked﴾, i.e., they seek to make it crooked for it by casting doubts and dubious arguments. What this involves has already been discussed in Surat Al 'Imran. ﴿and they are disbelievers in the Hereafter﴾, i.e., they conceal what has become evident to their intellects of its proofs. Thus, whenever these four attributes are found, the curse is justified.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 46:

﴿And between them⦁ that is, the condition of the two groups at this calling is that there is between them, or between the two abodes, ﴿a barrier⦁ that is, a wall, lest the people of the Garden find in their abode anything that disturbs its delight. ﴿And upon the heights⦁ plural of ʿurf (height), which is every elevated, raised thing, because it is more recognisable (aʿraf) than what is low; and these are the overlooking parts of that barrier ﴿are men⦁ whose good deeds and bad deeds are equal, so they are held back there until God decides concerning them, then He admits them to the Garden by the bounty of His mercy, as has been explained in the Musnad of Ibn Abi Khaythama from the hadith of Jabir (may Allah be pleased with him), from the Prophet (ﷺ). ﴿They will recognise each⦁ that is, the people of the Garden and the people of the Fire, before each of them enters its abode ﴿by their marks⦁ that is, their signs. ﴿And they will call out⦁ that is, the people of the heights ﴿to the companions of the Garden⦁ that is, after their entering it and settling in it ﴿Peace be upon you⦁ that is, safety and security from every harm.

Since this greeting might suggest that it came after the people of the heights had entered the Garden, it is as if it were said: was their calling after they had left the heights and entered it? It is answered: No.

﴿They had not entered it⦁ that is, the Garden, yet ﴿and they were hoping⦁ that is, while they were in the state of hoping to enter it. He expressed it with "hoping" because the servants have no means to God from themselves, even if they have deeds; how much more so for these who have no deeds.

When it was shown that those mentioned earlier are approaching Paradise and its people, he said, encouraging and warning: ﴿And when their eyes are turned﴾ (it is built in the passive voice because what frightens them is the turning itself, not who does it) ﴿toward﴾ (i.e., facing) ﴿the companions of the Fire﴾ (i.e., after they have settled in it, so they see what it contains of punishment), ﴿they say﴾ (i.e., the people of the Heights, while they have not entered it (p-407) and are fearful, seeking refuge from it), ﴿Our Lord﴾ (i.e., O You who have shown us every kind of kindness in this world and, in the Hereafter, by not having caused us to enter the Fire up to this time), ﴿do not place us with the wrongdoing people﴾ (by making us enter their place of entry).

When al-Biqa'i's discussion had earlier covered the speech of the people of Paradise to the people of Paradise with peace, he informed that they (the people of the Fire) would be addressed with rebuke and reproach. He said: ﴿And the companions of the heights shall call out﴾, and he made the agent explicit lest it be confused with the people of Paradise. Then he said ﴿to men﴾, meaning, the situation being that they turn their faces toward the people of the Fire, ﴿whom they recognize﴾, meaning, by their individual identities. As for their recognition in general, it was mentioned earlier. Here he said ﴿by their marks﴾ because the Fire had consumed them and altered their distinguishing features, along with their changes through fatness, blackness of faces, largeness of bodies and the like. ﴿They shall say﴾, either as a negation or as a question, in rebuke and censure: ﴿What did your gathering avail you﴾, meaning, of wealth and men? ﴿And what you used to be arrogant about﴾, meaning, you renewed by means of them this attribute and constantly established it in the world, claiming that no one could overcome you.

Then they increased their rebuke, reproach, grieving and regret, and their denunciation of them, by saying, pointing to people who used to belittle and despise them from among the people of Paradise: ﴿Are these the ones~﴾ and it is as if He uncovers them for them so that they see them, as an increase in their punishment, ﴿whom you swore~﴾ that is, in the world, ﴿that Allah would not grant them~﴾ that is, the One who possesses the attributes of perfection, ﴿mercy~﴾ so how then [would He grant it] with perfect mercy?

Since stating explicitly that they are to enter Paradise is a source of distress to the people of the Fire, for it negates what they swore to, [the Qur'an] says: ﴿Enter~﴾ that is, Allah says to them, or a speaker from His side says: Enter ﴿Paradise; no fear shall be upon you~﴾ that is, from anything whose harm can be anticipated, ﴿nor shall you grieve~﴾ that is, there will not recur for you a grief at any time over something that has passed, because of the good things you have, which cannot be described.

When the call of the people of the Garden was mentioned, in which they rejoice at entering it, in contrast to the people of the Fire, who suffer what grieves and brings tears, and when the passage concluded with this mercy, which makes the deprived hope for what delights and purifies, [Allah] informed that the people of the Fire call out to the people of the Garden when they experience distress from its entry, yet with something that should soften and make one weep. So He said what indicates that they possess all that was negated for the people of the Garden at the end of the preceding verse, namely fear and sorrow: ﴿And the companions of the Fire call out﴾, i.e., after their settling, ﴿to the companions of the Garden﴾, after He had made them known to them and commanded the Garden, so it was adorned. That was an increase in their torment. Then He explained what they called out for, saying: ﴿"Pour upon us some water"﴾, i.e., because you are higher than us, so if you pour it, it will reach us. This is due to the extreme affliction they are in, for between the Fire and the Garden there are abysses with no floor, and it is impossible for anything from either abode to reach the other.

Since pouring implies sending down, they said: ﴿"Or [give us] of what Allah has provided you"﴾, i.e., or send down to us something of what Allah has provided you, He to whom belongs absolute sufficiency, of whatever it is easy for you to send down. ﴿They will say﴾, i.e., the people of the Garden, ﴿"Indeed Allah has forbidden both"﴾, i.e., He has prevented them, through those abysses and other barriers, ﴿to the disbelievers﴾, i.e., those who conceal what sound reason and clear transmission have guided them to.

﴿Those who took﴾, that is, who burdened themselves with what their natural reason (al-'aql al-fitri) did not guide them to, when the legal reason (al-'aql al-shar'i) had alerted them, by taking ﴿their religion﴾ after they had destroyed its form and its reality, just as clay is destroyed when you make it into potsherds. Thus religion became ﴿amusement﴾, that is, occupation with what tends to distract and make one forget, and with every matter that pleases the soul and benefits nothing, without consideration of the outcome. So they were recompensed in kind for their deeds, in that no consideration was given to them for setting their outcome right.

When He had mentioned first what is more conducive to gathering around falsehood, which is the opposite of the surah's purpose of gathering around earnestness, and more conducive to heedlessness, and since it is among the nature of heedlessness of good that it drags one toward seeking pleasures and immersing oneself in desire, He confirmed this with His saying: ﴿and play﴾, that is, devotion to what brings joy and passes the present time with delusion. For this reason He followed it with His saying: ﴿and the life of this world deceived them﴾, that is, in doing that, ﴿the life of this world﴾, that is, with what it contains of passing accidents, such as hoping for long life, abundance of provision, and pleasant living, until by this they became veiled from looking at its meanings and from what He, exalted is He, called them to, namely turning away from it. So they did not reckon the reckoning of what lies beyond it.

And since their abandonment [of Him] was, by His mercy, glorified is He, eternal, He dropped the preposition, saying ﴿So today﴾, that is, as a consequence of that, on this day ﴿We will forget them﴾ (p-410), that is, We will leave them as one who is forgotten is left, ﴿as﴾ they did themselves, by ﴿forgetting﴾, that is, leaving behind, ﴿the meeting of this day of theirs﴾, so they did not prepare its provision for it. ﴿And as﴾, that is, and just as, ﴿they were﴾, that is, by natural disposition and temperament, ﴿with Our signs﴾, despite their great majesty by their being attributed to Us, ﴿deniers﴾, that is, they rejected them while they knew their reality, because it was in the utmost clarity.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 52:

When He mentioned their forgetting and their denial, He mentioned their state at that time, so He said: ﴿And indeed﴾, that is: they did that while the situation was that We—by Our might—﴿had brought them﴾, that is: in keeping with Our greatness, by sending Our Messenger to them from Us, ﴿a Book﴾ which is not at all a place for denial. Then He explained that in a context that encourages the one who accords with it and warns the one who opposes it, so He said: ﴿We have detailed it﴾, that is: We have made its meanings clear, leaving no ambiguity in them, and We made its verses into distinct sections, ﴿with knowledge﴾, that is: a great knowledge, so it came inimitable in its composition and its meaning, and in all its knowledge and its purpose; and it being ﴿a guidance﴾, that is: a clarification, ﴿and a mercy﴾, that is: a bestowal of honor. Then He specified those who benefit from it, because whoever does not benefit from a thing is, with respect to him, as if it were non-existent, so He said: ﴿for a people who believe﴾, that is: among whom there is the capacity for that. And in this there is a return to the description of the Book [which is one of the principal aims of the surah, in the most innovative manner and the finest style].

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 53:

When He had described the Book and mentioned those who benefit from it, the soul yearned to ask about the condition of those who do not believe in it, namely the deniers. So He said, indicating that their state, in their holding back from following it after knowing its truthfulness, owing to their inability to match it, is like that of one who awaits the fulfilment of its threat: ﴿Do they await anything but its fulfilment?﴾ That is, do they await anything but [its] fulfilment? But since they had no purpose in this beyond what the situation conveys, He stripped the verb [of any object], and to indicate that its coming is certain and exceedingly near, so that it is as if it were witnessed by them: ﴿except its fulfilment﴾, that is, the bringing of what it contains of promise and threat to its settling-place and the ends of its matter to which it informed that it would come.

Since it was as if it had been said: "What will their state be at that time?", He said: regret and submission where they will not benefit, and assent and belief when they will not be accepted. He expressed this by His saying: ﴿On the day its fulfilment comes﴾, that is, when the arrival of its threat reaches its full extent, in this world or in the Hereafter. When He placed the day first, out of concern for it, He followed it with its governing verb, saying: ﴿those who had forgotten it will say﴾, that is, they abandoned it as one abandons what is forgotten. It is also permissible that He counted that as forgetfulness, because it is fixed in human natures that every king must review his soldiers and call them to account; so when they turned away from this in what comes from the side of God, He counted it as forgetfulness on their part of what was fixed in their natures.

Since their forgetting was in some earlier time, He introduced the preposition, saying ﴿before﴾, that is, before the uncovering of the veil, confirming their assent: ﴿the messengers of our Lord had indeed come﴾, that is, in what preceded from the world, ﴿with the truth﴾, that is, conforming to this reality which we now see, of what they used to threaten us with. So they did not believe until they saw, and they did not place faith in the house of action, and therefore it did not benefit them.

Since they described Him, glorified is He, with goodness, because the situation disclosed of His forbearance and long patience, they made their saying a consequence of that: ﴿Have we then any intercessors?﴾, that is, on this day. It is as if they gathered the intercessors because they would be included among the people in the great intercession for the judgement to be decided. Then they made the confirmation of their being for them, specifically, a consequence of that, saying: ﴿that they may intercede for us﴾, that is, whether they are among our associates whom we used to imagine would benefit us, or others, so that He may forgive us the sins we committed; ﴿or are we to be sent back﴾, that is, if He does not forgive us, to the world, which is the house of action. The meaning is that there is no way for us to deliverance except by one of these two causes. Then they made their saying ﴿that we may do other than what we used to do﴾ a consequence of the answer to this second question, that is, in the world, ﴿other than what we used to do﴾, that is, by our natural dispositions without rational reflection.

Since it is known to whoever affirms the Qur'an and knows the placements of the reports within it that none of that will be theirs, its result was His saying: ﴿They have lost their souls﴾, that is, no one is more losing than they; ﴿and what they used to fabricate has gone astray from them﴾, that is, it vanished and became void, ﴿from them what they used to﴾, that is, by nature and disposition, which they cannot return from except at the sight of the calamity, ﴿invent﴾, that is, what they deliberately fabricated in the world of lies, in opposition to the messengers, through their claim that the idols would intercede for them, and other of their falsehoods.

The Qur'an's central concern is establishing the four foundational principles: tawhid (the oneness of God), prophethood, the Return (ma'ad), and knowledge (al-'ilm). The discourse is extensive in reporting God's commands, prohibitions, and actions toward His friends and enemies, which demonstrate His complete power and knowledge. It concludes that their associates cannot avail them. He explains this by stating that He alone is the Lord, in a context that points to the Oneness, which is the greatest purpose of the surah and is sufficient to manifest the proofs for it. It also points to the second purpose, the Return, whose circumstances He has finished establishing through the origination, which is established in the intellects as being harder than the return, with arguments that are elaborate and display complete power and knowledge. So He said: ﴿Indeed, your Lord﴾, meaning the One who benefits you by bringing you into existence from non-existence and arranging your interests, is ﴿Allah﴾, meaning the King who has no equal, alone, not an idol or anything else. Then He described Him with that which establishes this, saying: ﴿who created the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning in their vastness and greatness.

Since the disbelievers might have said: "Why does He not hasten the coming of what you promise, if He is capable and you are right in your message?", He clarified that His custom is deliberation, even though His command and His seizing are like a glance of the eye when He wills it. So He said: ﴿in six days﴾, meaning in the measure of them. Since the management of this creation is a dazzling matter that the intellects cannot contain, and for this reason the Quraysh used to say: "How can one God encompass creation?", He pointed to (p-414) His greatness and the loftiness of His rank with the particle of distance (adat al-bu'd, the demonstrative particle indicating remoteness), and said: ﴿Then He established Himself upon the Throne﴾, meaning He undertook the management of what He had brought into existence and created, a thorough, exhaustive undertaking, independent in it, because this is the manner of one who possesses a kingdom and takes up its administration, and to show that there is no contender with Him in any part of it. And so that the address to people is in terms of what they are accustomed to from their kings, so that His greatness, glory be to Him, becomes fixed in their minds, and the negation of comparison with Him is embedded in their original natures. It is said: "So-and-so sat upon the throne of kingship", even if there is no throne and no sitting. And as is said in the opposite sense: "So-and-so's throne was shattered", meaning his glory has gone, his kingdom has collapsed, and his affair has become corrupt. So this is a figurative expression (kinaya, metonymy) in which one does not look to applying the structure and the words to their apparent meanings, like their saying of a tall man: "long of sword-belt", and of a generous man: "great of ashes".

Since He, glory be to Him, is not preoccupied by one affair from another, He began with the management that is a sign of this, through witnessing it in the covering of the earth with its darkness at one instant. So He said, indicating the perfection of His power, which is meant by the establishing, with a matter witnessed every day, despite the abundance of its benefits by which He, glory be to Him, arranged the order of this existence: ﴿He covers﴾, meaning the state of His establishing is that He covers ﴿the night the day﴾. Abu Hayyan said: Humayd ibn Qays recited: "yaghshā al-laylu" (the night covers), with a fatha on the ya, sukun on the ghayn, fatha on the shin, and damma on the lam. This is what Abu 'Amr al-Dani reported from him. Abu al-Fath ibn Jinni said, on the authority of Humayd, with the accusative on "the night" and the nominative on (p-415) "the day". Ibn 'Atiyya said: "Abu al-Fath is more reliable." But what he said, that Abu al-Fath is more reliable, is an assertion that is not correct. For Abu 'Amr al-Dani's rank in recitation, his knowledge of it, his precision in its transmissions, and his distinction in this, is at a level that none of the imams of recitation approaches, let alone the grammarians, who are not reciters, nor did they transmit recitation from anyone, nor did anyone transmit recitation from them. This is in addition to his exceptional piety, his firmness in transmission, his avoidance of audacity, and his abundant share of Arabic. I have seen his book on "kallā" and his book on the idgham (assimilation) of Abu 'Amr al-Kabir, which demonstrate his mastery of what the imams of the grammarians and reciters barely attain, not to mention his other works. What Abu 'Amr al-Dani transmitted from Humayd is more probable in meaning, because that agrees with the recitation of the majority, since "al-layl" (the night), in their recitation, though it is in the accusative, is the subject in terms of meaning, as the hamzat al-naql (causative hamza) or the doubling made it an object. It cannot be a second object in terms of meaning, because the two accusatives that the verb transitively governs, one of them is the subject in terms of meaning, so the first of them necessarily is as it is necessary in "I made Zayd own 'Amr", since the order of precedence is what clarifies that it is the subject in terms of meaning, just as it is necessary in "Musa struck 'Isa". End of quotation. (p-416) When He, glory be to Him, informed that the night covers the day, this indicates that the day is likewise, through His saying, clarifying the state of the night: ﴿seeking it﴾, meaning the night draws on and always seeks the day, a seeking ﴿swiftly﴾, meaning very quickly, to cover the night. This is because a thing is not sought except after its existence, and when the day exists it covers the night, since they are opposites, the existence of one erasing the existence of the other. He, glory be to Him, began with mention of the night because its covering is the first occurrence after the completion of creation. Their movement is through the movement of the Throne, and therefore He linked them to it. It is the most rapid of movements and the most perfect in intensity. The sun has two kinds of motion: one according to its own essence, completed by traversing all the degrees of the whole sphere, from which the year results; and the second according to the motion of the Greatest Sphere, completed in a day and its night. The night and the day only come about through the motion of the outermost heaven, which is called the Throne, not through the motion of the two luminaries. Ibn Jinni permitted that "yatlubuhu" (seeking it) be a circumstantial clause (hal) describing the day in the recitation of the majority, even though it is an object, meaning the day is in the state of seeking the night swiftly in order to cover it. And that it be a circumstantial clause describing both together, because each of them seeks the other. By this, what he said about the recitation of Humayd is also harmonized, since each of them is covering the other. He said in his book, al-Muhtasab fi al-Qira'at al-Shawadhdh (The Reckoned: On the Irregular Readings): The correctness of both readings, and the meeting of their two meanings (p-417), is that the night and the day succeed each other, and each of them, though it removes its companion, its companion also removes it. Each of them, on this view, is a subject though it is an object, and an object though it is a subject. Moreover, what is apparent in the urging here is the day, since by its unveiling and its rising it has a more evident effect in urging than the night.

When He mentioned the two alternating phenomena, He followed each with its sign, saying: ﴿and the sun and the moon and the stars﴾, meaning He created them, or each category of them covers what is the sign of the other, the whole being ﴿subjected﴾, meaning for travelling and other purposes, ﴿by His command﴾, which is His will and His word. The angels guide them, as it is reported that God has angels who drive the sun and the moon.

Since it is established that everything we see of essences is His creation, and what we know of meanings is His command, He concluded with certainty His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, to Him belongs﴾, meaning to Him alone, and He placed the caused before the cause in ascending order, as the ruling requires, from the perceptible to the intelligible, saying: ﴿the creation﴾, which is what came about from origination through causation, growth, and development. Al-Razi said: Whatever is a body or corporeal is specified by a determinate measure, and so it is of the world of creation. So the world of creation is by His subjecting it, and the world of command is by His managing it, and the domination of the spiritual over the corporeal is by His determining. ﴿and the command﴾, which is what came about from that as bringing out of non-existence without causation, like the spirit, and what was preservation and management by speech (p-418), like religions and everything that involves the sustaining (qayyumiyya). Al-Razi also said: Whatever is free of volume and measure is of the world of command, and he counted the angels among the world of command. So this concluded with certainty His saying, as a praise beyond which necks are cut short and below whose height the peaks of the horizons fall short: ﴿Blessed be﴾, meaning He is established in a permanence which is, in truth, the permanence of none other, together with blessing, abundance of excellent effects, and noble results. ﴿Allah﴾, meaning the Possessor of majesty and honour.

Since He indicated that He deserves this praise for His essence, He indicated that He deserves it for His attributes, saying: ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, meaning the originator of all that, and its nurturer in creation and in directing it by His command. In the sixth part of (Fawa'id al-Mukhallis) it is related from Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna that he said: "What does this little creature say, meaning Bishr al-Marisi?" They said: "O Abu Muhammad! He claims that the Qur'an is created." He said: "He lied. God, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Unquestionably, to Him belongs the creation and the command﴾. So the creation is God's creation, and the command is the Qur'an." End of quotation. This interpretation, of what the verse may bear, is that the command is what is meant by His saying: ﴿by His command﴾, which is the will and the word, together with the possibility of what I have already put forward.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 55:

When He (exalted is He) mentioned His sole possession of creation and command, which necessitates His sole right to worship, in order to direct attention toward acquiring the inner knowledge (al-ma'arif al-nafsaniyyah) and the true sciences (al-ulum al-haqiqiyyah), He commanded according to this requirement, which is fitting for those cognitions, namely supplication (al-du'a'), which is the marrow (mukh) of worship. So He said: ﴿Call upon your Lord﴾, meaning the One who is constantly beneficent to you, calling upon Him in worship and submission, ﴿humbly and secretly﴾. "Humbly" means with outward humility (tadhallul zahir), and "secretly" means with inward humility (tadhallul batin). He praised His servant Zakariyya, peace be upon him, saying: ﴿When he called upon his Lord with a secret call﴾ [Maryam: 3]. That is, combine the humility of the outward with the humility of the inward. That is, make worship sincerely for Him. ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾ because His being called upon alone is what is fitting to the station of the might of lordship, and humbling oneself in this manner is what is fitting to the station of the humility of servanthood. This is the purpose of supplication, not changing the eternal knowledge, and it is the purpose of all acts of worship. For the servant does not supplicate except having brought to mind from himself humility, weakness and need, and from his Lord knowledge, power and sufficiency. This is the purpose of all acts of worship; therefore supplication was the marrow of worship. This statement, despite its brevity, has gathered every condition of supplication that is intended to be realized and attained, to the extent that nothing can be added to it. Whoever does the opposite has exceeded the limit. To this He alluded by His causal clause: ﴿Indeed, He does not love the transgressors﴾, meaning those who exceed what they were commanded in supplication and other matters. They said: the meaning is that whoever abandons this, Allah does not love him, that is, He does not reward him at all nor shows him kindness. The verse is of the type of ihtibak (concealment by mutual implication): its last part indicates the omission of its opposite from its first part, and its first part indicates that something was omitted before the last part: "And do not abandon sincerity, [lest] you be transgressors."

Since this was part of fulfilling the rights of Lordship and carrying out the rights of servanthood, which necessitates righteousness, He commanded its continuance by forbidding its opposite in His saying: ﴿And do not cause corruption﴾, i.e., do not commit corruption, ﴿in the earth﴾, i.e., through polytheism and wrongdoing. This is a prohibition against (p-420) bringing the essence of corruption into existence, and that requires the prohibition of all its types, so it encompasses the five universals upon which the religious communities agree: religion, life (bodies), intellect, lineage, and property. ﴿After its reformation﴾. The apparent meaning is that the idiom (iḍāfa) carries the sense of "to" (lām), and it is an iḍāfa of the object, i.e., do not defile it with corruption after He has reformed it for you in creation, by what He placed in it of benefits, indicated by His saying ﴿He covers the night with the day﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], which points to His oneness and calls to the truth, establishing the bodies; and He commanded, through the tongues of His messengers, what He sent down of His books, peace be upon them, establishing the religions. Thus He combined with the first origination the first preservation.

Since that might have implied restricting oneself, through perfect humility, to the station of fear alone, He negated that with His saying ﴿And call upon Him in fear﴾, i.e., of His justice. And since servants have no means of their own to reach Him — glory be to Him — He expressed it with hope, saying ﴿and in hope﴾, i.e., of His grace. For whoever combines fear and hope is in the station of ihsan, as if he were witnessing the All-Merciful: whenever the driver of majesty whips him with the lashes of His might, the caller of beauty summons him to the carpet of His compassion. And whoever attains the station of ihsan is fit for mercy. ﴿Indeed, the mercy of Allah﴾, i.e., the honoring of the Lord of Majesty and Generosity for whoever calls upon Him in this manner. He emphasized it by using the masculine form because it is attributed to a non-feminine noun, as Sibawayh said, and so He said ﴿near﴾, though the original would have been "near to you" ("minkum"); but He made it apparent in order to generalize and to attach the judgment to the attribute, so He said ﴿to the doers of good﴾.

(p-421) Since the lasting of goodness cannot occur except through rain, which is among the greatest kinds of mercy, and rain cannot occur except through clouds, and clouds cannot occur except through wind, God the Exalted said, conjoining it to ﴿Indeed, your Lord is God﴾ [al-A'raf: 54] as a reminder, after establishing the origin, of the establishment of the return: ﴿And He is the One who sends the winds﴾, that is, not other than Him, ﴿by way of glad tidings﴾, that is, by moving them. This is the reading of the majority. Its kinds are five: the south wind, the north wind, the east wind (ṣabā), the west wind (dabūr), and the nakbā, which is every wind that veers aside and falls between two winds. Ibn Kathir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it in the singular, intending the genus. ﴿Bushran﴾ with two dammas in the reading of the people of the Hijaz and Basra, meaning: spreading out, the plural of nushūr from al-nashr, which is the unfolding of what was folded. [Its scattering in every direction is not due to the wind's own essence, for otherwise that would persist from it, nor to the power of a celestial sphere or a star, because their relation to the air is one and the same.] ﴿Before His mercy﴾, that is, before ﴿His mercy﴾, that is, the rain. Perhaps He expressed it with the two hands, the right and the left, because this indicates, along with its grandeur, that it is sometimes mercy and sometimes punishment, as it was for the people of Noah, peace be upon him, though mercy in it predominates, and it is the right hand. Sometimes the winds gather the clouds to preserve the water; sometimes they scatter them, nullifying them; sometimes they are the fertilizing winds (al-lawāqiḥ) that establish the crops and trees and complete them; sometimes they make them grow or destroy them, as happens in autumn; and sometimes they are pleasant and sometimes destructive, either through extreme heat or extreme cold. Then He made the sending conditional with His saying: ﴿Until, when they carry a heavy cloud﴾, that is, they carry it (p-422) because of its lightness for them, being little in relation to them, ﴿heavy﴾, that is, with water. Since He indicated greatness through the plural and affirmed the matter through the description, He made the word singular to indicate the utmost greatness by driving it gathered together as if it were one piece, no part of it separating from the rest, for if it separated, its affair would be disordered. So He said: ﴿We drive it to a dead land﴾, that is, for its sake and toward it, ﴿dead﴾, that is, through the absence of vegetation. ﴿Then We cause to descend﴾, that is, by what We possess of greatness, ﴿therewith﴾, that is, the land, or by means of that cloud, ﴿water﴾, that is, this genus. He indicated the greatness of producing growth with the plural "We," and so He said: ﴿Then We bring forth therewith﴾, that is, through the water, ﴿from every kind of fruit﴾, that is, the literal fruits on trees and, figuratively, from plants and their grains. Since this, together with what it contains of reminding of the blessing which calls for His unity through worship, is a second proof most clearly indicating the power to resurrect, God the Exalted said: ﴿Thus﴾, that is, just as We brought forth this vegetation from the earth after it had not been, ﴿We bring forth the dead﴾, that is, from the earth after they have become dust, ﴿that perhaps you may remember﴾, that is, We have said this so that your state may be the state of one for whom it is hoped that he will remember this visible, near-at-hand sign, even at the least degree of remembrance, as indicated by the idghām; for He, glorified is He, just as He is able to restore vegetation by gathering water for it from within the earth after it had been hidden in the earth and become dust, and revived the tree after it had no spirit by depositing the fruit which is its spirit, is able (p-423) to restore bodies and deposit spirits in them as they were the first time; for there is no difference between the two bringings-forth.

The death is of two kinds, sensory (physical) and spiritual (ma'nawi), as indicated in Surat al-An'am in the verses: ﴿Only those who listen respond; as for the dead, Allah will raise them﴾ [al-An'am: 36] and ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life﴾ [al-An'am: 122]. It is as if it were said: there is no difference in this matter with Us between the dead of faith and the dead of bodies. Just as We have differentiated among the substances of the lands by creating some of them good and some of them bad, so too have We differentiated among the elements of human beings by making some of them pure and some of them impure. The one of noble origin finds faith easy, while the one of corrupt origin finds submission difficult, and his steadfastness and certainty are far off. ﴿And the good land﴾, i.e., the one whose soil is good, so that it is noble and fertile, ﴿its vegetation comes forth﴾, i.e., when water descends upon it, it yields abundant, good, easy and plentiful growth ﴿by the permission of﴾, i.e., by the enabling of, ﴿its Lord﴾, i.e., the One who nurtures it through what He has prepared for it. [And the land that is good in general but has not reached its full end brings forth growth less than that; and the bad land brings forth no growth at all, by the withholding of its Lord from it.] ﴿And that which is bad﴾, i.e., that in whose constitution corruption has come to be, by its land being salty or similar to that which Allah Most High does not prepare for growth, ﴿comes not forth﴾, i.e., its vegetation, ﴿except﴾, i.e., in a state of being ﴿meager﴾, i.e., little and weak in benefit. This is [an indication], together with the fact that this is only as described, while the lands are equal in origin and the waters are equal and their relation to the spheres and stars is the same, except by the Chooser who acts freely, like His striking, glorified is He, the believer and the disbeliever upon their hearing the Reminder from the Book and the Sunnah. [This verse is of al-Ihtibak.]

When these verses reached the summit of wondrous indications, the hearer was inclined to say: does all of these verses clarify this explanation? So it was said: ﴿Thus﴾, i.e., yes, in such a manner of variation, namely repetition with difference of modes, for the differing of indications and their display in the moulds of superior words and pleasing meanings, in inimitable compositions, in ways that scarcely can be counted: ﴿We vary the signs﴾, i.e., all of them. When this was completed in this strange method and wondrous pattern, reminding of blessings in a style indicating uniqueness and perfect power, it was most fitting to end it with His saying, specifying by them those who benefit, since they, in relation to others, are as if they had not been created: ﴿for a people who give thanks﴾, i.e., in whom gratitude for blessings is found in a continuous manner, so they do not associate partners, but benefit from what He has bestowed upon them, worshipping Him alone with it, and they reflect with their intellects that He has empowered them with His blessings to do what they are incapable of, so they are not deprived of any part of His power over resurrection or anything else. For they claim to be people of noble morals, among which is that the recompense of goodness is nothing but goodness.

[p. 425] When His threat, glory be to Him, was prolonged against those who persisted in corruption and did not turn back from their error and obstinacy, despite the fate of the earlier peoples and the destruction of those who passed away, and when He had varied in these verses the excellent indications of Tawhid (Divine Oneness) and the Return (ma'ad) through manifest proofs, overwhelming clear signs, decisive arguments, and shining evidences, He, glory be to Him, brought those stories as a sensory proof that among people there are both the wicked and the good. Together with this, there is a guarantee of the indication of His perfect power, and of His jealousy regarding association with Him in that presence. He detailed the conditions of those whose destruction was previously alluded to, explained their downfall, and showed that their strength and their numbers did not avail them anything at all, through His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How many a town have We destroyed﴾ [al-A'raf: 4] and His saying: ﴿So when their term comes, they cannot delay it by an hour﴾ [al-A'raf: 34], and the verse. This is a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) and a strengthening of his righteous followers, by alerting them that turning away from the signs is not a peculiarity of this Ummah but the custom of the earlier nations, and that blessings are specific to the grateful, which is why punishments are confined to the disbelievers. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿We certainly sent﴾, i.e., by Our greatness. He opened it with the particle of anticipation (harf al-tawaqqu', i.e., la-qad, "indeed") because of the eager expectation that the perceptive listener has toward mention of what has been repeatedly alluded to. Also, the lam that introduces the implied oath (al-qasam al-mahdhuf) is generally not uttered except accompanied by (qad), because the oath clause is only brought as emphasis for the clause sworn to, which is its answer. Thus it was a place of the meaning of anticipation, which is the meaning of (qad), upon the addressee's hearing the word of the oath. ﴿Noah﴾, meaning: the son of Lamak ibn [p. 426] Mattushalakh ibn Akhnukh, who is Idris, peace be upon him. At the time of his sending he was fifty years old.

Since his sending (ﷺ) preceded the tribes with their differing languages, He said: ﴿to his people﴾, i.e., those who were filling the earth, as in the hadith of intercession in the Two Sahihs and others, from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him: "Go to Noah, the first prophet Allah sent to the people of the earth." Among them was a strength for accomplishing what they willed, which is not hidden from one who reflects on their remains and knows their histories. If those remains are theirs, then the purpose has been achieved; and if they belong to those who came after them, it is known, by the rule of inductive reasoning (qiyas al-istiqra'), that they were stronger than these and higher than them. Since this is brought as proof of what was mentioned, it came without conjunctions. Along with all of this, it alerts that all the Messengers agree in calling to what a proof has indicated, ﴿Indeed your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 54], of Tawhid and righteousness, and beyond that from the seas of proofs and arguments whose waves crash together. And Allah is the guide to the path of right guidance. That Noah, peace be upon him, was a messenger to all the people of the earth, because they were his people through the unity of their tongue, does not conflict with the specification of our Prophet (ﷺ) with the universality of the message, because the meaning of universality is that he was sent to all the nations differing by the diversity of tongues, and to all who are alive among humans, jinn, and angels. Further explanation of this will come, Allah willing, in Surat al-Saffat.

Since among the great purposes is the announcement that what this Messenger called to has not ceased to be called to by all the Messengers, may the best prayers, peace, greetings, and honor be upon them all, and since Noah was the first messenger whose message is mentioned right after the mention of his sending, with the description of what he was sent with, by the particle fa (then), through His saying: ﴿So he said, "O my people"﴾, i.e., he endeared himself to them through this address, ﴿Worship Allah﴾, i.e., the One to whom belongs all greatness of creation and command, for He is deserving of that, and He has obligated His servants to it.

Since the aim is to single Him out for this, he justified it by His saying, emphasizing it by affirming the prepositional phrase: ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾, and he went to the extreme in negation, saying: ﴿other than Him﴾. Then he said, giving a reason or as a new statement, warning and emphasizing because of their denial: ﴿Indeed I fear for you﴾ in this world and the Hereafter. Perhaps he said here: ﴿the punishment of a great day﴾, and in (Hud): ﴿painful﴾ [Hud: 26], and in (al-Mu'minun) he said: ﴿Will you not fear Allah?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 23]. This is because the arrangement of the three surahs, although the correct view is that it was by the ijtihad of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, perhaps came in accordance with their order of revelation, since they are Meccan; and in accordance with the order of Noah's speech to them, peace be upon him. He first softened his speech to them, in that he gave the impression that the greatness described by "the day" was not because of the punishment but for another matter, so the punishment became absolute, encompassing any punishment whatsoever, even if small. When their denial persisted, he explained to them that its greatness was only due to the painful punishment that befalls in it. When they persisted in their rebellion, he said to them the words of one capable who threatens when his command is opposed: (p. 428) "Will you not do what I tell you?
