Whenever you oppose after this, I will hasten punishment upon you, and you know My power."

The passage is translated below.

When this was complete, and the situation called for them to respond with assent, in light of the clear proofs of God's oneness that had been set forth, it was as if it were said: "So what was their response?" He said: ﴿The chiefs (al-mala') said﴾, i.e., the nobles whose appearance fills the eyes with greatness, and toward whom eyes turn in assemblies. He did not describe them in this surah as disbelievers, because that is more effective in consolation; for it is the first surah in which he narrates something like this in the ordering of the Book, and because those who believed in him, unqualified, were in extreme minority compared with those who did not believe, so how much more so when they are qualified by nobility! He emphasized their blame as consolation for this noble Prophet by informing (of their closeness to him in lineage) through His saying: ﴿from among his people﴾; and they met his gentleness and courtesy with harshness, emphasizing the slander contained in what they said, because their own state contradicts them. So they said: ﴿Indeed, we see you﴾, i.e., each one of us holds a conviction which, in its certainty, is like sight, that you are ﴿in error﴾, i.e., in mistake and departure from the right course. The word "in" is a adverbial complement (zarf) for "you," encompassing you, ﴿evident﴾, i.e., manifest in itself, to the point that it seems to be evident to others.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 61:

When they accused him of "error" qualified by clarity, he negated absolute error, which is the more general category, and by negating it, all its specific forms are negated. Rather, he negated even the least amount of error. So Allah, the Exalted, said, reporting about him: ﴿He said: "O my people, there is no error in me"﴾, renewing his appeal to them. He negated an indefinite unit, and this is not true unless every individual instance is negated; thus it is more explicit than negating the verbal noun (al-masdar) itself. He did not describe the chiefs of his people here as "those who disbelieved," but he described them with that in Surah Hud. This is either because that description is one of blame not intended as a restriction, so the meaning is not disturbed by affirming it or negating it; or because they answered him with that twice: once before any of their nobles had become Muslim, and the second time after some of them had become Muslim.

When he had negated what they had charged him with in this eloquent manner, he affirmed for himself its opposite, in the most noble of the attributes of created beings. So he said, as a corrective after negating error, affirming the necessary consequence of its opposite: ﴿But I am a Messenger﴾, that is, to you, conveying what I have been commanded, so I am upon the most upright path ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾, that is, the One who is good to them by sending messengers to guide them, rescuing them from error. Thus he returned the matter to them with the most gentle allusion.

Then he resumed reporting his function, explaining his mission, and said: ﴿I convey to you﴾. It seems that the doors of their disbelief were many, so he gathered them together, either by considering them, or by considering the multiplicity of his miracles, or the multiplicity of the occasions of revelation over extended times and different meanings. Or it may be that he gathered together for him what those before him were sent with, such as Idris, his grandfather, whose scrolls were thirty, and Shith (Seth), whose scrolls were fifty, peace be upon them both. So he said: ﴿the messages of my Lord﴾, that is, of the One who has been good to me, of the commands and prohibitions and all kinds of obligations, concerning the affairs of the Hereafter and other matters, I add nothing to them and take nothing away from them, as is the way of every obedient messenger.

Since misguidance is among the attributes of action, he was content with the verbal sentence, which indicates occurrence, in his saying: ﴿and I give you sincere advice﴾. He restricted the act and indicated the specification of sincere advice to them and made it pure for them, so he said: ﴿for you﴾. Naṣīḥah (sincere counsel) is guiding to what is beneficial together with the purity of intention from any admixture of harm. Since misguidance stems from ignorance, he said: ﴿and I know from Allah﴾, that is, of the attributes of the One who possesses the attributes of perfection and all His affairs, ﴿what you do not know﴾, that is, of His great seizing of those who disobey Him and other matters which you have no capacity to know without my being sent. So take it from me and you will become scholars, and do not leave it, by attributing it to me as misguidance, lest you increase in misguidance.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 63:

Since what moved them to this was merely their astonishment that he (Noah) should be singled out from among them for a distinction, though he was one of them, as will come in another surah, He (God) denied this of them by saying: ﴿Do you wonder?﴾ That is: do you deny and marvel? ﴿that there has come to you﴾ — here (jā'a, "came") is made to imply the sense of (anzala, "sent down"), which is why its complement is introduced with (ʿalā, "upon"); so He says: ﴿a reminder﴾, that is, a message, ﴿from your Lord﴾, that is, the One who bestows favour upon you by bringing you into existence and nurturing you, ﴿sent down upon a man﴾, that is, one perfect in manhood, who is moreover of such a character that you cannot accuse him, for he is ﴿from among you﴾, in answer to your saying: ﴿We never heard of this among our fathers of old﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 24], that is, the sending of a human messenger, ﴿so that he may warn you﴾, so that you may beware of what he warns you of, ﴿and that you may be wary﴾, that is, that you may place between yourselves and what you fear a shield, ﴿so that perhaps you will be shown mercy﴾, that is, so that your state when you meet God may be that of one who hopes for His mercy, by His elevating him in both abodes.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 64:

When they first attributed to him error (ḍalāl), which may be a mistake arising from heedlessness and the like, and he established for them the proof that he was upon the truth, he informed them that nothing resulted from that except their explicit declaration of the denial which they had earlier only hinted at with the charge of error. So He said: ﴿So they denied him﴾, that is, the chiefs (al-Mala') and those who followed them from among their inferiors. Since their denial resulted in God's confirmation of what they had said by destroying them and saving him and those who believed with him, He said, placing the saving first out of concern for it: ﴿So We saved him﴾ by Our might, from all the people of the earth and from Our punishment with which We seized them, ﴿and those with him﴾, that is, by companionship in religious deeds, ﴿in the ark﴾, which is the ship that God graciously bestowed upon people by teaching them its construction, so that it would protect him from the flood, and it became a sign and a great benefit for those who came after them. ﴿And We drowned﴾, that is, by the flood, which is the water that covered the surface of the earth, leaving no place in it until it encompassed everything. The place of the pronoun was replaced by an explicit noun, linking the act to the description, to indicate that whoever does something to a messenger has done it to the one who sent him, and so He will repay him with what he deserves. So He said: ﴿those who denied Our signs﴾, that is, and they are so manifest that there is no concealment in them, given their greatness in relation to Us. The verb of salvation (najāh) is transitivized here with the hamza, which is the original form of transitivity, and it is joined with "alladhīna" because it is the most exclusive and clearest of the relative pronouns.

When the story was repeated in Surah Yunus, peace be upon him, the more fitting approach to the speech of eloquent speakers and more in keeping with the methods of the eloquent was variation in expression. So the doubling (ta'diyah by tadʿīf) was transitivized, along with what it contains of greater eloquence by conveying increased care, in harmony with the greater delegation mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿So decide your affair and your partners﴾ [Yunus: 71]. He used "min" to join branch to branch, since "min" is shared between connection and condition, and it is also sometimes applied to what does not reason, which suited that context. There it was added in describing the saved: ﴿and We made them successors﴾ [Yunus: 73], in view of His words at the beginning of the surah: ﴿And We destroyed the generations before you when they wronged﴾ [Yunus: 13], then He said: ﴿Then We made you successors in the land after them, that We might see how you would act﴾ [Yunus: 14]. Thus He hinted to them of destruction if they wronged, then He indicated to them, in the story of Nuh, peace be upon him, that He had made known to them that the successors are the saved whose mention and descendants remain, and that He graciously bestowed upon them the grace of responding to faith and showed them mercy through this noble Prophet, upon whom be the best prayers and peace, so He decreed that they would not be destroyed.

When the story was opened with their attribution to him of error falsely, which arises from blindness of insight or of sight, it was fitting that the matter be reversed upon them in the manner of truth. So He said, emphasizing their denial of that: ﴿Indeed they were﴾, that is, by what I created in them of crookedness, ﴿a blind people﴾, that is, stamped with blindness of heart, along with their strength in what they attempt, which is established for them, by what the verb indicates without saying "a doer." The story in Yunus was concluded with His words: ﴿Then see how was the end of those warned﴾ [Yunus: 73], corresponding to His words at its beginning: ﴿If my standing and my reminding are grievous to you﴾ [Yunus: 71], that is, my warning, for He knows that it was grievous to them; had it been good tidings, it would not have been hard upon them.

When Ad came after them, and there was nothing here requiring a disruption of the order, he followed them with them, placing the recipient of the message first so that it would convey that his mission was restricted to them, and they are a part of the people of the earth. So He said: ﴿And to ʿĀd﴾ [We sent] specifically, ﴿their brother﴾, i.e., by lineage, because they would understand him better than others and would know his state of trustworthiness and honesty better. When He joined him to Noah, peace be upon both of them, after mentioning the people to whom he was sent, He clarified him with His saying: ﴿Hūd﴾. This differs from the people of Noah, for they were all the people of the earth, because the tribes had not yet dispersed the people, nor the languages, since the language of all was one. The languages were not divided until after the ṣarḥ (the tower). For this reason the flood covered all the people of the earth. Therefore the meaning of his story at that point does not differ in order, neither in advancing nor in delaying, so it was appropriate to place the message or the messenger first, because it is more important.

Since the story of Noah, peace be upon him, was the first of the stories of the prophets with their peoples, and the Arabs had no prior acquaintance with the neighbors of the prophets and those sent to them, He used in it the original form (arsalnāhu) [in the sense of "We sent him"]. He spoke in one continuous context, addressing one whose mind is free of every part of its details. The story of Hūd, peace be upon him, came after the hearers had knowledge of the story of Noah, peace be upon him, of what occurred in his conveying the message to them and their rejection of him. So when He mentioned his being sent, the listener became eager to know whether he said to them what Noah had said, and whether they responded to him as his people had responded, or whether the matter was different from that? So the question of the one eager to know was answered by His saying: ﴿He said﴾, like the saying of Noah, peace be upon him, exactly, ﴿O my people﴾, reminding them that he is one of them, that what concerns them concerns him, ﴿Worship Allah﴾, i.e., because He alone deserves that for His own essence. Then He gave the reason, or resumed, with His saying: ﴿You have no﴾ and He went to the extreme in negation, so He said: ﴿god other than Him﴾. Since they were aware of what befell the people of Noah, He said: ﴿Will you not then be wary?﴾, i.e., will you not place between yourselves and the punishment of this one mighty tyrant a protection?

When the listener was eager to hear their reply, after this exhortation mixed with warning, the answer came with His words: ﴿The chiefs said﴾. That is, the nobles, who fill the eyes with splendour and the hearts with awe. Since 'Ad were few compared with the people of Noah, peace be upon him, and some of their nobles had accepted Islam and had a measure of wealth, the verse restricts them with His words: ﴿who disbelieved﴾. That is, who concealed what ought to be manifest of the proofs of God's oneness. They are described in this way to console this noble Prophet regarding the harshness he sees from his people, since the same had happened to his fellow prophets, by His words: ﴿from among his people﴾. They reinforced the harshness they showed him, because they knew that his state, in his knowledge and judgment, refutes them. Their words were: ﴿Indeed, we see you﴾. That is, we know you with certain knowledge, (p-435) so much so that it is as though it were perceived by the senses, ﴿in folly﴾ (سفاهة). That is, enclosed by lightness of intellect, so that it surrounds you from all sides, with no escape for you from it, and therefore it has led you to a claim that has no reality. The tanwin (nunation) here is for magnification. If it is said that it is for belittlement, then it is as though they hesitated to describe him with this, just as they hesitated to assert outright that he was lying. So they said: ﴿And indeed, we think you are among the liars﴾. That is, among those who deliberately lie. This is because they had knowledge from the messengers and of the punishment that comes upon those who oppose them, from the story of Noah, peace be upon him, and the time had not been long. As for the people of Noah, they asserted error with certainty and reinforced it by describing him as ﴿manifest﴾, because they had no awareness of the circumstances of the messengers and the punishment of nations before that. For this reason they said: ﴿We have not heard of this among our earliest fathers﴾ (23:24). It is said: it is not so, for something similar appears in the reply of the people of Noah in Surah Hud: ﴿Rather, we think you are liars﴾ (11:27). If it is said: this occurred only in the later stage, after he had set forth for them the proofs and established the demonstrations for the soundness of his claim, and personal interests were stirred up by dispute, it is unlikely that his people answered him with this at the very first time he called them. It is said: the matter is the same in the story of Hud, peace be upon him, for none said this to him except the disbelievers among his people. Their being qualified by this description indicates that among them were those who followed him, and indeed that his followers were among their nobles, by conjecture. The expression "among the liars" is used because they intended that, in describing him with the folly they alleged, it suffices that he went ahead with what makes their assumption of his lying plausible. Or their words, "not the truth" in their view, may be understood as being undecided between his having said it deliberately, or having been moved to it by the folly they charged him with, without reflection.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 67:

When they met his gentleness toward them and his compassion for them with this harshness, he turned away from that and dealt with them, with forbearance, by its opposite, in response to what they called him. So he ﴿said﴾, teaching good manners in addressing foolish people, ﴿"O my people"﴾, reminding them of the kinship between them, which calls for affection, sincere counsel, tenderness and gentle treatment. ﴿"There is no foolishness in me"﴾. So he denied that there was in him any trace of lightness of forbearance. He avoided saying that he was lying, because what prompts a person to lie is lightness and recklessness, so he had no need to single it out for denial.

When he denied foolishness, he affirmed what necessarily follows from it, its opposite, by his saying: ﴿"But I am a messenger"﴾. He specified the one who sent him, to magnify the matter, by his saying ﴿"from the Lord of the worlds"﴾, meaning: the One who does good to them after the blessing of their creation and their provisions, by sending messengers to them so that they may gain for them the lofty qualities of character through which the blessing of continuance is orderly maintained.

﴿I convey to you﴾, and he used the plural form of "message" (*risalah*), as he did in the story of Noah, peace be upon him, when he said ﴿the messages of my Lord﴾. That is, the One who has been good to me by teaching me what I did not know and by qualifying me for what was not within my reckoning.

Since they had accused him of *safah* (foolishness), which is among the dispositions of the soul because it is the opposite of forbearance (*hilm*) and gravity (*raz̲anah*), he expressed the content of the negating sentence with a form that implies permanence, saying ﴿and I am a sincere adviser to you﴾. That is, sincere counsel has never ceased to be one of my attributes. It is not something I acquired through effort, but an innate disposition in me, and you have tested me in it before the prophethood and before the declaring of this statement (p-٤٣٧) for a long age and a lengthy time. Then, when they said that they thought him a liar, he added to them the attribute of trustworthiness, saying ﴿trustworthy﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 69:

When he knew what they believed of his trustworthiness and intellect, and he thought that what had moved them to this was nothing but conceit at the idea that he might be given knowledge of what they had not been given, he denounced them for it, mentioning what he thought had moved them, hinting at the connection to denial, so he said: ﴿Do you wonder﴾, i.e., do you deny and wonder, ﴿that there has come to you a reminder﴾, i.e., a nobility and an admonition, ﴿from your Lord﴾, i.e., the One who has never cut off His favour from you at all, ﴿upon a man from among you﴾, i.e., his might is your might and his nobility is your nobility, so nothing has escaped you, ﴿that he may warn you﴾, i.e., that he may caution you against what awaits those who are in your condition of wretched outcome.

Since the implied meaning is: "so beware," he followed it with reminding them of the blessing, pointing by it to warning against the great retribution, in His saying: ﴿And remember when﴾, i.e., when, ﴿He made you successors﴾, i.e., over what you are in of the earth. And since their time was distant after them, he used the prepositional phrase, saying: ﴿after the people of Noah﴾. Or the omitted element may be what the interrogative in His saying ﴿Do you wonder﴾ requires of a request for an answer, i.e., "answer, and remember," meaning: do not hasten to answer until you remember what He has bestowed upon you, and in this is an indication of warning against what befell the people of Noah. Or the conjunction may be upon the sense of the denying interrogative in ﴿Will you not then fear God?﴾ [al-A'raf: 65], ﴿Do you wonder﴾, i.e., fear God, do not wonder, and remember. Or the conjunction, which is better, is upon ﴿Worship God﴾ [al-A'raf: 65]. As for His saying ﴿successors﴾, it has been said that it implies they had taken the place of those people, and it is known that the people of Noah filled the earth, while 'Ad were only in a small part of it, namely the tract from the direction of Yemen. It has been said that this is because Shaddad ibn 'Ad ruled the whole earth, so it is as if it were said: your forefather was made a successor over the whole earth. So if gratitude is achieved, the blessing is complete; so obey, and He will increase you from His bounty. It has also been said that the story of Thamud is similar, and there was none among them who ruled the earth, nor the land of 'Ad; so it is answered with what is generally accepted, namely that 'Ad, since they were the strongest people of the earth in bodies, greatest in physique, most vigorous in creation, and most famous in tribe and mention, all other people were followers of them; and likewise Thamud in what they were given of the power to hew mountains and the like into houses. In my view, the question from its origin is not to be rejected, for there is a difference that is not hidden between our saying "So-and-so is successor of So-and-so" and "So-and-so is a successor after So-and-so." In the second, the one succeeded is not mentioned, so it is as if it were said: He made you successors to those who were before you in this earth in which you are. He singled out the people of Noah and 'Ad for mention, as a reminder of the punishment that befell them. For this very reason God singled out these nations mentioned in the Qur'an for mention; otherwise the nations were very numerous, exceeding measure, and greatly dispersed in all regions, and it is known that God Most High did not leave any one of them without a messenger: ﴿And We never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isra': 15].

In the story of Hud in the surah of al-Ahqaf there is ﴿Warners had already come before him and after him﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 21]. It has another secret, namely that these nations were known to the Arabs, with many reports about them, so their circumstances were detailed to them, while those of whom they had no awareness were passed over, and so they were mentioned only in summary, lest they hasten to denial of what descends upon them without a visible proof established against them.

When He reminded them of the bare survival after that general drowning, He followed it with a reminder of the increase, so He said: ﴿And He increased you﴾, i.e., beyond those before you or beyond those who exist on the earth in your time, ﴿in creation﴾, i.e., specifically among you, ﴿in stature﴾, i.e., in sensible form, in the length of bodies, and the meaning is in strength of frame. It has been said that the height of each of them was twelve cubits, and it has been said more.

When the blessing became great, He repeated the reminder to them, saying, as a consequence of that: ﴿So remember the bounties of God﴾, i.e., the blessings of the One who combined the attributes of greatness, which He bestowed upon you, of succession, strength and others, and remember that there is no blessing with you from anyone other than Him at all, so He is deserving that you single Him out with worship, ﴿that you may prosper﴾, i.e., so that your state may be that of one whose success is hoped for, which is attaining all his aims; because remembrance necessitates gratitude, which necessitates increase.

(p-440) Since this (the call to worship God alone) was necessarily compelling, and every fair-minded listener must hasten to submit to this decisive proof, namely that He alone deserves worship because He alone bestows blessings, the eagerness of the addressee to hear their answer increased, so it was answered with His saying: ﴿They said﴾, denying it upon him and relying on mere imitation (taqlid) alone, ﴿"Have you come to us﴾, that is, from the One whom you claim to be His messenger, ﴿that we may worship God﴾, that is, the Supreme King, ﴿alone?"﴾ And since this statement of theirs was in the extreme of conceit, which deserves denunciation, they followed it with what serves as the reason for their rejection of what he called them to, so they said: ﴿and abandon﴾, that is, leave aside in a state of no good quality, ﴿what our fathers used to worship﴾, that is, persistently devoted to worshipping it, as indicated by (kāna) and the form of the present tense, together with the indication thereby to depicting their fathers in that state, ﴿so that it would be fitting, in their assumption,﴾ to deny that they oppose them.

And since the meaning of this denial was "We will not give you (what you ask)", and he had alluded to them, through the reminder of the people of Noah and his saying ﴿Will you not then fear God?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 23], to the punishment should they persist, they based on that their saying: ﴿So bring us﴾, that is, swiftly, ﴿what you promise us﴾, that is, of the punishment, through what their gestures had hinted at of denial by their saying: ﴿if you are of the truthful.﴾ And their calling the warning of punishment a "promise" was by way of mockery.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 71:

Since they had gone to extremes of foolishness in this statement, and it was known from his (ﷺ) dealings with them that he was forbearing towards them, their longing to hear what his reply would be grew intense, and they anticipated it. So he satisfied the thirst of this longing with his words: (p-٤٤١)﴿He said: "There has already fallen﴾, meaning: it has been decreed, has become binding, and is close to occurring, ﴿upon you from your Lord﴾, meaning: the One who deceived you by the continuous succession of His favours upon you and the prolonging of His respite for you, ﴿an abomination﴾, meaning: a punishment of severe turmoil that seizes both the farthest and the nearest of you, which necessitates the intensity of your turmoil, ﴿and wrath﴾, meaning: an intensity in that punishment from which you will not escape."

When he had informed them of this, he made clear to them that its cause was this speech of theirs, in a context of denial, so he said: ﴿Do you dispute with me﴾. And since the gods they were disputing about were nothing beyond names, being devoid of any meaning, he said: ﴿about names﴾. Then he made clear that the one who named them gods was not the one they worship, so he said: ﴿which you have named, you and your fathers﴾. And since it belongs to Allah the Exalted to do what He wills and to command submission to whomever He wills, he said, negating the sending down (al-tanzil), for the negation of sending down (al-inzal) entails it: ﴿Allah has not sent down﴾, meaning: He to whom alone the command belongs, ﴿any authority for them﴾, meaning: for your worship of them or for your naming of them. He went to the utmost in negation, saying: ﴿any authority﴾. Perhaps he used the form of tanzil (tanzil, from the verbal form tafʿīl) because the tafʿīl form comes to mean a renewed act and also an act occurring gradually. So he intended the negation in every respect, whether as renewal or as gradual revelation, since it is in the context of disputation, and in a surah whose purpose is to warn those who turn away from what this Book, revealed gradually, calls to. This also indicates that if a single command to worship them had been sent down to them, they would have hesitated over it because they did not understand its meaning, until the command was repeated to them again and again, so that they would know that it is a decisive matter that cannot be avoided, just as the Children of Israel did with the command to slaughter a cow for the sake of the slain man, because they did not comprehend (p-٤٤٢) its meaning. This clearly shows that the command for them to worship these idols is nothing but the darkness of desire, for it is pure blindness, and it is part of human nature to ride it without any proof whatsoever.

When he had informed them of the occurrence of the punishment and its cause, he made clear to them that the occurrence is not to be taken literally as to immediate fulfilment; rather its meaning is the necessity that cannot be avoided. So he said: ﴿Then wait﴾. Then he resumed informing them about his own state with his words: ﴿Indeed I﴾, and he indicated with his words: ﴿am with you﴾ that he does not leave them, neither out of fear of them nor of anything else, ﴿among those who wait﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 72:

When this (the warning) ought to have been a cause for belief, which is the cause of mercy, he made clear that He had only brought about punishment for them, while salvation was for Him and for those who followed him. So he began with the believers, showing concern for their situation, with his saying: ﴿So We saved him﴾, that is, by what We possess of greatness, a rescue (injā') by revelation, swift, We drew them out from that punishment as a hair is drawn out of dough (kasall al-sha'ra min al-'ajīn). ﴿And those who were with him﴾, that is, in obedience. He indicated that nothing is obligatory upon God by his saying: ﴿by mercy﴾, that is, by honour and protection, ﴿from Us﴾, that is, not by any deed or anything else.

When he had put the rescue first, out of concern for it, he followed it with their state, saying, informing that their seizure was not like the seizure of kings who are unable to pursue thoroughly, so that the last of the armies, the stragglers of the troops and the followers escape them. ﴿And We cut off﴾ their last remnant (dābir), that is, their last ones. This was the original wording, but He expressed the intended meaning more clearly and explained the reason for their seizure, so He said: ﴿the last remnant (dābir)﴾, that is, the last ones, meaning: We uprooted them, and We made that uprooting a sign (mu'jiza) for Hūd, peace be upon him, ﴿of those who denied Our signs﴾, that is, who did not regard their greatness in relation to Us. And his saying: ﴿and they were not﴾, that is, by nature and disposition, ﴿believers﴾ is conjoined to the relative clause of "those who" (alladhīna), namely: ﴿denied Our signs﴾ [al-A'rāf: 64], and it functions as the reason for their seizure, indicating that no righteousness would come from them, just as He concluded the story of Noah with his saying: ﴿Indeed, they were a blind people﴾ [al-A'rāf: 64], as the cause of their drowning. That is: We cut off their last remnant while they deserved that, because they were not receptive to belief, due to the intensity of their obstinacy and their persistence in atheism. So the meaning is: belief was not among their characteristics, that is, they did not believe in the past and will not believe in the future. Thereby excluded from this is one who believed after having denied before his belief, and one who did not believe at the time of Hūd's supplication for them while God knew that he would believe. What adds beauty is that when they opened their speech by ascribing foolishness to him, falsely, it was fitting to conclude the story by turning the matter upon them, so that they are described with the like of that truthfully, in a statement that makes clear that their being characterized by it is what necessitated what was done to them; for belief arises only from complete steadfastness, sobriety, abandoning desire, restraining the follies of the self, and submitting to clear proofs and manifest evidence. Whoever abandons it despite all that is in the utmost recklessness, levity and lack of reason. Also, describing them with denial in the past tense does not convey its continuance upon them; so He, glorified is He, said that to negate the possibility that they believed after denying and that their seizure was only for the mere occurrence of denial from them, and that they did not hasten to belief before denial. It is also possible that the clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the meaning in either case: We cut off their last remnant while they were in a state of denial and non-belief.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 73:

When He, glory be to Him, had completed what He intended of the story of ʿĀd, He followed it with Thamūd, saying: ﴿And to Thamūd⟩ — i.e., a particular people — [the name] is not declined (mamnūʿ min al-ṣarf) because it refers to a tribe; it is derived from al-thamd (ṯamd), which is a little water. Their dwellings were in the rocky land between the Ḥijāz and al-Shām, as far as Wādī al-Qurā. ﴿We sent their brother Ṣāliḥ.⟩ Then He resumed the report of his speech — as it passed in Hūd — peace be upon him — saying: ﴿He said, "O my people,"⟩ seeking their sympathy by reminding them of kinship and the bond of lineage, ﴿"Worship God"⟩ — i.e., the One in whom alone perfection lies — ﴿"You have no god other than Him."⟩ He emphasized the negation with His words: ﴿"other than Him"⟩.

When it was shown that his truthfulness in this matter was evident, since they called upon their idols and they did not answer them, and he (ﷺ) called upon his Lord, glory be to Him, and He brought forth the she-camel for them — he gave the reason for the soundness of what he called to with His words: ﴿"There has certainly come to you a clear proof"⟩ — i.e., a very manifest sign of the truth of my claim to messengerhood and of the soundness of what I commanded you. He increased their desire with His words: ﴿"from your Lord"⟩ — i.e., the One who has never ceased to be good to you. Then he resumed explaining it with His words: ﴿"This"⟩, pointing to it after its creation, to confirm it and to magnify its status and the status of the One who brought it into being, given the greatness of its creation and the swiftness of its formation for their sake.

When he pointed to it, he named it, saying: ﴿"the she-camel of God"⟩; He honored it by attributing it to the Greatest Name, and He indicated its being specific to them with His words: ﴿"for you"⟩, in the state of it being ﴿a sign⟩ — i.e., for whoever witnessed it and for whoever heard of it and whose affair was confirmed to him. Then, as a consequence of that, He said: ﴿"So leave her"⟩ — i.e., let her be, even in the least manner of leaving — ﴿"to eat"⟩, i.e., of the vegetation, and ﴿"in God's earth"⟩, i.e., of what God has caused to grow, to whom all things belong, (p-445) and she is His she-camel just as the whole earth is absolutely His earth and the vegetation His provision. For this reason it was made manifest, so that her eating would not be restricted to one land over another.

When he had commanded them to leave her for this reason, he confirmed the command by forbidding them from harming her, saying: ﴿"And do not touch her with harm"⟩ — let alone what comes after touching — ﴿"lest there seize you"⟩, i.e., a seizing of overpowering by reason of that touching and in its wake, ﴿"a painful punishment"⟩, i.e., one that causes pain.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 74:

When He had commanded them and forbidden them, He mentioned to them, as encouragement while alluding to warning, saying: ﴿And remember﴾, that is: the blessing of Allah upon you ﴿when He made you successors﴾, that is: in what you are in ﴿after ʿĀd﴾, that is: after their destruction ﴿and settled you in the land﴾, that is: He made for you in its substance dwellings in which you take up residence (tabawwu'), that is: you return to them at the time of your rest. He made easy for you, in whatever land you wished, its working, what He did not make easy for others. For this reason he explained the intended meaning with His words: ﴿you take for yourselves﴾, that is: by the crafts you possess, ﴿from its plains, palaces﴾, that is: buildings, of clay, mud-brick and baked brick, spacious, lofty and fine, in which the hope of the hopeful and the gaze of the beholder are kept short by what they contain of amenities and beauties. ﴿And you hew out the mountains﴾, that is: whatever mountain you wished, you are able to shape it ﴿as houses﴾.

When He reminded them of these blessings, encouraging and warning them, He repeated that by allusion and by explicit expression, saying, as a consequence of what He had reminded them of: ﴿So remember﴾, that is: remembrance of submission, desire and awe, ﴿the bounties of Allah﴾, that is: the blessings of Allah, the One who possesses the attributes of perfection, so that He has no need of anyone, and His beneficence is in truth the beneficence ﴿and do not commit corruption in the land﴾ (ta'thaw, from al-ʿathy, which is corruption; it is an inversion of al-ʿayth, as Ibn al-Qaṭṭāʿ said), and in that case His saying ﴿causing corruption﴾ means ones who deliberately pursue corruption.

When the turn of address to their reply took place, it was said: ﴿The chiefs (al-mala'), that is, the nobles, said﴾. He identified them by his words: ﴿who were arrogant﴾, that is, who had committed arrogance and characterized themselves by it, so that it became a disposition for them, and therefore they did not believe. He drew attention to their being pitied by his words: ﴿from among his people﴾. When He said: ﴿to those who were deemed weak﴾, it might have been understood that all of them had believed, so He negated that with His words, in apposition (mubdilan minhu, i.e., as a badal, substitute or appositive) to it: ﴿to those of them who believed﴾, that is, of the weakened ones. This is more striking to the soul and more captivating to the heart than an explicit statement at first encounter, together with an indication that the followers of the truth are the weak, and that only some of them believed. In it there is a hint that weakness is among the greatest of blessings, because it accompanies the abandonment of self-conceit, which leads to submission to the truth. Its being built in the passive form (bina'uhu lil-maf'ul, the passive construction) is evidence that they were in the utmost weakness, to the extent that everyone would regard them as weak. ﴿Do you know﴾, that is, they began with denial, turning them away from belief: ﴿that Salih﴾. They called him by his name, out of harshness, roughness, and intimidation toward those being questioned, so that they would answer them in a way that pleased them. ﴿is one sent from his Lord﴾. It is as though they said this in order to learn their condition, so as to build upon it what they would do, because the arrogant do not complete their arrogance except through the obedience of the weak.

When they knew this from them, they informed them of their rejection, relying upon the Great, the Exalted (al-Kabir al-Muta'al), before whom every arrogance collapses and to whose command no command of anyone is considered, by saying: ﴿They said﴾, admonishing them about their coarseness and their error in their assessment of their state, expressing themselves with what indicates knowledge of that and submission to it: ﴿Indeed, we are in what he has been sent with﴾. It was built in the passive to indicate the generality of affirmation, and that his being from God is a matter decided upon, not requiring specification: ﴿believers﴾, that is, deeply immersed in belief in it (p. 447).

So for this reason, ﴿Those who were arrogant said﴾ — that is, in their reply, expressing themselves in a manner that indicates opposition to them and obstinacy — ﴿Indeed, we are disbelievers in that which﴾ — and they placed (in the position of "was sent with it") — as a rejection of what they had taken to be known and accepted as settled — ﴿you believe in﴾, that is, whatever it may be ﴿.﴾

Then He attributed to their saying their (other) saying: ﴿So they hamstrung the she-camel﴾, that is, the one which Allah had made a sign for them. He used the word "hamstrung" (ʿaqr) rather than "slaughtered" (naḥr) because it covers every means of killing her, for Ibn Ishaq mentioned that a group of them gathered around her: one of them shot her with an arrow, another struck her legs with a sword, and another slaughtered her. So the name of the cause was applied to the effect. However, the words of the Most High: ﴿Then they called their companion, and he took up (the sword) and hamstrung [her]﴾ [al-Qamar: 29], and His words ﴿when the most wretched of them rose up﴾ [al-Shams: 12], and the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "There rose up for her a mighty, violent, powerful man among his people" — they said: he was Qudar ibn Salif, whom a woman of his people had promised her daughter if he hamstrung her, so he did it, and he was the most wretched of the first (generation) and the most wretched of the last: ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Muljam al-Muradi, the slayer of ʿAli ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), (p-448) for Qatam — a beautiful woman of the Banu ʿIjl — had offered herself to him if he killed him. The connection between them is that each of them cast himself into the greatest disobedience for the sake of the desire of his private parts, in marriage to a woman. And his (ﷺ) saying: "The most wretched of the first (generations) is the hamstringer of the she-camel" indicates that her hamstringer was one man, and in that case the intended meaning is cutting the legs. So where (the Qur'an) uses the plural, it intends both the literal and the figurative sense together, and where (the Prophet) uses the singular, he intends only the literal sense. The expression with (ʿaqr) is used because it is the root and the greatest cause of slaughtering camels. Al-Baghawi said: al-Azhari said: ʿaqr is cutting the hamstring of the camel; then naḥr (slaughter) was called ʿaqr because the one who slaughters a camel hamstrings it and then slaughters it. End of quote. It seems that this is an indication that what is meant by ʿaqr in his speech is naḥr. There is no doubt that the original meaning of ʿaqr in the language is cutting, and its root revolves around that: ʿaqara al-nakhla means he cut its top so it dried out, and ʿaqara al-faras means he struck its legs with a sword. The term ʿaqr is mostly used for corruption, whereas naḥr is generally used for benefiting from the slaughtered animal, its meat, hide, and other parts. So perhaps the use of ʿaqr rather than naḥr is an indication that they intended by slaughtering her nothing but her destruction, out of insolence toward Allah, obstinacy, and doing evil in opposition to the prohibition of Salih (peace be upon him). This is not contradicted by what has been reported that they divided up her meat, because (the verse) does not claim that hamstringing necessarily prevents benefit from the slaughtered animal; and even if so, they did not intend by that to benefit from the meat, but since they could not all share in the hamstringing, they intended to share in its consequence, as a display of their approval of it and their participation in it by what was possible for them. ﴿And they defied﴾, that is, they exceeded the limit in harshness and arrogance ﴿the command﴾, that is, the carrying out of the command ﴿of their Lord﴾, that is, the One who does good to them, who had come to them through His messenger, to leave her alone ﴿and they said﴾, adding to their defiance: ﴿O Salih, bring us﴾

And when they treated his threat against them — since they did not believe in it — as a promise and good tidings, they said: ﴿what you threaten us with﴾, out of contempt and exaggeration in denial, [as if they were saying: we are certain that you cannot bring us anything of that, and if you are truthful, then do it and do not delay it, out of gentleness and compassion toward us, for we are not harmed by it; rather we take pleasure in it, as one who meets a good promise]. The summary of this is their mockery of him and an indication of his inability; and they emphasized this by their saying with the particle of doubt: ﴿if you are of the messengers﴾, that is, those whose reports we have heard of in the past;

Then He traced the cause of their arrogance to His words: ﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾, that is, the one from which or by which the Shout (al-sayha) came, a seizing of one who is in the grip, in a state of utmost humiliation and abasement. Perhaps the singular "dar" (abode) here, together with the earthquake in the story of Salih and Shu'ayb, peace be upon them, in His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So they were found lying prostrate in their abode﴾, that is, their dwellings, and the plural form in the two stories together with the Shout in Surat Hud (peace be upon him), is to indicate the greatness of the quake and the Shout in both places. This is because when the quake is confined to a single thing it is more firm, and so it is greater in the intended punishment. The Shout, by its nature, spreads; so when it covers distant places and remote abodes, destroying their people, tearing apart their community and scattering their unity, it attains such extreme force and intensity that souls are disturbed upon contemplating its description and hearts are struck with awe. The upshot is that where He expressed it with "al-rajfa" (the earthquake) He used the singular "dar", indicating the severity of the punishment through the greatness of the convulsion; and where He expressed it with "al-sayha" (the Shout) He used the plural, as a hint at the universality of death through the intensity of the sound. There is no contradiction, for their punishment was by each of them, and perhaps one of them was a cause of the other. Perhaps the intended meaning of "al-rajfa" is the trembling of hearts, a trembling that cut them off, or that the abode quaked and so the hearts quaked; and this is closer. The Surat al-A'raf was singled out for what is mentioned in it, because its purpose is to warn those who turn away, and the earthquake is more striking in its impact due to people's unfamiliarity with it. And Allah knows best. ﴿Lying prostrate﴾, that is, kneeling on their knees, remaining in their places, with none of them stirring. No one remained among them at that hour except one man who was in the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram). When he left it, there befell him what befell his people, and he was Abu Righal. The distance of the Haram from their land exceeds a ten-day journey. Among the great signs is that this event, which tore loose their hearts and removed their spirits, had no effect whatsoever on Salih, peace be upon him, or the weak believers with him. This is like the wind that shook the confederates (al-ahzab), inflicted upon them the most severe punishment, and pelted them with stones and dust until it routed them, yet it did not cause the Prophet ﷺ and his companions any great harm, and Allah restrained it from Hudhayfah. Likewise was the hail that came in his time, when the Prophet ﷺ sent him to gain knowledge of their news.

When this calamity befell them, it caused him to be driven out of their lands, the lands of evil, wrath and curse. So God Most High said, informing us of this: ﴿So he turned away from them﴾, meaning he imposed upon himself the turning away from them. ﴿And said﴾, meaning, when he was overcome by the tenderness of human nature over the loss of their faith, since they were his own origin and kin: ﴿O my people﴾, meaning those whose harm distresses me. ﴿I had certainly conveyed to you﴾. He perhaps used the singular for his words ﴿the message of my Lord﴾ because its wording is one. ﴿And I advised you﴾, where he left the verb without an object and made it transitive with the particle lam, saying ﴿to you﴾, to indicate that it was specifically for them. It is narrated that he went out from them with one hundred and ten Muslims, weeping, while his people numbered fifteen hundred households. It is also narrated that he returned with those who were with him, and they settled in their homes.

Since the implied sense was: "So I did with you what calls for your loving me because of it," he joined to it his words ﴿but﴾ you did not love me. This was the original form, but he expressed it in a way that conveys that this was their habit and disposition toward every advisor. So he said ﴿you do not love﴾, meaning recounting their past condition, ﴿the advisors﴾, meaning every one who does what I did of complete advice.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on surah 7, verse 80:

When He, glory be to Him, had completed what fulfils the purpose of this surah in this context concerning their story, He followed it with the one after them, from among those the Arabs know, as He had done before, and said: (p-452) ﴿And Lot, when he said﴾. Since his mission was to several cities, as though they were various tribes, it was said that they were five, and these are the *Mu'tafikat* (the overturned cities). It was also said that they were four thousand, between al-Sham and the noble city of Madinah. He said: ﴿to his people﴾. It has been permitted that the governing element (*al-'amil*) for this could be "We sent" or "remember." It does not necessarily follow, if "We sent" is the governing element, that his sending was not prior to the time when he spoke these words to them, because just as that time, which encompasses the beginning and end of his statement, is a time for him, so also the day on which this statement occurred is a time for him, and indeed that month, that year and that century. For it is the custom of the Arabs to call the days shared in a single action by one name "a day." They say "the Day of al-Qadisiyyah," which lasted four days if we consider only the duration of the fighting, or several months if we consider the gathering for it. Likewise "the Day of Siffin." God, the Exalted, said in the story of Badr: ﴿And when God promised you one of the two groups, that it would be yours﴾ [al-Anfal: 7], up to His saying: ﴿when you sought help from your Lord﴾ [al-Anfal: 9], up to His saying: ﴿when He covered you with drowsiness as a security from Him﴾ [al-Anfal: 11], ﴿when your Lord revealed to the angels﴾ [al-Anfal: 12]. All of these are a substitution (*badal*) for His saying: ﴿when God promised you one of the two groups﴾ [al-Anfal: 7]. There is no doubt that the time of all of these was not one unified time except by interpreting all the days connected with the event, of march, fighting and other things, as one. And God knows best. In the story of Noah [peace be upon him] He expressed it as ﴿We sent Noah to his people﴾ [al-A'raf: 59], then the ones after him were coordinated (*nassaqa*) with it, so it was said: ﴿And to 'Ad their brother Hud﴾ [al-A'raf: 65], ﴿And to Thamud their brother Salih﴾ [al-A'raf: 73], ﴿And to Madyan their brother Shu'ayb﴾ [al-A'raf: 85]. He departed from this style in the story of Lot, [so He did not say: "And to the people of Adum their brother Lot"], (p-453) or "To the people of Sodom, Lot," or "And We sent Lot to his people," and similar, as will come in the story of Moses [peace be upon him]. This is because among the greatest purposes of the context of these stories is to console the Prophet ﷺ regarding the opposition of his people to him, their non-response and the severity of their harm, and to warn his people that there would befall them what befell these nations of punishment. The stories of all the others are similar to the story of Quraysh in associating partners with God and in harming His believing servants. As for the story of the people of Lot, it exceeds that in a matter that is monstrous, of very great ugliness, of severe shame and indecency. So He departed from that coordinated style to draw attention to it, to magnify the matter and to make it abhorrent, so that the consolation would be stronger and the call to praise and gratitude more complete. At that point it becomes preferable that the governing element be "remember" and not "We sent." That is: remember Lot and what befell him from his people, in addition to their polytheism, from seeing among them this matter that left no room for further abomination. Thus the story is in reality a consolation and a reminder of the blessing of the Arabs being spared from such a condition, and a warning to them of the evil outcome, together with what it shares with its sister stories in indicating the evil nature of these people and the wickedness of their essence, which required their being singled out from the people of the earth by that gross matter. The proof that it is the most abominable of abominations after polytheism, despite God having placed in every sound nature an aversion to it, is that it is singled out by sharing with polytheism in that it has never been permitted in any religion (*millah*) at any time, nor with any attribute. The rest of the prohibited matters are not like this. As for killing souls, it is permitted in retaliation (*qisas*), in jihad and in other cases. Sexual intercourse in the vagina is not prohibited except under the condition that it be fornication (*zina*); without that attribute it would be permitted. Consuming property is originally permitted, and it is prohibited only under the condition that it be by falsehood (*bil-batil*). And so is the rest. Abu Hayyan said: Since this act's ugliness is well known and its indecency is embedded in minds, it came defined: that is, in His saying after rebuking them, reproaching them and censuring them: ﴿Do you commit the indecency?﴾, meaning: do you commit the evil that continues in ugliness, even if there is a great distance between you and it. Or the (*al-*) in it is for the genus, as an emphasis, as though, because of its extreme ugliness, all indecencies were made into it, and because the Arabs were far, a complete distance, from that. This is unlike fornication, for He said about it: ﴿And do not approach fornication; indeed it is an indecency﴾ [al-Isra: 32]. Since it was not unlikely, given the brazenness of their faces and their shamelessness, that they would say: "Why should our deed be an abomination censured for it?", He said: ﴿No one in the worlds preceded you in it﴾, and He intensified the negation with His saying: ﴿from anyone﴾, and magnified that by generalizing it in His saying: ﴿from the worlds﴾. So you have invented something whose like of indecency has not existed, so that you may be remembered for it with the worst remembrance. Just as (p-455) people of lofty aspirations, excellence and perfection devise from good deeds and benefits what will leave them a lasting remembrance and whose reward will benefit them, and in this there is a greater indication of condemning innovations (*bida'*) and censuring their doers, because minds cannot independently know good deeds.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 81:

When he left the indecency unspecified so that the desire to know what it was would arise, he specified it in another interrogation, similar to the first in its denunciation and rebuke, so that it would be more indicative of the extreme restraint against it. So He said: ﴿Indeed, you approach men with desire⦆... 

Note: the verse as quoted here reads ﴿إنَّكم لَتَأْتُونَ الرِّجالَ﴾, which is rendered as: ﴿Indeed, you come upon men﴾. Its meaning is: you cover them with the covering of men over women (i.e., you have intercourse with them as one does with women). When he left no room for curiosity, he specified with His words ﴿shahwatan﴾, meaning: desiring, or for the sake of desire; no motive moves you to that except desire, like the beasts which have no call from the intellect. And he stated explicitly ﴿min dun al-nisa'﴾, "instead of women." So when he left no ambiguity, and this might have suggested that they had an excuse for not finding women or for women's failing to satisfy them, he turned away from that with His words: ﴿Nay, you are a people﴾...

When the purpose of this surah is warning, the most fitting thing for it was excess (al-israf), which is the extreme of the ignorance mentioned in Surah al-Naml. So He said: ﴿who exceed (musrifun)﴾, meaning: no necessity of desire that you claim compelled you to this; rather, the habit of transgressing the limits. He did not name the people of Lut in any surah of the surahs, as Ad and Thamud and others were named, in order to keep the speech free from naming them. As for the people of Nuh, they were not named because the tribes had not yet dispersed at that time; so they were, for that reason, all the people of the earth, and therefore the drowning covered them all. And Allah knows best.

[p. 456]

Since it is as if it were said: this rebuke necessarily produces the utmost shame, indeed it drives each of them who hears it to a place where he finds no cover for his condition. So I wonder, what was their state in his sight? It was said: it is as if they answered him with great impudence and extreme wickedness beyond all bounds. Their answer was nothing but harm toward Lot, peace be upon him, and his family, for which they deserved from him a severe warning, which is the aim of the surah. He linked to it His saying: ﴿And the answer of his people was not but that they said﴾, meaning: those who possessed great strength, firm resolve, and power to carry out what they intended, ﴿except that they said﴾

Since the purpose is to show that they hastened to answer him with what would distress him, He omitted what does not become unclear through omission [or: since the context is to explain the wicked, He made clear that there is no one more wicked than these people, whose baseness reached the point that they regarded the pure and purifying ones, those whose tongues are kept from mentioning such things, as deserving expulsion]. So He said, Exalted is He, indicating this in relating their words: ﴿Expel them﴾, meaning: those spoken of, namely Lot and whoever joined him, ﴿from your town﴾. The purpose of showing their haste in this is to console the Prophet ﷺ over his people's rejection of his words, so that no distress would remain in his breast over their warning. Then they gave a reason for their expulsion of them by their saying: ﴿Indeed they are people﴾, meaning: weak ones, ﴿who purify themselves﴾. It seems they intended, by the form with the tafa''ul prefix (the taf'ul form, using the tā' of tafa''ul), to attribute to them a love of this vile deed, and that their abstaining from it was only affectation and forcing of their souls to turn back from what they inclined toward, and a turning to purity without a true motive, and a display of it out of showing off. This is what the appearance of the tā' of the taf'īl form indicates. Along with this there is in it a tinge of mockery. Restricting their answer to this meaning, expressed in this wording, does not contradict the verse of al-'Ankabut which says: ﴿So the answer of his people was not but that they said: Bring us the punishment of God﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 29]. This is because applying the term "answer" to this is permissible, and the meaning is: their saying in reply to him was nothing but bringing what is not fit to be an answer, and that is the implication of this statement and others that have no connection to the answer. Or, since this answer, by its denial and its announcing persistence and harshness toward the Messenger of God ﷺ, entailed punishment, they were as if they had spoken it, saying ﴿Bring us the punishment of God﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 29]; He made their speaking the cause as speaking the effect. Or, they used for every situation a fitting speech. What supports this is that the meaning is one here and in al-Naml, namely the restriction of the answer to this: that is, their answer to this statement was nothing but this. When in al-'Ankabut He added to the rebuke, saying: ﴿Do you indeed approach men, and cut off the road, and commit the evil in your gatherings?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 29], they answered with something more eloquent in denial and mockery, saying: ﴿Bring us the punishment of God﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 29], and so on in the verse.

"Then, since their obstinacy resulted in their destruction and his deliverance, and since informing about his deliverance—even though he understands their destruction—was more important, He said: ﴿So We delivered him and his family﴾, i.e., those who obeyed him, ﴿except his wife﴾. And since it was as if it were said, "What about her?", He said: ﴿She was among those who remained behind﴾, i.e., those who stayed behind, whom the punishment overtook, so that the lesson and the reminder are an indication that she suffered the same punishment as the men, not lesser than them, because she was an unbeliever like them."

(p-458) When this had made clear their destruction, he explained it, indicating its kind, with His saying: ﴿And We rained﴾, i.e., rocks of brimstone (kibrit), after their cities had been uprooted, raised up, and overturned, until those who traveled among them and their stragglers were stoned with them, because it was a punishment of annihilation (al-isti'sal) from One whom nothing can frustrate. He clarified it by restricting the verb and transitivizing it with the preposition of elevation, saying: ﴿upon them﴾. He emphasized that it was from the sky, not from a plain, a mountain, or the like, with His saying: ﴿a rain﴾. He indicated its greatness, entirely removing any ambiguity, by what he made its consequence, with His saying: ﴿Then see how was the end of the criminals﴾, i.e., the final outcome of their affair. He made the explicit noun stand in place of the pronoun, attaching the ruling to the descriptive of severance (al-qat') for what is due to be connected (al-wasl) by joining it to the gross disobedience that is due to be severed, as evidence that stoning is the recompense of whoever does this act under its condition, because the ruling revolves with its cause ('illah). In Surah Hud, upon him be peace, the account of their story from the Torah will come, after the beginning of their affair was already mentioned in al-Baqarah at His saying: ﴿When his Lord said to him, "Submit"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 131]. This is like the stones being marked (sawwamat) for the Quraysh when, after they resolved to return from the road following their turning away from the Battle of Uhud, they intended to frighten the Prophet ﷺ and his companions by their assumption, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is! Stones were indeed marked for them, and had they returned, they would have been like yesterday's departed." But when he ﷺ was a messenger of mercy, Allah did not decree their return, so they went on until many of them later embraced Islam. And like when Allah rained stones upon the companions of the Elephant in the year of the Prophet's ﷺ birth, as a protection for his city, by his blessing.

(p. 459) When this wondrous story in the narratives had concluded, he returned to the first arrangement (nasaq) and said, ﴿And to Madyan﴾, meaning: We sent. Madyan is a town, and it is said to be a tribe descended from Madyan ibn Ibrahim al-Khalil (peace be upon him). ﴿their brother﴾, meaning by lineage. He clarified this with His words, ﴿Shu'ayb﴾, who is described as the "orator of the prophets" (peace be upon them) because of the excellence of his debate with his people. Then he resumed his speech in the same arrangement: ﴿He said: O my people﴾, indicating sincere advice and compassion by reminding them of kinship. He began with the foundation that is upheld in all the laws transmitted from the prophets (peace be upon them), so he said: ﴿Worship Allah﴾, meaning the One who deserves worship in His essence, by virtue of His Beautiful Names and Sublime Attributes.

Since the purpose is to single Him out for worship, because He does not accept association (shirk), because He is self-sufficient (ghani), he justified this with His words, ﴿You have no god other than Him﴾, and he emphasized the negation with His words, ﴿other than Him﴾. Then he resumed the reminder with what indicates the soundness of his claim in itself and his truthfulness in his claim to messengerhood, with His words, ﴿There has certainly come to you﴾, meaning through me, ﴿a clear proof﴾. Since we know from the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), which al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) narrated from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him): "There is no prophet among the prophets except that he was given signs of the kind that people believed in on their account," that this clear proof is a miracle, and that the like of it is sufficient for the soundness of the claim, and there was no necessity to mention it to us, it was not specified. Then he increased them in encouragement with His words, ﴿from your Lord﴾, meaning the One from whom you have seen no blessing except from Him.

Since his bringing the clear proofs was a cause for the obligation of obeying his command, he said, consequently: ﴿So give full measure﴾, meaning the measuring vessel and the weight, ﴿and the scale﴾, meaning give what you give with them in full. (p. 460) So the verse is of the type of al-ihtibak (a rhetorical device in which one term is omitted where its counterpart is mentioned, and vice versa). What is reported of him here is from the early part of his speech to them, so he omitted the emphasis that removes the figurative sense of approximation by mentioning equity (al-qist).

Since the command to fulfill includes the prohibition of diminishing, he stated it explicitly in a way that encompasses others, so he said: ﴿And do not diminish﴾, meaning do not reduce or corrupt, as diminution corrupts, ﴿people's things﴾, meaning any diminution in measure, weight, or anything else. And "people" (al-nas), said al-Qamus, may refer to humans and jinn; it is the plural of insan (human), its origin being unas, a rare plural to which the definite article (al-) was added. Abu 'Abd Allah al-Qazzaz said: "The origin of al-nas according to the Basrans is unas; then they added the alif and lam to that and dropped the hamza, and al-nas remained. Its original form was fu'al from anistu bihi (I was comfortable with him), as if it was said unas, meaning by inversion, he said, because they are a source of comfort." End. When this is known, it is known that his prohibition, peace be upon him, against diminishing the group in which there is strength of resistance is a prohibition against diminishing the individual by the way of the other (al-ukhra, i.e., by the principle of a fortiori), because the laws came only to strengthen the weak in his right.

Since he prohibited corruption by diminution, he generalized every corruption, so he said: ﴿And do not cause corruption﴾, meaning do not bring about corruption, ﴿in the earth﴾, by placing something of the right of the Truth or of creation in other than its place. Since he forbade them from these vices, he reminded them of Allah's blessing as an emphasis on the prohibition, with what is in that of frightening and as an incitement to adopt the attribute of the Master, so he said: ﴿after its reformation﴾, meaning the reformation by Allah of it through the blessing of the first origination, by creating it and creating its benefits and what is in it in this wondrous, well-ordered system; then through the blessing of the first sustaining (al-ibqa'), (p. 461) by sending down the Books, dispatching the Messengers, and establishing the laws through which benefit is achieved and the blessing is completed by reforming the affairs of livelihood and the hereafter, by exalting the command of Allah and by compassion toward the creation of Allah. All of that is comprised by abstaining from doing harm.

Since he had laid down to them the command and prohibition, he pointed to the greatness of what that entails, as an incitement for them to comply with it, so he said: ﴿That﴾, meaning this great matter of high rank from what has been mentioned in this story, ﴿is better for you﴾. And since the disbeliever is deficient in perceptions yet complete in ruin, he indicated this with His words, ﴿if you are believers﴾, meaning: then do not cause corruption, or: you know the soundness of what I have said, and when you know its soundness you act upon it, and when you act upon it you prosper entirely. It is permissible, and it is the better reading, that the estimate is: "then it is better for you," because the believer is rewarded for his action since he has built it upon the foundation of faith, whereas the disbeliever's deeds are corrupt, so his doing of these things is not good for him in terms of his happiness in the Hereafter, since he has no reward.

Since the generality follows the specification, and the detail follows the summary, and since prohibiting corruption by blocking the way of God is the primary aim, because it forbids every kind of corruption, He singled it out for mention, indicating that it is the essence of the intended meaning after the general statement. So He said: ﴿And do not sit﴾, meaning, do not act like one who lies in wait, fully turned toward it, ﴿on every path﴾, meaning, every road of the world and of the religion, of lawful and unlawful things, of commands and prohibitions, of the clear and the ambiguous, and of the parables, (p-٤٦٢) ﴿threatening﴾, meaning, you threaten whoever walks it with every evil, if he does not agree with what you want.

Since the path of religion is more important, He singled it out for mention, saying: ﴿and barring﴾, meaning, you continually practice barring, ﴿from the way of God﴾, meaning, the road of Him to whom all command belongs. Having mentioned barring from it, He mentioned the one who is barred, saying: ﴿those who believe in Him﴾, meaning, in God, and so follow His way, which has no straighter path. Since they were not satisfied with mere barring by threats and the like, but presented the one being barred with doubts that make him think he is in error, He said, joining it by conjunction: ﴿and seeking to make it crooked﴾, meaning, you seek the path while it is crooked, that is, you seek its distortion by casting doubts and suspicions, as you say: "I want so-and-so a king," meaning, I want his kingship. It has been mentioned in (Al 'Imran) that its being put in the accusative as a hal (circumstantial accusative) is more preferred, and that his saying (ﷺ) in the Sahih: "«Get me stones that I may wipe with them»" favours its being in the accusative as a maf'ul (direct object). And God knows best.

Since their actions diminished people, either in wealth through defrauding, or in faith and support through barring, He reminded them that God, exalted is He, did the opposite of that with them, namely increasing them after their paucity, in a context warning them of being uprooted from the face of the earth, and He singled them out with favour beyond their being few and diminished. So He said, joining it to His words: ﴿Worship God﴾ [Al-A'raf: 85] and what follows it of commands and prohibitions: ﴿And remember when﴾, meaning, at the time when ﴿you were few﴾, meaning, in number and in resources, ﴿so He multiplied you﴾, meaning, He multiplied your numbers, your wealth, and everything that is attributed to you. So do not repay the blessing with its opposite, for remembering the blessing encourages gratitude.

(p-٤٦٣) Since He encouraged them by reminding them of the blessing, He warned them by reminding them of those who received punishment, saying: ﴿And look at how was the end﴾, meaning, the final outcome of ﴿the corrupters﴾, meaning, in the general destruction through kinds of punishment, so that you may beware lest there befall you the like of what befell them, as He stated explicitly in Surah (Hud), because the situation there called for elaboration, as will come, God willing, Exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 87:

When He had warned them of the gravity of the corruption He had forbidden them, and had made their cessation from it conditional on the attribute of faith, He returned to the other part of what He had stipulated as the condition for ceasing from corruption, and said: ﴿And if there is a group among you﴾, that is, a company, numerous enough that they can form a circle around those they wish to [protect], ﴿who have believed in that with which I have been sent﴾. He framed the verb in the passive (ublitha, "I have been sent") as an indication that the one who sends (the agent) is known from what preceded in the context, and that [the matter] has reached a point where no doubt can reach it, because of the proofs that have been established. ﴿And a group﴾, that is, from among you, ﴿has not believed﴾, that is, in that with which He sent me, [the One] who strengthened me with what you know of the clear signs. And He warned them of His might by His saying: ﴿So be patient﴾, that is, O both groups, ﴿until Allah judges﴾, that is, the One to whom belongs all greatness, ﴿between us﴾, that is, between our two groups, by granting victory to the reformer and destroying the corrupter, as He has made this His custom. ﴿And He is﴾, that is, the state is that He is ﴿the best of judges﴾, because He decides the dispute in the most complete and most perfect manner.

[p-1]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

When his speech, peace be upon him, had ended in this wondrous manner, God, glorified be He, informed of what made clear that his people had found no answer to him at all, because they had turned to resisting by deed, which is a sign of having run out of argument. So He said, beginning a new clause (isti'naf): ﴿The chiefs (al-mala', i.e., the notables) among his people who were arrogant said﴾, that is: the nobles,

﴿who were arrogant﴾, meaning: they brought pride into being, in the manner of one who seeks it with the utmost desire. He singled them out so that the consolation would be complete with His words: ﴿"We will surely expel you, O Shu'ayb, from our town"﴾. He showed their harshness and their coarseness by their saying, ﴿"O Shu'ayb"﴾, without any courtesy or reverence, ﴿"and those who believed"﴾. It is permissible for His words ﴿"with you"﴾ to be connected to "believed" and to "will expel,"

﴿"from our town"﴾, that is: from the place that gathers us, since you separate yourselves from us,

﴿"or you will return"﴾, that is: unless you return, meaning: the outcome will be one of two things, either expulsion or return,

﴿"to our religion"﴾, that is: by remaining silent about us as you were. They did not mean by it a return to disbelief, because he, peace be upon him, had been protected before prophethood, like his fellow prophets, peace be upon them. Rather, they used to count his silence, before he was sent to them, from calling them, reviling their gods and faulting their religion, as being a state within their religion. What they now intend is his return, peace be upon him, to that condition [p-2] and to the contentment of those who followed him in it. Thus their meaning of "return" is literal in all cases.

Since both the expulsion and the restoration were considered grave, God, exalted be He, informed that Shu'ayb rejected it with his words: ﴿He said: "Even if"﴾, that is: will you expel us or restore us, even if we were content with the expulsion and the return, and even if ﴿"we were unwilling"﴾.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 89:

Since the Arabs were the furthest of people from lying in general, the most avoidant of it, and the most averse to it, how much more so would lying about the great ones (be far from them), and how much more so about kings, and how much more so about the King of kings! He attached the lie against God, the Exalted, to returning to their religion, with his words, beginning a new statement for whoever longs to know what happened after this gentle speech and anticipates something else: ﴿We would have invented against God a lie﴾, meaning: we would then be deliberately fabricating, by what we tell you, that God has forbidden disbelief and acquiescence in it,

﴿against God﴾, that is, the One who possesses all greatness,

﴿a lie﴾. Its tanwin may be for magnification, and it may be for belittlement; each has an aspect that the context calls for, which is not hidden.

﴿if we return﴾, that is, even for an hour of time,

﴿to your religion﴾, that is, by our silence, or by my silence and the disbelief of those who followed me while they were disbelievers,

﴿after God has delivered us﴾, that is, the Supreme King, by a miracle breaking custom, from that into which we were worthy of being immersed, following the fathers, grandfathers and clan, by His power and majesty,

﴿from it﴾, that is: if we did that, we would have committed the most abhorrent of abominations with full insight on our part. This is a conditional on what is customarily impossible, and it is of the kind of the saying of al-Ashtar al-Nakha'i:

I remained with my wealth and turned away from lofty things, and met my guests with a frowning face.

If I do not raid the son of Hind, a raid, my soul will never be free of being plundered.

Yet the conditional in the verse is my assessment; the conditional in the poem is my estimation of it, since they informed them that God forbade disbelief and commanded them to warn every disbeliever, so when they abandon that, lying is necessarily entailed.

﴿It is not for us﴾, that is: it is not valid and does not fit ﴿that we return to it﴾, that is, your religion.

Since it is for God, glorified be He, to do what He wills, with nothing obligatory upon Him and nothing abhorrent from Him, He indicated this by His words: ﴿unless God wills﴾. He mentioned the name of the Essence, indicating that all praise belongs to Him by His essence; then He mentioned the attribute of benevolence, seeking refuge from His being intended to humiliate them, so He said: ﴿our Lord﴾, that is, the breaker of custom; so it is for Him. This belongs to the category of reminding oneself of fears and of looking upon the possibility of evil outcomes, out of sincerity in supplicating to God, the Exalted, and seeking refuge in Him and seeking protection from His plotting. For this reason He used the name of majesty, which comprises all the meanings of the Most Beautiful Names, and the attribute of lordship, the call to which in mention is the action performed by a compassionate nurturer. It is as if he said: our return to your religion is not customarily possible, and what is customarily impossible cannot be done except by a power from God; indeed, aspirations are not directed toward it. God, the Exalted, is too generous to return on what He has bestowed upon us of this great matter, and to strip us of this beautiful garment, (p-4) and this is explicit that disbelief occurs by the will of God, indeed it does not occur except by His will. His words ﴿Our Lord has encompassed﴾, that is, the Benefactor to us,

﴿all things in knowledge﴾ is an increase in urging His community to seek refuge and to disavow strength and power, that is: we have no knowledge of the final outcomes of deeds, and knowledge belongs to God; He is the Perfect in knowledge, the Complete in power. This sentence is thus like the reason for the conditioning by the will, [definitively], for whatever may arise from the hope of those addressed for their return; as if it were said: we only made the return conditional on the will because of the deficiency of our knowledge, for perhaps in the breadth of His knowledge there is a third possibility, namely that we remain in the town on our religion and you remain or not, or you agree with us in what we are upon. Thus it befits the one who is nurtured, and it does not befit to affirm with certainty a matter that is yet to come except for God our Lord, because of the comprehensiveness of His knowledge. The verse indicates that He has been, from eternity, knowing of everything, both universals and particulars, because "encompassed" is in the past tense; and it has been mentioned in al-An'am that the words of the Friend (Abraham), peace be upon him, "this" and the verse of al-Kahf are from one informant. And God knows best.
