Since the meaning of this is what has been mentioned, it was alarming to hearts, unsettling to souls, shaking to thoughts, and disturbing to minds by contemplating these dangers that threaten the utmost loss; so it was as if the believers said: what is the course of action and where is the refuge? So He said: ﴿upon God﴾, that is, the One to whom the entire command belongs, and no command is with anyone besides Him, alone, not upon anyone else,

﴿we have put our trust﴾, that is: we have entrusted all our affairs to Him. He is too generous to choose for us other than what is most rightly guided (p-5), and we have disavowed our own power and strength, clung to His power and strength, and made all our affairs wholly borne upon His power, as the agent bears the affair of his principal on his behalf and relieves him of his worry and anxiety.

Since the custom is that the principal informs the agent of what he wants him to do, He followed this with supplication for judgment according to what the apparent state requires, namely the victory of the righteous and the abandonment of the wrongdoer, so He said: ﴿our Lord﴾, that is, O You who benefit us,

﴿decide﴾, that is, judge ﴿between us﴾. And since he intended to win their compassion for their happiness, he said: ﴿and between our people﴾, and in this is an indication of his inclination to supplicate for their guidance, and a courtesy of not stating explicitly what he was not permitted to state,

﴿in truth﴾, that is: by the decisive matter in dealing with each of the righteous and the wrongdoer according to what he deserves in law and custom, such that each party has a door leading it to the utmost end of its affair. This is the station of fairness. From the allusion of his words the care for his people is known, and from his expression the fairness toward himself is known; had he intended to prefer himself and his followers, he would have prayed that they be treated with favor and that their opponents be treated with justice. The verse informs that He, the Exalted, may do what He wills: abandoning the wrongdoer, granting victory to the oppressed, punishing the disobedient, rewarding the obedient, and the reverse of that.

﴿He is not questioned about what He does﴾ [al-Anbiya': 23], because He is the Perfect in dominion, the Great in sovereignty, the All-encompassing in power, the Wise, the All-Aware. It is also possible that the meaning is: we will not return to what we were upon of silence concerning your calling to God and forbidding you from acts of error; for we have been commanded to warn you, except that God wills our silence by a command He brings to us in that (p-6) for a benefit whose wisdom He has decreed and which our knowledge falls short of. So when He wills that and commands us to it, we comply; to Him belong creation and command.

When he alluded to supplication for his people, he alluded, by conjunction with no apparent antecedent, to the sense that the implied meaning is: "So You are the best of the merciful": ﴿and You are the best of those who open﴾, that is, for those upon whom doors have been closed and who find no deliverer.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 90:

When the answer to the distinction (al-fasl), which was built upon nullifying favour (al-fadl) and manifesting justice (al-'adl), had been completed, He, glorified is He, mentioned their statement after it, conjoining it (ʿaṭfan) to what had passed of their statement or of his statement. The original form would have been to say: "And they said," but He made manifest the description by nobility (al-sharaf) as an indication that it was he who had driven them to the outcome of arrogance (al-istikbar), which is disbelief (al-kufr). Then they were not content with this until they added to it the declaring of others to be disbelievers (takfir), so He said: ﴿And the chiefs (al-mala') said﴾, that is, the eminent ones (al-akabir),

﴿who disbelieved﴾, those who fill the eyes with their appearance and the hearts with awe. So pride (al-takabbur) led them to the point that they ﴿disbelieved﴾.

Since it was improbable that his own kinsmen would shun what he had brought them of good out of envy (hasad), or suspicion (ittiham), or other than these two, it might have been thought that these people who treated him with this error were strangers to him. So He said: ﴿from his people﴾, as a clarification that favour (al-fadl) is in the hand of Allah, so He may give it to the hated and distant, and withhold it from the beloved and near,

﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾ [al-Qasas: 56]. They prepared the way for the oath (al-qasam) by their saying: ﴿If you follow Shu'ayb﴾, that is, O followers, among those who have not yet believed, ﴿Shu'ayb﴾, or you abandon what you are upon, which your fathers bequeathed to you. They answered the oath with what stood in place of the answer of the condition (sadda ʿan jawab al-shart), by His saying: ﴿then you would indeed be ﴾, that is, at the time of following him,

﴿losers (khasirun)﴾, that is, because you have exchanged the religion of your fathers for another and have forfeited the benefits of cheating in measure and weight (al-bakhs wa-l-tatfif) and of highway robbery (qat' al-subul).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 91:

When their sin was complete through misguidance and misleading others, they became deserving of being seized. So He said: ﴿So the earthquake seized them﴾, meaning: as a consequence of these their statements and deeds, the earthquake seized them. ﴿The earthquake﴾, that is, the great tremor in the hearts or in the dwellings, which was a cause of the shout or was caused by it.

﴿So they were in their abode﴾, that is, their dwellings. The secret of using the singular for it has already been mentioned.

﴿Lying prostrate﴾, that is, kneeling on their knees, or remaining in their places, with no movement in them. This is less than what happened to the Prophet ﷺ when the angels descended at Hunayn, so that the disbelievers would hear in their insides something like the sound of a pebble in a basin; and less than what his opponent would feel of terror from a month's journey behind him and a month's journey in front of him. And because he was the Prophet of mercy, that did not require destruction but rather deliverance.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 92:

When Allah, glorified is He, informed of their destruction and of the words and deeds that caused it, and since there is no hidden benefit in the hearts, through the depiction of the one who delivers [the greatness] to the minds, [He] summarized that, mentioning that what befell them specifically was what they attributed to the believers of loss, so He said: ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb﴾, that is, they attributed to him lying in what he said on Our behalf, and We supported him in it with clear proofs,

﴿as if﴾, that is, they were the ones specially singled out for destruction, until it was as if they,

﴿had never prospered﴾, that is, had never dwelt and settled, and their standing had ceased, being heedless of joys, singing, and self-sufficiency from the homes, which are the dwellings, and self-sufficiency,

﴿therein﴾, that is, in the abode, because of their denial.

And since the denial of truthful ones, especially messengers, is of utmost heinousness, He repeated it as a signal to that and as an announcement that it was a cause for them of something greater than the destruction of bodies, in contrast to what belief caused for the believers, so He said: ﴿Those who denied Shu'ayb﴾, that is, so his denial was the cause of their destruction,

﴿they were﴾, that is, by reason of the denial as well,

﴿the ones﴾, that is, specifically,

﴿who were the losers﴾, that is, they lost their souls just as they lost their bodies; for everything else they are even more losing. As for those who followed him, no loss befell them. In this resumption, beginning and repetition there is emphasis in refuting the claim of the chiefs to their followers, a belittling of their opinions, a mockery of their counsel to their people, and a magnification of what befell them.

When that abode became a place of wrath, he withdrew from it, as was the custom of the prophets before him, peace be upon them. So He said: ﴿Then he turned away from them﴾ after the descent of the punishment, and before it, upon seeing its signs, going off to another place to worship his Lord there.

﴿And he said﴾ grieving over what he had lost of their guidance:

﴿O my people﴾, that is, O my kinsmen and the people nearest to me.

﴿Indeed I have conveyed to you﴾. Perhaps he used the plural because of the great number of miracles that came to them, so He said: ﴿the messages of my Lord﴾, that is, of the One who has been good to me by saving me and those who followed me from your punishment, by granting us success in what pleases Him.

﴿And I gave you counsel﴾, that is, I sincerely offered counsel (p-9) ﴿to you﴾, that is, specifically.

Since this conveys what human nature is inclined to feel of sorrow over one's family and kinsmen, He followed it with his disapproval of himself, saying: ﴿So how should I grieve﴾, that is, how should I feel intense sorrow,

﴿over a people who are disbelievers﴾, that is, who are deeply steeped in disbelief. Thus it is known that he grieved over them because of their nearness to him and the loss of faith for them, not grieving over them because of their disbelief. The repetition of these five stories in this order in many surahs of the Qur'an, without the story of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), who is the greatest of them, is for the sake of their unity in that their eyes were gratified by seeing the downfall of those who opposed them. As for Ibrahim (peace be upon him), the text in His saying: ﴿Indeed I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [al-Saffat: 99] states that he departed from among his people before their punishment, and He did not make his case like theirs in gratifying his eyes by the destruction of those who denied him in his presence. He is the most excellent of them, because what occurred in his story is greater in excellence. This matches what befell his son, the most excellent of mankind, our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). Consider His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33], and you will know the honour in this station, and that the matter is as it has been said: "For one eye, a thousand eyes are repaid, and it is honoured."

When Glorified is He had presented in summary the warning, with what the nations shared in terms of destruction, by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And how many a town have We destroyed﴾ [al-A'raf: 4], and the verse...

Then He followed this—after presenting what was needed ahead of the arrangement (nazm) that was previously pointed out—with a detailed account of the punishment that each nation was singled out for, which befell them in the manner of a just recompense. He followed that with another summary, broader than the first, in a striking style that indicates His constant custom and His settled way in describing the condition of these nations that He mentioned and others besides them, lest it be thought that the condition of others was other than their condition. So He made clear that all of them follow one path, and that the cause of their annihilation is one: denial (al-takdhib) and arrogance toward the truth (al-istikbar), so that the summary would serve as the governing principles and universal rules (al-dawabit wa al-qawa'id al-kulliyya) that apply to the particulars. This insight into what results in benefit or harm, and the avoidance of being deceived by the conditions of the ones led on gradually to ruin (al-mustadrajin) who are wicked, serves to console (al-tasliyah) His Prophet (ﷺ) and to bring him comfort (al-ta'siyah). It precedes the story of Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both, because that story is lengthy, and in order to hasten the mention of what it contains of the outcomes of warning, through His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We did not send﴾, that is: We sent this one and it happened thus, and that one and it happened thus, and "We did not send" means: by Our greatness,

﴿into a town﴾, that is: from the towns of those (peoples) and others,

﴿any prophet﴾, that is: from the prophets who came before you, ﴿but﴾ what We tell of their being made to fear Our might was that We ﴿seized﴾, that is: by Our majesty,

﴿its people﴾, that is: with a seizing of subjugation and might, meaning: because of their arrogance toward the truth,

﴿with misfortune﴾, that is: the subjugation of men, ﴿and adversity﴾, that is: sickness and poverty,

﴿that they might humble themselves﴾, that is: so that their state at the time of hardship would be the state of one whose humbling, submission, and lowliness is hoped for before One who does not remove that from him except Him, even if the humbling is at its lowest degree, as the idgham (assimilation) indicates, because that suffices for deliverance from the punishment of the warning which is the theme of this surah, unlike what passed in al-An'am.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 95:

When they did not humble themselves sincerely from their hearts, acknowledging the truth to its people as it is due, He lured them on by pouring out blessings. He said, pointing to the length of the period of trial and their deeming the removal of that trial unlikely: ﴿Then We replaced﴾, and the manifestation of greatness supports the second possibility. ﴿In place of﴾, meaning: We made in place of ﴿the evil﴾, that is, the retribution,

﴿the good﴾, that is, the blessing. He made clear that He extended the blessing by His saying: ﴿until they multiplied﴾, meaning: they increased in number and their blessings multiplied, yet they did not give thanks,

﴿and they said﴾, attributing the matter to other than its people: ﴿Indeed, adversity and ease have touched our fathers﴾, meaning: hardship and prosperity, and comfort and blessing, believing that this is merely the custom of time and not the act of a free, choosing Agent.

When they did not take heed or come to know that this is from One who loves that His door not be turned away from and that His court not be neglected, and they thought that this was the habit of the age and the action of time, and they persisted in their corruption in both hardship and ease, the following was consequent upon this: ﴿So We seized them﴾, meaning: by Our greatness, with the most severe and dreadful seizing, outwardly and inwardly,

﴿suddenly﴾, meaning: unexpectedly, so that repentance would no longer benefit them. He emphasized the meaning of suddenness, confirming His matter, by His saying: ﴿while they did not perceive﴾. Whoever hears this is obliged to hasten to turn back from every act of disobedience he is engaged in, out of fear of being seized suddenly.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 96:

When Allah (Exalted) had explained what their saying was that caused the sudden seizure, He explained what would have been the opposite of their saying, causing blessings for them had it occurred, with His words: ﴿And if the people of the towns﴾, meaning these towns whose accounts We have related,

﴿had believed﴾, meaning in what their messengers brought them, [p. 12] ﴿and had been mindful of God﴾, meaning they feared God's command and placed between themselves and His displeasure a shield of obedience to Him, so that they persisted in their faith,

﴿We would have opened for them blessings﴾, meaning lasting goods that no one could remove,

﴿from the heaven﴾, meaning by rain, which comes down like the mouths of waterskins and the like,

﴿and the earth﴾, meaning by thick vegetation and what is near to it. The recitation of Ibn 'Amir (a canonical mode of recitation) with the doubled letter indicates the abundance of those blessings. The root meaning of barakah (blessing) is persistence in good.

Since what the word "law" (if) conveyed was, in effect, that they did not believe, He expressed it with His words: ﴿But they denied﴾, meaning denial was their habit and their nature, so for that reason they did not confirm Our messengers in anything. Since denial is the place of coarseness and obstinacy, which is the cause of not considering the evidence, He made the punishment its consequence, saying: ﴿So We seized them﴾, meaning by Our majesty,

﴿for what﴾, meaning because of what ﴿they were earning﴾, meaning by their wicked natures, through the deeds suited to them.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 97:

Since they had gone far astray in their error, in making prosperity and adversity a cause for feeling secure from the cunning (makr) of God, He spoke, rebuking them for their sense of security and linking it by the conjunction (ʿaṭf) to "they denied," because it is the cause of the error and it is the cause of the security. So He said: ﴿Do the people of the towns feel secure﴾, meaning: they denied, forgetting Our deeds that terrify with harms and encourage with delights, and so they felt secure ﴿that Our might will come upon them﴾, meaning: that which arises from Our greatness, which none forgets except a loser, ﴿by night﴾, meaning: during the night, while they have taken their rest in their houses. And since sleep is one single state that overwhelms the senses and thus requires stability, He expressed it with the nominal form that indicates permanence, saying: ﴿while they are sleeping﴾, meaning: in the utmost state of heedlessness of it.

Since someone might say, "If He had come upon them while they were awake, they could have defended themselves!", He says: ﴿Do the people of the cities feel secure that Our punishment will not come upon them by day,﴾ that is, gathered or dispersed, for there is no difference with Us in that, ﴿while they are at play?﴾ That is, at a time of their ease, the gathering of their strength and their vigor. And since wakefulness entails movement, He used the present tense in His words ﴿while they are at play﴾, meaning that their play is renewed moment by moment at that time. In this there is a rebuke to them, by attributing to them the state of children of intellect, having no attention for anything other than play.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 99:

Since their error, in which they attributed the matter to other than its rightful people, was the most abominable error, for it entailed denial (ta'til) of God's attributes and what leads from it of falsehoods, he repeated the rebuke against them in a manner more intense than the first. So he said, giving as the cause of the rebuke what this discourse established of the greatness about which no person of intellect disputes: ﴿Do they then feel secure from the plan of God?﴾ That is, from His action which resembles a plan, by seizing a person from where he does not perceive, through gradual leading on (istidraj) with what He wills of blessings and retributions. He made the following consequence of this: ﴿None feels secure from the plan of God﴾ That is, the plan than which there is no greater, so no command of His is turned back ﴿except the people who are lost﴾ That is, those whose powers were the cause of their being well-versed (i'raqa) in harmful deeds and destructive traits.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 100:

When the state of the disbelievers was made clear, both in summary and in detail, by what preceded, and the purpose of that was to be a lesson for the listeners, and their being seized by misfortune and adversity, while their lives were preserved, their souls and their understanding kept intact after the destruction of those before them, in some of what befell them of that, and their inheritance of the land after them, a condition in which they find themselves within the sphere of those from whom fear is hoped for, which calls for humility, and knowledge with certainty that the One who does that is Allah, and that had He willed He would have destroyed them for their sins, or veiled their understanding such that they became like cattle, hearing nothing but call and cry, so their hearing, where there is no understanding, is like no hearing, yet they made that a cause for security; He denounced this for them by His saying: ﴿Do they then feel secure﴾ [al-A'raf: 97] to the end of it. Then He denounced for them their failure to draw inference from the power (of Allah), saying, conjoining [with] "Do they then feel secure":

﴿Has it not become clear﴾, i.e., has it not been made manifest to them, the seizing of the earlier nations with misfortune and adversity, and then their destruction if they do not take heed,

﴿to those who inherit the land﴾. He placed the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, for generality, and to attach the judgment to the attribute, and as an indication of their dullness, through their not searching out the reports, so that they might know from them what harms and what benefits, and so not be like cattle. For if they had reflected upon their own state, and the state of those who inherited their land, and the state of the land, that would have sufficed them for guidance to the right path.

And since their inheritance was not all-encompassing of time, He used the preposition, saying: ﴿after its people﴾. Then He mentioned the object of "yahdi" by His saying: "an", meaning: that We,

﴿if We willed﴾, i.e., at whatever time We desired,

﴿to smite them for their sins﴾, i.e., a smiting by which We would annihilate them, as We did to those who inherited their land. And since this was a warning to those existing after the destroyed, among them Quraysh and the rest of the Arabs who are addressed by this Qur'an, as though what they were warned of had not yet occurred, He conjoined to "We smote" His saying: ﴿and We seal upon their hearts﴾, i.e., by removing their intellects until they become like cattle. And for this He made His saying a consequence of it:

﴿so they do not hear﴾, i.e., they do not hear with understanding. He expressed the smiting in the past tense, indicating the swiftness of destruction together with its being one single thing not divisible, and He expressed the sealing in the present tense, as an intimation of renewal, such that no time passes except that they are in it in a fresh sealing.

When that had been completed in this most magnificent manner and most eloquent and wise arrangement, and these towns were such that the Arabs knew them and saw them, He pointed to them, urging reflection (i'tibar, taking a lesson) from them. And since their people deserved to be distanced from and fled from, He referred to them with a demonstrative of distance and said: ﴿Those towns﴾, that is, the dwelling places of the five tribes. It is possible that the distance is due to the greatness of the punishment that befell their people, and His words, clarifying their condition, support this: ﴿We relate to you﴾.

Since the sensible person is satisfied with the least thing, He magnified the matter by saying that their reports are beyond counting, and that what has been related of them suffices for the one who takes heed. So He said: ﴿of their reports﴾, that is, their great and terrifying reports, corresponding to reality, one after another, as one does who follows a trace. He made the pronoun feminine because seeing the towns themselves has a role in knowing the reports of their people.

Since the situation was one of wonder at their denial after that clarification, someone might imagine that they had not been given a clear proof. So God the Exalted bore witness to the Messengers, peace be upon them, confirming the words of those among them who said: "Indeed a clear sign has come to you," by His saying: ﴿And certainly﴾, that is, while the state is that indeed ﴿there came to them﴾, that is, the people of the towns, since they are the ones directly intended,

﴿their messengers﴾, that is, those whom We sent to them,

﴿with the clear signs. But﴾, that is, it did not result from that, through the cause of Our sealing their hearts, anything except that they ﴿were not﴾ granted success

﴿to believe﴾, that is, when the signs came. He has stressed the incompatibility of their state with faith by the lam (of purpose) and by the verb "to be" in the most complete emphasis, ﴿in what﴾, that is, in that which ﴿they denied﴾, that is, they denied it. [Omitting it is more effective in rebuke than mere denial, and more suited to the aim of the surah.]

Since their denial did not encompass all of past time, He introduced the preposition, saying: ﴿before﴾, that is, before the Messengers came to them, or with their denial, which occurred from them toward the Messengers regarding what they brought from God, before being seized suddenly; or before the coming of the Messengers with the signs, for at the first coming they confronted them with denial. Thus they were held to account for denying the truth without examining evidence, by nature [upon their hearts; then the Messengers brought them miracles, but they persisted in that denial and stood firm in that sealing], along with their own desires. Their arrogance and their intense stubbornness prevented them from faith, lest it be said: they first feared what they had committed of denial, so they were in it without insight; or they feared a second time what the Messengers threatened them with, so they entered out of cowardice into what they knew to be false. So this adornment for them became a sealing upon their hearts. It is as if it were said: Does such a wonder occur in anyone like this? It was said: Yes, like what We sealed upon their hearts, until with understanding they no longer benefit, as if they do not understand, as if they do not hear.

﴿Thus does God seal﴾, that is, He who unites the attributes of greatness and the qualities of majesty, by making that which constitutes rust, along with His greatness,

﴿upon the hearts of the disbelievers﴾, that is, everyone who covers the light of intellect God has given him with what his soul calls him to of desire, persisting deeply in that attribute, so he abandons God's signs.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 102:

Since breaking a covenant is the most heinous of things, especially among the Arabs, He said, conjoining it with "So they were not" (fa-ma kanu): ﴿And We did not find﴾, that is: in the world of witnessing (ʿalam al-shahada),

﴿for most of them﴾, that is: of the people, and He emphasised the comprehensiveness by saying: ﴿any covenant﴾, in accordance with what was with Us in the world of the unseen (ʿalam al-ghayb). This refers either to the covenant on the day of ﴿Am I not your Lord?﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 172], if that was in its literal sense, or to what they do in times of hardship by way of desisting from sins and pledging to be grateful: ﴿If You deliver us from this, we will surely be among the grateful﴾ [Yunus: 22]; or to the establishment of proofs through the bestowal of intellects and the setting up of evidences. Thus, by setting them up and clarifying them to the intellects, it is as if He took the covenant from whoever has reason that he will exert effort in reflection and will not go beyond what sound reasoning has shown him.

﴿And indeed﴾, that is: and indeed We,

﴿found﴾, that is: knew, in the world of witnessing,

﴿most of them to be defiantly disobedient (fasiqin)﴾, that is: departing from the circle of covenants, transgressing what has restrained them from the limit, and going astray in that, in accordance with what We knew of them in the world of the unseen. And We did not bring it forth in the world of witnessing except to establish the proof against them by it, according to what they recognise among themselves in the courses of their customs and the perceptions of their intellects.

When the explanation of this general summary, which captivates men's hearts, was complete, he followed it with the disclosure (p-١٨) of what came after the story of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, namely the story of Musa, peace be upon him, the son-in-law of Shu'ayb, [with] Pharaoh and his people. It serves as evidence for the verses of the general summary (ijmal), just as the earlier stories served as evidence for the generalities at the beginning of the surah. The story of Pharaoh includes being seized with adversity and hardship, then being favored with ease and prosperity, then being seized suddenly because of their persistent adherence to misguidance after the clear disclosure and explanation of what was upon their hearts of sealing, and of what their appetites had led them to of wickedness. It seems he separated it from the earlier stories to draw attention to it and to alert the reader to its lofty rank, because the miracles of its bearer are among the miracles of those before him, and the ignorance of those he dealt with was greater and more shameful than the ignorance of those nations. For this reason he introduced it with the particle of distance, despite the closeness of its time to the one before it, indicating the remoteness of its rank because of the wonders it contains and the desirable and strange matters it includes. For this reason he extended the field for it and loosened the reins of the steed within its context, saying: ﴿Then We sent﴾, that is, by Our greatness,

﴿after them﴾, that is, after the messengers mentioned and the nations destroyed,

﴿Musa with Our signs﴾, that is, those which deserve greatness by their being attributed to Us, by which prophethood was established, to ﴿Pharaoh﴾, which is a proper name (ʿalam jins) for the kings of Egypt, like Kisra for the kings of Persia and Qayṣar for the kings of Rome. The name of Pharaoh at the time of Musa, peace be upon him, was Qabus, and it has been said: al-Walid ibn Mus'ab ibn al-Rayyan.

﴿and his chiefs﴾, that is, the great men of his people. He singled them out because when they submit, those beneath them submit, so they are in effect the intended recipients, and sending to them is sending to all.

When the wrongs had led them [to it], He said: ﴿so they wronged﴾, that is, they fell into something like darkness until they placed things in other than their proper places, so they placed denial where acknowledgment belonged,

﴿by them﴾, that is, because of seeing them, out of fear for their leadership and their perishable kingdom that it might slip from their hands. Since this was among the most astonishing of wonders, namely that the cause of justice becomes the cause of wrongdoing, and since this wrongdoing was the greatest corruption, he consequently said, expressing wonder: ﴿So look﴾, that is, with the eye of insight,

﴿how was the end of the corrupters﴾, that is, the final outcome of their affair. Thus in this verse, despite its brevity, he summarized their whole story despite its length, and he placed the mention of the signs first out of concern for them and because they are the evidence for the soundness of the claim of resurrection.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 104:

Since the implied sense is an continuation (ʿaṭf) upon ﴿so they wronged them﴾ [al-A'raf: 103], and Musa placed things in their proper places, he expressed this by his saying: ﴿And Musa said, "O Pharaoh"﴾. He addressed him with what would please him, in compliance with the command of Allah the Exalted to him that he should speak gently in his address, because "Pharaoh" is a title of praise for whoever ruled Egypt.

When he (peace be upon him) came to them, they knew of his trustworthiness, his truthfulness, the greatness of his standing, the nobility of his character, the honour of his lineage and the excellence of his background, and Pharaoh was the most knowledgeable of them concerning him, since he had been raised in his care. This situation called for the message to be delivered to them without emphasis. However, since sending from Allah is an extremely great matter, and since the purpose (of the mission) was to free the path of the Children of Israel, and since Pharaoh was stingy about this, he emphasised it to some degree and said: ﴿Indeed, I am a messenger﴾. Then he specified the One who sent him by his saying: ﴿from the Lord of the worlds﴾, meaning: the One who does good to all of them, including you, by bringing them into existence and nurturing them. Thus it is an admonition to whoever hears it that Pharaoh is a created being who is subjugated.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 105:

When he (Moses) had sent him (Pharaoh) away with this, which he claimed of lordship, indicating his equality with the rest of the worlds, both those who speak and those who are mute, and this being far from submitting to this speech, he followed it, by way of emphasis, with his saying, beginning a new sentence to explain what is incumbent upon the Messenger: ﴿It is my duty not to say about Allah﴾ — i.e., "Him to whom belongs all perfection, and there is no greatness or majesty besides Him" — ﴿except the truth﴾ — i.e., the established truth about which no dispute at all is possible, owing to the miracles that confirm it. The sum and implication of the expression is: it is incumbent upon my saying, which I attribute to Allah, that it be nothing but the truth, i.e., not untrue. For this reason he expressed it with the Greatest Name, which encompasses all attributes. The reading of Nafi' with the doubling of the ya' of the first person in "ʿalā" (ʿalayya) has the same meaning, because whoever has a duty (ḥaqqa ʿalayhi shayʾ) is bound in respect of his speech (ḥaqqa ʿalā kalāmihi).

Since the situation at that time required the expectation that Moses, peace be upon him, would produce a clear proof of the soundness of his mission, it was as if it were said: "What is the proof of your truthfulness?" He said, beginning with the particle of expectation and affirmation: ﴿I have certainly come to you﴾ — i.e., all of you, not singling out any one of you — ﴿with a clear proof﴾ (p-21), a proof of my mission and of my saying the truth — ﴿from your Lord﴾ — i.e., the One who benefits you with every blessing you see in your possession, from your creation and your provision, and His restraining the nations from snatching this kingdom from you and destroying you. That clear proof is the miracle. Thus he repeated the explanation in this speech, to show that Pharaoh is not as he claims, because he is a creature being sustained (marbūb), with no difference between him and the rest of the worlds in this respect.

Since it is known that a man of his complete intellect and nobility of disposition would not claim, in those assemblies, anything but the truth, together with what he pointed out of the clarification that Allah alone is God just as He alone bestows favour, it was as if he had displayed the clear proof, the least of which was their restraint from destroying them. He then followed this by asking for the outcome, informing them of the ultimate aim he desired from them, with his saying, as a consequence of mere this report which he had already made its content effective: ﴿So send with me the Children of Israel﴾ — i.e., O Pharaoh — meaning: the cause of my producing the proof for the soundness of what I have said is that the command concerning what I came for, namely their sending with me, is the command of one who has authority, with the production of proof, so that we may all go to [the House of] the Holy Land, the homeland of our fathers, which Allah swore to them that He would bequeath to their descendants. In making that the outcome of the sending to him is an indication that his mission is confined to his own people.

Then it was as if it were said: "What did Pharaoh say in reply to this clear command?" So it is said: "He said," turning away from it and concealing it from them, out of fear of its harm (ghā'ila) among those who know Musa, peace be upon him, in the truest knowledge, expressing it with the particle of doubt (adāt al-shakk) so as to halt them: ﴿If you have come with a sign﴾, that is, a proof of the truth of your message, ﴿then produce it﴾. He thereby gave the impression that he did not understand anything except that what was meant was that he would bring it about, without there being in his earlier speech any indication of its truthfulness. He emphasized the vagueness and the doubt with his saying: ﴿If you are﴾, that is, by nature and disposition, ﴿of the truthful﴾, that is, among the company of the people of truthfulness, those who are deeply rooted in it, so that your claim may be valid and established in my sight.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 107:

When he (Allah) had presented this request in a manner that indicated that he (Pharaoh) was doubtful about the matter, Allah, exalted is He, informed that He suddenly brought about the manifestation of the sign, indicating this by the particle fa' (fa', "then") which expresses causation and immediate succession without any delay. So He said, concerning the action of Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿So he threw down his staff﴾, and concerning His own action, glorified is He: ﴿and behold, it was a serpent, plainly visible﴾. That is, the staff became a serpent (tho'ban, a large serpent) manifest in its size and the swiftness of its movement, to such an extent that, because of how plainly visible it was, it was as if it were calling out to the people so that its matter would become clear to them. It also clarified the truthfulness of the one through whose action it came about, in all that he had said. It was narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that it was a serpent with bristling hair, its mouth gaping, between its two jaws eighty cubits; it placed its lower jaw on the ground and its upper jaw on the top of the palace wall, then it turned towards Pharaoh, and he leapt from his throne fleeing and soiled himself. It charged at the people, and they fled and cried out, and twenty-five thousand of them died; some of them trampled others. Pharaoh cried out: "O Musa, take it, and I will believe [in you]," so he took it and it returned to being a staff.

Then he said: "Do you have another sign?" He said: "Yes." ﴿And he drew out his hand﴾, that is, he took it out of his pocket after he had shown him it scorched and dark, as it had been while it was at his side, ﴿and behold, it was white﴾. He drew attention to the lasting whiteness of it and to the increase of its wonder with his words ﴿to the onlookers﴾. Abu Hayyan said: that is, to the spectators. And in mentioning that there is an indication of the great whiteness of it, because wonder only comes upon them if its whiteness is outside the ordinary custom. Ibn 'Abbas said: it became a radiant light that illuminated what is between the heaven and the earth, having a sheen like the flash of lightning, so they fell down upon their faces. How wondrous is the matter of these two great miracles: one of them is in himself, and that is the white hand, and the other is outside himself, and it is the staff which he holds in his hand. By these two he combined the change of essences from wood to animal, and the change of accidents from brown to brilliant white, so they were two signs indicating the permissibility of both matters. End.

The Nazm al-Durar is by al-Biqa'i; I'll translate the passage as given.

When he had brought the clear proof and established the manifest evidence, the circumstance required asking about what they had put forward as their statement in reply to him, so he said: ﴿The chiefs among the people of Pharaoh said﴾, i.e., the eminent ones, ﴿"Indeed, this is a skilled sorcerer"﴾, i.e., this which you have seen, O people, of his imagery is something with no reality, so do not hasten to follow him.

And since that was outside what they had become accustomed to from sorcerers, they said: ﴿"Knowing"﴾ (p-24), i.e., with regard to what they are engaged in, reaching in his knowledge a great degree, so this is what came of what you have seen from him, beyond the usual. It is as if Pharaoh said this at the outset, as in Surat al-Shura, and they took it from him and hastened to repeat his words, one of them saying it to another, to make known that they were in utmost obedience to him, out of fear for their leadership, confirming the saying of Him, the Exalted: ﴿So he made light of his people and they obeyed him﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 54]. The attribution of the speech to them is chosen here because the context is the argument for the corruption of the majority, whereas there the context is different; for if He, glorified is He, had sent down a sign they would have submitted to it, just as Pharaoh submitted upon seeing what he saw from Musa, peace be upon him, until he was content for himself to address his subjects, by his claim, with words implying that they had some command over him. Therefore attributing the saying to him is better, because victory in confronting the head is more manifest, and the submission of the neck is more vast and greater.

When they had bewildered them until they were halted from the eagerness they had sensed in them to follow him, by claiming that he is a sorcerer, they made them recoil from that and frightened them by saying that he wants to put his people, who had been their slaves, in charge of them and drive them out of their lands, which are for their bodies what their bodies are for their souls, through his saying: ﴿He wants to drive you out﴾, meaning, O Copts, ﴿from your land﴾, meaning this one which your forefathers established for you and on which your livelihood depends. And since the context was to explain their wickedness, he omitted their saying "with his sorcery" in the other place ﴿with his sorcery﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 35], to convey their haste in settling the matter to harm him [indicating their excess in wickedness, while knowing that he is truthful and not a sorcerer] (p-25).

Since the aim of this speech was to win over the addressees, they sought to win them over after they had halted them. Then they frightened them with what they had set in motion from the previous address, namely their saying: ﴿So what do you advise?﴾, meaning, what do you say in this counsel, O lords, so that it may be carried out.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on Surah 7, verse 111:

Since it was as if it were said: "Upon what did their opinion settle?" it was said: "Upon postponing the matter until the sorcerers are gathered for the contest." Almighty God informed—indicating that the origin of the speech of the chiefs (al-mala') came from him—that they turned to him, addressing him, drawing attention to those who conveyed it to him, glorifying him, attributing the matter to him by His saying: ﴿They said﴾, i.e., [the chiefs] of Pharaoh [after the intention had settled in their minds], ﴿Put him off﴾, i.e., Moses, peace be upon him, ﴿and his brother﴾, i.e., postpone the two of them, giving us relief from this strait for a while, until we look into their affair, ﴿and send into the cities﴾, i.e., [from] the kingdom of Egypt, ﴿gatherers﴾, who will gather for you the sorcerers and collect them from every deep valley. Al-hashr (gathering) is the assembling by compulsion.

﴿They will bring you every﴾ [And since the indication of the context regarding Pharaoh's eagerness was less than in al-Shu'ara', owing to what the situation required in each of the two surahs, the majority (al-Jumhur) recited]: ﴿skilled sorcerer who has knowledge﴾, meaning: one who has reached the utmost in knowledge of sorcery. In the recitation of [Hamzah and al-Kisa'i]: "sahhar" (sahhar, an intensive form), an additional emphasis of exaggeration as well [because they saw Pharaoh's anxiety in general]. This indicates that sorcerers in that era were in great abundance among them, and it indicates that human nature inclines toward opposition (mu'aradah, contesting a challenge with its like). So whenever it is possible, the claim of prophethood is refuted, and when it is impossible, the claim is established.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 113:

Since the implied sense was: "Delay their affair and send [agents], as they said," they gathered whomever they could find of them. He joined to it His saying: ﴿And the sorcerers came to Pharaoh﴾. When the listener became eager to learn their news, He answered him, beginning a new clause: ﴿They said﴾, that is, to Pharaoh, when they had come before him, seeking assurance for their own benefit, making him understand that they were the victors, with nothing preventing them from that except that he was not fair to them, driving their speech, in the recitation of the majority, in the manner of a question, out of courtesy toward him in seeking reward: ﴿Will we indeed have a reward﴾ [al-A'raf: 113 / ash-Shu'ara: 41], and they emphasized the request, in order to draw out the promise under conditions of denial: ﴿if we are indeed﴾, that is, exclusively, ﴿the victors﴾. Whoever reads it as a declarative intends the sense of a question. They are: Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Hafs from 'Asim.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 114:

﴿Qāla﴾ i.e., Pharaoh, ﴿Naʿam﴾ i.e., "Yes, for you there is a reward," the news of which is emphasized; and he added to the emphasis of the statement by what he gave them, desiring to make his words firm, ﴿wa-innakum﴾ i.e., in addition to that, ﴿la-mina al-muqarrabīn﴾ i.e., "you will be among those brought near," in my presence in the court.

They (the magicians) finished their dialogue with him, and the listener became eager to hear what they said to Musa, peace be upon him. So He resumed their speech as a reply, saying: ﴿They said﴾, beginning with his name, ﴿O Musa﴾, showing him courtesy as is the custom of intelligent adversaries before the contest begins, in a context that conveys that their intention is that the throwing be first: that is, their saying: ﴿Either you throw﴾, meaning: you first (p-27) what you wish to throw, for the contest in demonstrating the validity of your claim, ﴿or we will be﴾, meaning: by ourselves, ﴿the throwers﴾, meaning: what is with us first.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 116:

When Musa (peace be upon him) understood their intention from what this composition expressed of the reality of its meaning, through the emphasis of their connected pronoun with the separated one, the definition of the predicate, and the insertion of the separator (al-fasl), and he was confident in God Most High, in what He had promised him, acting in accordance with His purpose, there being no difference between going first or later, he answered their request, and this is more effective in belittling their status. So God, glorified is He, resumed the report about him with His saying: ﴿He said: "Throw"﴾, meaning: you, O sorcerers, throw what you intend to throw, and this is a command of challenge (amr ta'jiz).

When he gave them permission, they hastened to do that, as the conjunction with fa' (then) in His saying indicates: ﴿So when they threw﴾, meaning: what they had prepared for sorcery, ﴿they bewitched the eyes of the people﴾, meaning: they deceived their perception so that they imagined to them what has no reality, namely that their ropes and staffs, which were very numerous indeed, began to move and some of them coiled around others. They also sent a group calling out: "O people, beware!" ﴿and they struck terror into them﴾, meaning: they produced fear in them, bringing it about as one who desires it and seeks it with utmost eagerness.

When this was said, one might have thought that they feared something of which one would not normally be afraid, so God Most High, explaining that they were excused in their fear, said: ﴿And they came with a great sorcery﴾. The author of Kitab al-Zina said: Sorcery (al-sihr) takes many forms; among it is the affecting of the eye (al-akhdh bil-'ayn), and among it is that by which a man is separated from his wife, and among it is other than that. Its root is derived from pretending to be something by falsehood and turning a matter from its true direction, as we have mentioned from the language of the Arabs.

When the matter had reached its height and the longing to see what Moses (peace be upon him) would do had intensified, He said, informing about it, by way of conjunction (ʿaṭf, the connecting of one clause to another by a conjunction) upon ﴿And they came﴾ [al-Aʿrāf 7:116], ﴿And We revealed﴾, that is, manifesting Our greatness before the eyes of the witnesses, with a thing that no one can match: ﴿to Moses: "Throw down your staff"﴾, that is, so he threw it. ﴿Then behold, it﴾, from the moment he threw it, ﴿was swallowing﴾, that is, devouring with a true, intense, and very swift swallowing, as indicated by the deletion of the (تاء) taa' in (تَلْقَفُ, talqafu). It also indicates the abundance of what they did by His saying: ﴿what they were faking﴾, that is, they were renewing, at the moment of their throwing, their deception and their turning of it away from its reality. So it swallowed what had filled the valley of staves and ropes. Then Moses (peace be upon him) took it, and behold, it returned to what it had been, with nothing of its size added to what it had been. In this context, which informs us of Moses (peace be upon him) remaining steadfast after what he had seen of their magic, and of the revelation to him, there is an explanation of his good manners (peace be upon him) in that tight situation, and of his calm, under the closeness (of danger) and with his Sender, glorified is He, until His noble commands appeared.

When it became known that what they had produced was only an illusion, and that what Musa (peace be upon him) had produced was firmer than the mountains, the verse was connected to his statement, ﴿So the truth came to pass﴾. That is, the truth is that than which nothing is firmer. What actually happens corresponds to it, because the inner reality agrees with what appeared outwardly of it, namely the swallowing of their ropes (p-٢٩) and staffs. Therefore, reporting it is true. This also alerts that their act was only an illusion relative to the outward appearance. As for the inner reality and what actually happened, it has no substance. So the report that what they had cast moved is false.

When he reported the firmness of the truth, he followed it with the passing away of falsehood, saying: ﴿And what they had been doing was annulled﴾, to the extent that it was utterly erased from its very root. The use of ﴿kāna﴾ (was) with the present tense (ya'malūn) indicates that they, even with the annulment of what they had done, had forgotten their knowledge to such a degree that the practice of work was ascribed to them after they had possessed a faculty for it, like a faculty that is almost innate. And God knows best.

Then He made a consequence of this His statement: ﴿So they were overcome there﴾, that is, at this great matter of lofty rank, ﴿and they returned﴾, that is, as a requital for their turning those realities away from their faces, ﴿humbled﴾, that is, after they had been, in their own estimation and in the estimation of those who held their view (and that is the majority), exalted. Nor is there any humiliation or abasement greater for the one who holds falsehood than the manifestation of the falsity of his claim in a manner that leaves no room for stratagem.

Since courtesy and humbling of the self only bring about good, for they are what befits servants, it led many of them to eternal happiness. Therefore He said: ﴿And the magicians were thrown down﴾, meaning He cast them down in the posture of those fearful of God and eager to submit before Him and to abase themselves in His presence, when they knew that what Moses, peace be upon him, had done was a heavenly matter, by which God Most High confirmed Moses, peace be upon him, in his being His messenger. They did not delay at all after that, to the extent that it was as if they fell down without choice ﴿prostrating﴾, thanking God Most High, casting off disbelief, and as a sign of the utmost degrees of submission. God did this to them so that Pharaoh and his chiefs would be dazzled by it and their minds bewildered.

Now that they were in a state of great eagerness to know what they would say after their deed, Allah, glory be to Him, informed about that with His words: ﴿They said﴾, that is, at the moment of their throwing themselves down in prostration, ﴿"We believe"﴾, that is, all of us, ﴿"in the Lord of the worlds"﴾, that is, the One who created Pharaoh and those before him, and the things by which they live;

Then they singled out those whom Allah guided at their hands, to state the intended meaning explicitly and to honour the two of them, so they said: ﴿The Lord of Moses﴾. Then they removed the doubt in its entirety, because Pharaoh might have claimed, on account of having raised Moses (peace be upon him), that he was the one intended, by their saying: ﴿and Aaron﴾. In the verse there is evidence that the manifestation of a sign necessitates faith for the one to whom it becomes manifest, even if the Messenger is not the one sent to him.

When they openly declared that they believed in him, which prevented Pharaoh from deceiving them with anything that would mislead his people, he began to threaten them in a way by which he would scheme against his people and confuse them, in order to stop them from hastening to faith, as the sorcerers had hastened, until some time had passed. So he resumed the report about him, may He be exalted, with His words [naming him explicitly and not using a pronoun for him, as in other surahs, because the aim of this surah is warning, and he is the best of people to be called out to in that setting, and his story is brought to explain the wickedness of most people, and he was the most wicked person of that age]: ﴿Pharaoh said﴾, denouncing them [and rebuking them] with his words: ﴿"Have you believed in him"﴾, that is, have you affirmed ﴿"him"﴾, that is, Moses, with an affirmation that secures against your turning back from him. The one who reports intended a question, and Pharaoh gave the impression to those among the Copts who understood from them that they intended belief, because of the signs of Moses's truthfulness that they had seen, and following the sorcerers, [with his words: ﴿"before I give you permission"﴾, to make them stop, out of fear of opposing him, by what he hoped they would gain from his permission. When he thought that they had halted their horses, by what would entirely and fundamentally remove that thought from them, he said, emphasizing a negation of what his words contained of the marks of falsehood]: ﴿"Indeed, this is a plot"﴾, that is, a very great one. He lengthened his speech to clarify what they intended and to dull the thought of faith, so he said: ﴿"You plotted it in the city"﴾, that is, by an appointment between you and Moses, and a stratagem you devised before you gathered, and your faith is not because his truthfulness appeared to you. Then he gave a reason connected to what occupies their thinking and disturbs their hearts, so he said: ﴿"so that you might expel"﴾, that is, you and Moses, peace be upon him, ﴿"its people from it"﴾, and you and the Children of Israel might dwell in it.

When his intended subtle guile was firmly established for him, he began to threaten them with what would deter others and perhaps turn them back. So he said, making this the consequence of that: ﴿"Then you will come to know"﴾, that is, by a promise that admits no failure, what I will do to you of a punishment that cannot be borne,

Then he explained what was general in this threat with his words: ﴿I will surely cut off your hands﴾, meaning the right ones for example, ﴿and your feet﴾, meaning the left ones. For this reason he explained it with his words: ﴿on opposite sides﴾, meaning the side from which the hand is cut off opposes the side from which the foot is cut off.

Since the purpose of this surah is warning, it mentions what befell Musa (peace be upon him) and the magicians in a manner that magnifies the report of what Pharaoh did in a manner close to that. So he used the particle of delay (thumma), because in it, together with the lengthy elaboration that occupies his companions from what had astonished them of what they had seen, there is a magnification of the matter of crucifixion. Thus it is more terrifying to the magicians and to whoever among his people was shaken by them. So he said: ﴿Then I will surely crucify you﴾, meaning: I will hang you with your hands stretched out so that you take the form of the cross, or until your cross, which is the grease within you, drips. ﴿All of you﴾, meaning: I will leave none of you, so that I make you an example for others.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 125:

When this was a state that stirs souls toward their answer, He resumed it with His saying: ﴿They said﴾, that is, all of them; not one of them wavered, nor was any of them shaken from what Allah had bestowed upon him of the rank of faith: ﴿Indeed, to our Lord﴾, that is, the One who never ceased to show us kindness with His manifest and hidden blessings, until He made the end of that the greatest of blessings, not to anyone else ﴿we will be returned﴾, that is, by death, a return that is firm, from which we have no escape, whether you crucify us or leave us. We have no hope of remaining in this world. So we do not mind, after our knowledge that we are in the state of the blessed, dying in whatever state it may be. Or the meaning is that we will be returned, if you kill us, to One who is kind to us, by which You will take revenge on you. For this reason they followed it with their saying:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 126:

﴿And you resent﴾ i.e., you disapprove of, ﴿from us﴾ i.e., your doing that to us and you find fault with us, ﴿except that we believed﴾ (p-33) i.e., except for that which is the root of all virtues, which is faith, ﴿in the signs of our Lord﴾ i.e., those which are great by virtue of their having come from Him, and who has never ceased to be good to us, so that it is obligatory upon us to be grateful to Him, ﴿when﴾ [i.e., when] ﴿they came to us﴾, we did not delay in recognizing the truth [of the one who confirms it]. This necessitates honour, not retribution. Then they informed him that they were resolved to face whatever might be done to them, so they said: ﴿Our Lord﴾ i.e., O You who are good to us and able to deliver us, ﴿pour out﴾ i.e., pour out abundantly, ﴿upon us﴾ i.e., in what You have threatened us with, this which You have strengthened against us, ﴿patience﴾ i.e., much patience, that will overwhelm us as water overwhelms the one upon whom it is poured out, so that what frightens us will not terrify us. ﴿And take us in death﴾ i.e., take our souls complete, while we are ﴿Muslims﴾ i.e., thoroughly submissive outwardly and inwardly to the proofs of the truth. The apparent meaning is that God Most High answered them in what they asked, by allusion through the mention of "Lord," so He did not impose it upon them, according to His saying, Most High: ﴿You and whoever follows you will be the victors﴾ [al-Qasas: 35]. No reliable report has come that He killed them. And it will come at the end of al-Hadid, from the History of Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, what is explicit regarding their deliverance.

(p-34) When Pharaoh was content with this state of affairs, in which that manifest miracle had dazzled his people, and it had separated in this manner, leaving him no trick except that he had tried it, and Musa (peace be upon him) escaped with his people, having some measure of power over them, and the context was to explain that most of creation are corrupt, Allah the Exalted informed us of what Pharaoh's people said after they saw the overpowering miracle as evidence of that. He said, coordinating it with ﴿And the sorcerers were cast down prostrating﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:120) and what follows it, or with the words of Pharaoh: ﴿And the chiefs﴾, that is, the nobles, ﴿of Pharaoh's people said﴾, that is, supposing that Pharaoh had the power to do to Musa (peace be upon him) whatever harm he wished, disapproving of what the situation had come to regarding the affair of Musa (peace be upon him) when he did what he did and the sorcerers believed in him, while Pharaoh had done nothing, neither killing him nor imprisoning him, because he was not able to do that and would not admit it to his people: ﴿Will you leave Musa and his people﴾

When what had happened at the first assembly, the faith of the sorcerers, was bound to draw others like them to it, they named it corruption and made it a target for Pharaoh, to incite and enrage him, so they said: ﴿to spread corruption﴾, that is, to bring about corruption, which is the changing of the religion, ﴿in the land﴾, that is, the land which is the whole earth, or this land of ours, or the whole earth, because such an act is bound to turn all the people of the earth away from their beliefs. ﴿And leave you and your gods﴾. It was said: he had commanded his people to worship idols to draw near to him. The Imam said: the more likely view is that he was a materialist (dahri) denying the existence of the Creator, and he used to say that the manager of this lower world is the stars, and that he was the one served in the world by creation, or by that group, and its nurturer. He then said: if his doctrine was that, it is not far-fetched to say that he had made idols in the shapes of the stars and worshipped them, according to the religion of the star-worshippers. [End.] For this reason he said: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾ (An-Nazi'at 79:24). This is what has been said, and it is the apparent meaning of the expression of the Tawrah (Torah) that follows in the verse of the lice. But his intention is not suitable to this balancing. Rather, the apparent meaning is that he had named his governors "gods" and named for each governor a people who would deify him, that is, obey him. It has been reported about them that they would call the ruler, and even the great man, a god, as will come from the expression of the Tawrah. So where the comparison occurs between Musa (peace be upon him) and his people and Pharaoh and his people, he used the word "gods" to magnify his side, indicating that he is a god, that is, a ruler who is worshipped, with no end beyond him, and all his council are gods, that is, rulers beneath him. Musa (peace be upon him) is not a god, and there is no god among his people; rather they are those ruled over, and they are weak, so how could they be left alone! Where he denied divinity of anyone else, this is in view of his address to the council: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:38). Where he gathered the subjects, he called them with his words: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾ (An-Nazi'at 79:24). It seems that this was applied to the ruler figuratively, and they made it literal, and they began doing what is specific to gods, [of permitting and forbidding, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾ (At-Tawbah 9:31)], so they disbelieved by claiming lordship in the sense of servitude, and by denying the true object of worship, as is shown by the verse "I have not done". The summary is that they reproached him for being content to be a chief over the Copts while Musa (peace be upon him) was a chief over the Children of Israel, so that by this abandonment they would be equals to the Copts.

When Allah the Exalted rendered him unable to do more than he had been doing before the coming of Musa (peace be upon him), because of what was intended for him of istidraj (gradual leading toward ruin), He informed us of him in a way that conveys this. So He said, beginning a new statement: ﴿He said﴾, that is, Pharaoh: ﴿We will kill﴾, that is, a great slaughter, ﴿their sons﴾, that is, as we used to do, ﴿and spare their women﴾, that is, keep them alive, humiliating them and securing ourselves against their harm in the future, ﴿and indeed we are above them﴾, that is, now, ﴿dominant﴾. There is no trace of Musa's victory over us in these scenes, lest the common people imagine that he is the child whom the astrologers and soothsayers spoke of, through whose hand their kingdom would perish, and that would discourage them from obedience, thereby giving the impression that his leaving off harming Musa (peace be upon him) is because he did not care about him, and that nothing could render him powerless.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 128:

When this matter was something that increased the anxiety of the Children of Israel, since they had caught the scent of relief, Allah, glorified is He, resumed the report about what Musa, peace be upon him, used to firm them up, saying: ﴿Musa said to his people﴾, that is, the Children of Israel, who possessed strength and resolve [in] what they sought of affairs, if their hearts were united: ﴿Seek help﴾, that is, attach yourselves to seeking aid ﴿from Allah﴾, Whom there is none greater than, through what pleases Him of worship, ﴿and be patient﴾. Then he gave the reason for that, that He is one who does whatever He wills, and there is no objection to Him and no escape from His judgment, so he said: (p-37) ﴿Indeed, the earth﴾, that is, all of it, Egypt and other than it, ﴿belongs to Allah﴾, that is, the One with Whom there is no command for anyone, He repeated it to remind of His greatness, to make it clear, and for blessing; then he resumed his speech: ﴿He gives it as inheritance to whomever He wills of His servants﴾.

When he informed that the relation of all of it to Him is one, he informed of what elevates some of them above others, so he said: ﴿And the final outcome is for the God-conscious﴾, that is, and the situation is that the end of the matter, even if trial occurs, ﴿is for those who are mindful of Allah﴾, that is, those who protect themselves from Allah's wrath by doing what pleases Him. So there is no regard for what you see in the immediate, for it may be a gradual leading on (istidraj).

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 129:

When the listener became eager to know what their response had been, God, exalted is He, indicated, by His saying (in a resumptive construction), that their distress had reached a point beyond which there was no patience: ﴿They said﴾. Since what causes pain is the harm itself and not its coming from a specific source, they used the passive form in their saying: ﴿We have been harmed﴾, that is, by killing and enslavement.

Since their harm did not encompass all time, they affirmed the prepositional phrase and said: ﴿Before you came to us﴾, that is, as you know, ﴿and after you came to us﴾, that is, what benefit has your coming brought us? ﴿He said﴾, consoling them, calling them to hope, and giving them good expectation by what he had alluded to earlier: ﴿It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy﴾, that is, the One who has shown kindness to your forefathers by what you know and to you by sending me to you, ﴿and make you successors in the land﴾, so that what you see should not frighten you. ﴿And make you successors﴾, that is, bring into being your succession over them, firmly established, with none other than you ruling over you, ﴿in the land﴾, that is, its entirety, if you are God-fearing (muttaqun). Then he made the successorship the cause of his following statement, reminding them and warning them against the assaults of Him, glorified is He: ﴿so that He may see how you act﴾, that is, while you are firmly established successors. ﴿How you act﴾, that is, He deals with you in the manner of one who tests, though He is eternally aware of what you will do after you have performed your deeds, but He does this so that the proof may be established against you according to the patterns of your customs.

When Moses, peace be upon him, gave them hope with this, Allah, glorified is He, reported that He had done what He had told them He would do. So He mentioned its preliminaries, saying: ﴿And indeed﴾, meaning: He said to them what He said, while the situation was that We, by Our might, had ﴿seized﴾, meaning subdued, ﴿the people of Pharaoh﴾, softened their stubbornness and eased their obstinacy, ﴿with years﴾, meaning with drought and famine. The word *sanah* (year) is used with the meaning of hardship through dominance, just as it is used for a year. Since *sanah* is used for a shortage of grain, He specified fruits, saying: ﴿and a shortage of fruits﴾, meaning through blights, if the water was abundant. Alternatively, *al-sanah* applies to the desert dwellers and *al-naqs* (shortage) applies to the settled people. ﴿So that they might take heed﴾, meaning that their condition would be that of one whom the observer hopes will remember within himself, even by the least degree of remembrance, as indicated by the *idgham* (assimilation of consonants, here the merging of the *ta'* of *yatadhakkaruna* into the *dhal*). Harm removes the arrogance which is the likely cause of clinging to one's fortunes, and it makes a person tender, so he says: "This has only befallen me because of my denial of this Messenger and my worship of one who cannot remove evil from himself or from anyone else."

When they neither took heed nor humbled themselves, He attributed to their being seized by Him the saying (of theirs), disclosing their foolishness, and expressing the good with the particle of certainty (idha, "when") as an indication that it is the more prevalent over evil, as an incitement to gratitude: ﴿But when﴾, that is, nothing resulted from that except that they, whenever ﴿good came to them﴾, that is, the complete state that they love, of abundance and other things, and he defined it after its realization as an indication of its completeness, ﴿they said, "This is ours by right"﴾, that is, we are worthy of it. And the fact that good is more frequent than other than it is shown by his saying, with the particle of doubt together with indefiniteness: ﴿but if evil befalls them﴾, that is, a state they dislike.

[Since being struck by evil is specific to them and nothing of it reaches the Children of Israel, and their display of ill omen regarding them was evident in their rejecting them and denying it, He, glorified is He, indicated by the assimilation of the taa' that they were only slipping it in to those among the ignorant and foolish whom they could deceive, in a manner of concealment and secrecy, unlike what is in Ya-Sin. So He said]: ﴿they consider it an omen from Moses and those with him﴾, that is, they regard them as a bad omen, by saying: this evil has befallen us only because of their ill omen. It is a form of tafa''ul from the tayr (bird), which is deliberately aiming at the flight of a bird in order to take an omen from it, for good or for ill. Its origin is that when an Arab saw a bird pass from their right side toward their left, they said: "bariḥ," that is, ill-omened, from al-barḥ, which is hardship; but if it flew from the left toward the right, they counted it blessed, and they said: "Who gives me the sanih after the barih?", that is, the blessed after the ill-omened. And it is known that what is meant here is taking an ill omen, because of its association with evil.

When they had lied in both places, He said, resuming in a manner of emphasis: (p-40) ﴿Behold, their omen is only with Allah﴾, that is, their lot, which was decreed from eternity, of good and evil, so it does not increase or decrease. ﴿with Allah﴾, that is, the King to whom no command belongs to anyone else, and who has decreed everything, so no one other than Him can bring about anything at all. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾, that is, they have no knowledge at all, so they do not guide themselves to what benefits them, and they suppose that the servants have a part in that, which is why you see them attributing things to causes they imagine.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 132:

Since what they said indicates bad temperament and coarseness of disposition that does not accept treatment, he followed it with something worse than it, namely that they were resolute that whenever anything came to them in the future, they would confront it with disbelief. So He said: ﴿And they said, "Whatever]</br>

Translation follows the exegetical structure:

Since what they said indicates bad temperament and coarseness of disposition that does not accept treatment, He followed it with something worse than it, namely that they were resolute that whenever anything came to them in the future, they would confront it with disbelief. So He said: ﴿And they said, "Whatever sign you bring us to enchant us with it, we will not be believers in you."﴾

The phrase ﴿mahma﴾ is composed of "ma" twice: the first is the conditional (ma al-shartiyyah, "whatever"), and the second is for emphasis (ta'kid). The alif of the first was changed to a ha' (hā') to ease pronunciation, and it is said that [mah] is the sound used to restrain, and the conditional ma means: restrain yourself from what you are in. Then they resumed with "mā" in ﴿ta'tinā bihi﴾, meaning: at whatever time and in whatever state it occurs. Then they specified what is brought by their saying: ﴿min āyah﴾, meaning: a sign (ʿalāmah) of your truthfulness, and this is according to their claim; for this reason they gave as the reason their saying: ﴿li-tasḥaranā﴾, meaning: that you may bewitch our minds ﴿bihā﴾ and turn us away from what we are upon toward what you desire. So we call it sorcery and you call it a sign. Then they answered the condition with their saying: ﴿fa-mā naḥnu﴾, meaning: all of us, ﴿laka﴾, meaning: specifically for you, ﴿bi-mu'minīn﴾, meaning: as believers in order to refrain from denying you.

(p-41) When they confronted [Moses] with this magnitude [of signs], they deserved punishment. Therefore He made the following statement a consequence of that: ﴿So We sent upon them﴾, meaning a punishment for them, as the preposition "upon" (ʿalā) conveys elevation and domination, ﴿the flood﴾, meaning the thunder, the lightning, and the fire along with the rain and the large hailstones that kill cattle and whatever is smaller than them, as well as the darkness and the violent wind that covered their land and surrounded it. Since such [a calamity] may sometimes leave the land fertile, He informed [them] that He also sent what would spoil that, so He said: ﴿and the locusts﴾.

Since locusts may sometimes fly away while leaving something behind, He informed [them] of what remains clinging to the ground until it leaves nothing on it, so He said: ﴿and the lice﴾. In al-Qamus [the dictionary], it says: "al-qummal, like al-sukkar, are the small ants and wingless locusts, or the smallest of locusts, or a small thing with a red wing, or something resembling the bedbug that has a foul smell, or small creatures like ticks, meaning the ṭurād (ticks)." Al-Bukhari said in the chapter on the Children of Israel in his Ṣaḥīḥ: "al-qummal: al-ḥamnān, which resembles the small bedbugs."

Since there may have been something stored among them that this [plague] did not reach, He informed [them] of what would fall into their food and spoil or diminish it, so He said: ﴿and the frogs﴾, for they covered all their places, would fall into their food, and sometimes would leap into their mouths when they opened them to eat.

When what harms food was complete, He followed it with what spoiled drink, so He said: ﴿and the blood﴾, for all their water turned into foul-smelling blood. The blood covered the trees, the stones, and the entire land with respect to the Copts (al-Qibṭ). As for the Children of Israel (Banū Isrāʾīl), they were safe from all of that.

When the Exalted mentioned these great signs, He drew attention to their greatness by mentioning their condition, so He said: ﴿signs﴾, meaning proofs of His truthfulness, great ones, ﴿detailed﴾, meaning some follow others, and between each one and its sibling there is a period in which they are tested, although the distinction of each one from its sibling is extremely evident, and likewise the knowledge that they are among the signs of God which no one other than Him is able to produce.

Since they were deserving that faith should result from them when the heart is sound, He made the following statement a consequence of them: ﴿but they acted arrogantly﴾, clarifying that what prevented them from faith was a sickness of the heart through arrogance and transgression, ﴿and they were a criminal people﴾, meaning that it is in their nature to sever what ought to be joined, together with their power over what they attempt.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 134:

Since this was in reality a breach of what God had taken from the servants by the covenant of reason, He followed it with a real breach, saying, clarifying their state at every sign. Perhaps he expressed it with what encompasses them and did not state the repetition explicitly, because that is sufficient for what was mentioned of breaking (naqd) and transgression (fisq): ﴿And when the plague (rijz) fell upon them﴾, meaning the detailed punishment that necessitates turmoil, ﴿they said, "O Moses, pray to your Lord for us"﴾, i.e., the one who has been good to you. Out of arrogance and pride, they did not permit themselves to identify Him by saying "our Lord," ﴿by what He has covenanted with you﴾, i.e., of prophethood, of which this kindness that you see Him showing you is part. Then they reinforced the covenant with their statement, either as a fresh start or as a reason (p-43): ﴿If You remove from us the plague﴾, i.e., the punishment by which our hearts and all our states were thrown into turmoil, ﴿we will surely believe in you﴾, i.e., we will make you secure from denial by bringing about belief, and that will be purely for your sake and specifically for you, ﴿and we will surely send with you﴾, i.e., in your company, we will not hold back any of you from the other, ﴿the Children of Israel﴾, i.e., as you requested. It indicated the nearness of the answer by the particle "fa" (then) in His saying:

ۚ﴿So when We removed from them the punishment﴾, i.e., by Our greatness, ﴿the plague﴾ — He repeated it for clarity and to convey its severity — and We extended the removal ﴿until a term﴾, i.e., a limit of time, ﴿which they would reach﴾, i.e., in Our knowledge, ﴿behold, they broke their oath﴾, i.e., by their inner intentions, according to which their outward conduct proceeds ﴿they break [their word]﴾.

When He had informed that they hastily broke the covenant and repeated it, He made the following statement its consequence: ﴿So We took retribution from them﴾, i.e., a retribution unlike that with which We had been punishing them, but a retribution of destruction, as a lesson, because they had arrived, after all doubts had been removed, at pure obstinacy. Then He explained it with His words: ﴿So We drowned them﴾ with the majesty that is Ours ﴿in the sea﴾, i.e., in the sea which is sought for its benefits, ﴿because they﴾, i.e., because of the fact that they ﴿denied Our signs﴾, i.e., in spite of their greatness, as it is known that they are truly attributed to Us. And Glorified is He, by His words ﴿and they were﴾, i.e., by nature and disposition, ﴿heedless of them﴾, i.e., their state after them would be like their state before them, so it is as though the signs had never come to them at all, and so they deserved the seizing, since it was established that the signs would not benefit them, indicated that they denied without any doubt that had presented itself to them, but out of obstinacy.
