(p-٤٤)When he had informed of their destruction, he followed it with what He did for the Children of Israel, so he said: ﴿And We made them inherit﴾, that is, after their destruction, by what We possess of greatness, ﴿the people﴾. When he indicated with this expression, whose meaning is that they had strength, abundance, and firm resolve in what they attempted and undertook, to the point that it was He who humbled them and not Pharaoh, he followed it with what indicates this, saying: ﴿who were deemed weak﴾, that is, whose weakness was sought and exploited, by a ruler whose greatness had taken hold of hearts that are dominated by illusion, and they were the Children of Israel. ﴿The eastern and western parts of the land﴾, that is, the parts full of its blessings; ﴿and its western parts﴾, that is, the land of al-Sham from the Euphrates to the Sea of Suf, the place from which they emerged from the sea and in which Pharaoh and his household drowned, as its transmission was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Ma'idah from the Torah. This means Our decree to make them inherit that and Our fulfilling it for the sons of those who had left Egypt after the destruction of their fathers in the wilderness (al-tih). Then he described it, expressing admiration for it, by his saying: ﴿which We had blessed﴾, that is, in its land with water, trees, fruits and fertility; and in its provisions with abundance and goodness; and in its men with knowledge and prophethood; and in their dispositions with uprightness; and in their resolves with courage, bravery and noble qualities; and in all their conditions with the fact that no oppressor transgresses against them except that he is quickly struck with retribution. ﴿And was fulfilled﴾, that is, its truthfulness was realized through the existence of its content in the world of witnessing and its manifestation from the veils of the unseen; ﴿the word of your Lord﴾ [Hud: 119], that is, the Bestower of good upon you by sending down these reports in these ways, which are beneficial together with their inimitability, for the ultimate knowledge and wisdom; ﴿the best﴾ prevailing ﴿upon the Children of Israel﴾ (p-٤٥), that is, the word that is the best of speech, and it is His promise to them of deliverance from servitude and of making them inherit the dwellings of their fathers, as they used to hear from their predecessors. When it prevails over them, it prevents their enemies from reaching them. ﴿Because they were patient﴾, that is, because of their patience under enslavement and the slaughter of their sons and what came after that of long afflictions. ﴿And We destroyed﴾, that is, We destroyed with a great destruction, making it crumble like ashes, with no good whatsoever remaining in it at all; ﴿what Pharaoh and his people had been making﴾, that is, the making with complete devotion to it, to the point that it is as if they were created for it; ﴿and what they had been building﴾, that is, of the magnificent, marvelous crafts that amaze everyone who sees them or hears of them, even though they had become accustomed to them, so they became the easiest thing for them. ﴿And what they had been building﴾, that is, with what is almost like innate nature and disposition, ﴿lofty structures﴾, that is, of gardens and palaces with high pillars. This verse suffices as an incitement to patience and as a guarantee for every one who deserves reward, through relieving the oppressed, supporting him, destroying the oppressor, and subduing him.

He explained what needs explaining here from the Torah that exists today among the Jews. He said, translating in the third chapter of the second book, the text of which is:

And the LORD said to Moses in Midian:
"Go back to Egypt, for all the men who were seeking your life have died." So Moses took his wife and his sons and set them on his donkey, and he took in his hand the rod of the LORD. And the LORD said to Moses:
"See all the wonders that I have put in your hand; do them before Pharaoh. But I will harden his heart so that he will not let the people go. And say to Pharaoh:
'Thus says the LORD:
Israel is My firstborn son. Let My son go that he may serve Me; but if you refuse to let My son go, I will kill your firstborn son.'" And when Moses was on the way, at the lodging place, the angel of the LORD met him and sought to kill him. Then Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son's foreskin and touched his feet with it, and said:
"Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me" (in the text of the Septuagint: "and she fell at his feet"), meaning circumcision. Then the LORD said to Aaron:
"Go into the wilderness to meet Moses." So he went and met him at the mountain of God in Horeb, and kissed him. And Moses told Aaron all the words of the LORD with which He had sent him and all the signs He had commanded him. Then Moses and Aaron went and gathered all the elders of the children of Israel, and Aaron spoke all the words that the LORD had spoken to Moses, and did the signs in the sight of the people. (In the text of the Septuagint: "So they gathered the elders of the children of Israel, and Aaron spoke all the words which God had spoken to Moses and did the signs before the people.") The people believed, and when they heard that the LORD had visited the children of Israel and had seen their affliction, they bowed their heads and worshipped. After these signs and troubles, Moses and Aaron went in and said to Pharaoh:
"Thus says the LORD God of Israel:
'Let My people go, that they may hold a feast to Me in the wilderness'" (in the text of the Septuagint: "that they may serve Me in the wilderness," instead of "hold a feast in the wilderness"). Pharaoh said:
"Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice? I do not know the LORD, nor will I let Israel go." They said:
"The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Let us go three days' journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the LORD our God, lest He strike us with pestilence or with the sword" (in the text of the Septuagint: "lest death or slaughter suddenly fall upon us"). Pharaoh said:
"Why do you, Moses and Aaron, take the people away from their work? Get back to your burdens!"
So Pharaoh commanded that same day the taskmasters of the people and their officers, saying:
"You shall no longer give the people straw to make bricks as before; let them go and gather straw for themselves. But the quota of bricks which they made before you shall lay on them; you shall not reduce it, for they are idle; therefore they cry out, saying, 'Let us go and sacrifice to our God.' Let more work be laid on the men, that they may labor in it and not regard vain words." (In the text of the Septuagint: "Let the labor of these people be multiplied, that they may be occupied with it and not pay attention to lying words.") So the taskmasters and officers of the people went out and spoke to the people, saying, "Thus says Pharaoh: 'I will not give you straw. Go, gather straw for yourselves wherever you can find it; yet not one bit of your work shall be reduced.'" So the people were scattered throughout all the land of Egypt to gather stubble instead of straw. And the taskmasters were urgent, saying:
"Fulfill your daily quotas, as when there was straw." And the officers of the children of Israel, whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over them, were beaten and were asked:
"Why have you not fulfilled your task of making bricks both yesterday and today, as before?" Then the officers of the children of Israel came and cried out to Pharaoh, saying:
"Why are you dealing thus with your servants? No straw is given to your servants, yet they say to us, 'Make bricks!' And look, your servants are beaten, but the fault is in your own people."
But he said:
"You are idle, you are idle! Therefore you say, 'Let us go and sacrifice to the LORD.' Go now and work; for no straw shall be given you, yet you shall deliver the quota of bricks." And the officers of the children of Israel saw that they were in trouble, when they were told, "You shall not reduce your daily quota of bricks." So they met Moses and Aaron, who were standing there to meet them as they came from Pharaoh (in the text of the Septuagint: "as they were coming toward them when they came out from before Pharaoh"). And they said to them:
"May the LORD look upon you and judge, because you have made us abhorrent in the sight of Pharaoh and his servants, to put a sword in their hand to kill us."
So Moses returned to the LORD and said:
"Lord, why have You caused trouble to this people? Why did You ever send me? For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in Your name, he has done evil to this people, and You have not delivered Your people at all."
Then the LORD said to Moses:
"Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh; for with a strong hand he will let them go" (in the text of the Septuagint: "Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh, and how he will let them go with a mighty hand and a great arm, and he will drive them out of the land of Egypt!" (p-٤٩)). "I am the LORD who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty, but by My name LORD I was not known to them. I also established My covenant with them, to give them the land of Canaan, the land of their sojourning in which they dwelt" (in the text of the Septuagint: "and My name is LORD, but I did not reveal it to them"). "And I have also heard the groaning of the children of Israel, whom the Egyptians keep in bondage, and I have remembered My covenant. Therefore say to the children of Israel: 'I am the LORD; I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, I will rescue you from their bondage, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great judgments. I will take you as My people, and I will be your God; then you shall know that I am the LORD your God who brings you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians. And I will bring you to the land which I swore to give to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and I will give it to you as a heritage: I am the LORD.'"
So Moses spoke thus to the children of Israel; but they did not heed Moses, because of anguish of spirit and cruel bondage.
And the LORD spoke to Moses, saying: "Go in, tell Pharaoh king of Egypt to let the children of Israel go out of his land." But Moses spoke before the LORD, saying: "Indeed the children of Israel have not heeded me; how then will Pharaoh heed me, since I am of uncircumcised lips?" So the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, and gave them a command for the children of Israel and for Pharaoh king of Egypt, to bring the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt.
The LORD said to Moses:
"See, I have made you as God to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet. You shall speak all that I command you, and Aaron your brother shall speak to Pharaoh, that he send the children of Israel out of his land. But I will harden Pharaoh's heart and multiply My signs and wonders in the land of Egypt. But Pharaoh will not heed you, so that I may lay My hand on Egypt and bring My armies and My people, the children of Israel, out of the land of Egypt by great judgments. And the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out My hand on Egypt and bring out the children of Israel from among them." (In the text of the Septuagint: "And Aaron your brother shall be a prophet for you, and you shall speak all that I command you, and Aaron your brother shall speak to Pharaoh" (p-٥٠)...) So Moses and Aaron did so; as the LORD commanded them, so they did. Moses was eighty years old and Aaron eighty-three years old when they spoke to Pharaoh.
Then the LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: "When Pharaoh speaks to you, saying, 'Show a wonder for yourselves,' then you shall say to Aaron, 'Take your rod and cast it before Pharaoh, and it will become a serpent.'" So Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh, and they did so as the LORD had commanded. Aaron cast down his rod before Pharaoh and his servants (in the text of the Septuagint: "Aaron cast down his rod before Pharaoh and before his officials and his servants"), and it became a serpent. Then Pharaoh also called the wise men and the sorcerers, and the magicians of Egypt also did the same with their enchantments. For each man cast down his rod, and they became serpents; but Aaron's rod swallowed up their rods. Yet Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he did not heed them, as the LORD had said.
And the LORD said to Moses:
"Pharaoh's heart is hardened; he refuses to let the people go. Go to Pharaoh in the morning, when he goes out to the water; stand by the river's bank to meet him, and take in your hand the rod which was turned into a serpent (p-٥١), and say to him: 'The LORD God of the Hebrews has sent me to you, saying, "Let My people go, that they may serve Me in the wilderness"; but until now you would not hear.' Thus says the LORD: 'By this you shall know that I am the LORD. Behold, I will strike the waters that are in the river with the rod that is in my hand, and they shall be turned to blood. The fish that are in the river shall die, the river shall stink' (in the text of the Septuagint: 'and the Egyptians shall not be able to drink water from this river')." And the LORD said to Moses:
"Tell Aaron, 'Take your rod and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, over their canals, over their ponds, and over all their pools of water' (in the text of the Septuagint: 'And the LORD said to Moses: say to Aaron: take your rod and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, their reeds, their marshes, and over all their standing waters'), that they may become blood; and there shall be blood throughout all the land of Egypt, in both wooden vessels and stone vessels." So Moses and Aaron did so, as the LORD had commanded. He lifted up the rod and struck the waters that were in the river, in the sight of Pharaoh and of his servants, and all the waters that were in the river were turned to blood. The fish that were in the river died, the river became foul, and the Egyptians could not drink water from the river; there was blood throughout all the land of Egypt. Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not heed them, as the LORD had said. Pharaoh turned and went into his house, and he did not take even this to heart. All the Egyptians dug around the river for water to drink, for they could not drink of the river's water. And seven days were fulfilled after the LORD had struck the river. And the LORD said to Moses:
"Go in to Pharaoh and say to him, 'Thus says the LORD (p-٥٢):'"

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 137 (part 2 of 4):

Let my people go that they may serve me. But if you refuse to let him go, behold, I will smite all your territory with frogs, and the frogs will swarm and climb up and enter your house, your bedchamber, your bed, the houses of your servants and your people, your ovens and your kneading-troughs. The frogs will crawl upon you and upon all your people.

The Lord said to Moses:

Say to Aaron your brother:

Stretch out your hand with your staff over the rivers, over the canals and over the reed-beds, and bring up the frogs upon the land of Egypt. So Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of the Egyptians, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt. Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said to them:

Pray before the Lord that the frogs may depart from me and from my people, and I will let the people go to sacrifice before the Lord. Moses said to Pharaoh:

Set the time for me to pray for you, for your servants and for your people, that the frogs may depart from you and from your houses, except those remaining in the river. (In a version of the Septuagint: "from you and from your nation and from your houses.") He said:

Tomorrow.

Moses said to him:

It shall be as you have said, so that you may know that there is no god besides our God. The frogs will depart from you and from your house (in a version of the Septuagint: "houses") and from your servants and your people, except the frogs that are in the river. Moses and Aaron went out from before Pharaoh, and Moses prayed before the Lord, and the Lord answered Moses. The frogs died in the houses, the dwellings and the fields, and they gathered them into heaps upon heaps, and the land became foul and rotten. (In a version of the Septuagint: "they gathered them in heaps, heap by heap, and the land stank.") Pharaoh saw that there was relief and rest, and his heart became hardened, and he did not heed them, just as the Lord had said.

The Lord said to Moses:

Tell Aaron to raise his staff and strike the dust of the earth, so that lice will come upon all the land of Egypt. They did so: Aaron stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the earth, and the lice came upon men and beasts, and all the dust of the earth became lice throughout the land of Egypt. The magicians tried to do the same with their sorcery, but they could not bring forth lice, either on men or on beasts. The magicians said to Pharaoh:

This is the finger of the Lord of the worlds. But Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he did not heed them, just as the Lord had said.

The Lord said to Moses:

Rise early in the morning and stand before Pharaoh, for he goes out to the water (in a version of the Septuagint: "for he goes out to the water"). Say to him:

Thus says the Lord:

Let my people go that they may serve me. But if you refuse, behold, I am sending (in a version of the Septuagint: "I am sending") upon you, upon your people and upon your households, swarms of flies and vermin of every kind, and the houses of the Egyptians will be filled with flies and vermin, as well as the ground on which they stand. (In another version: "dog-flies".) On that day I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people dwell, so that no swarms of flies or vermin will be there, that you may know that I am the Lord. I will make a distinction between my people and your people, and this sign will be tomorrow. The Lord did so, and sent swarms of flies upon the house (in another version: "houses") of Pharaoh, his servants and all the land of Egypt, and the land was ruined by the flies. Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said to them:

Go, sacrifice to the Lord your God in this land. Moses said:

It is not right for us to do so, for we sacrifice to the Lord our God what is abominable to the Egyptians. If we sacrifice before the gods of the Egyptians, they will stone us. Rather, we will go three days' journey into the wilderness and sacrifice there to the Lord our God as he commands us. Pharaoh said:

I will let you go to sacrifice to the Lord your God in the wilderness, but do not go far away; and pray for me too. (In a version of the Septuagint: "but do not go far away, and pray for me too, to your Lord.") Moses said to Pharaoh:

I will go out from before you and pray to the Lord, and tomorrow the flies will depart from Pharaoh, his servants and his people. But let Pharaoh not deceive again by his word and refuse to let the people go to sacrifice. Moses went out from before Pharaoh and prayed to the Lord, and the Lord accepted Moses' prayer and removed the flies, so that not one remained. Pharaoh's heart was hardened again, and he did not let the people go.

The Lord said to Moses:

Go to Pharaoh and say to him:

Thus says the Lord, God of the Hebrews:

Let my people go that they may serve me. But if you refuse to let them go (in a version of the Septuagint: "and you hold on to them"), behold, the hand of the Lord will strike your livestock in the field, the horses, the donkeys, the cattle and the sheep, with a very severe pestilence. The Lord will make a distinction between the livestock of the Israelites and the livestock of the Egyptians, so that not one of the livestock of the children of Israel will die. The Lord set a time, saying, "Tomorrow the Lord will do this thing in the land." The Lord did this thing the next day, and all the livestock of the Egyptians died, but not one of the livestock of the children of Israel died. Pharaoh sent, and behold, not one of the livestock of the Israelites had died. Yet Pharaoh's heart was hardened again, and he refused to let the people go.

The Lord said to Moses and Aaron:

Take handfuls of soot from the furnace, and let Moses throw it toward the sky in the presence of Pharaoh, and it will become fine dust over all the land of Egypt, and it will cause festering boils breaking out on men and beasts throughout the land of Egypt. They took soot from the furnace and stood before Pharaoh, and Moses threw it toward the sky, and it caused festering boils to break out on men and beasts. The magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils, which had appeared on the magicians and on all the people of Egypt. The Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not listen to them, just as the Lord had said to Moses.

The Lord said to Moses:

Rise early in the morning and stand before Pharaoh and say to him:

Thus says the Lord, God of the Hebrews:

Let my people go that they may serve me. Otherwise, I am sending at this time my full plague upon your heart, your servants and your people, so that you may know that there is no god like me in all the earth. For by now I could have stretched out my hand and struck you and your people with pestilence, and you would have been wiped off the face of the earth. But I have kept you alive for this very purpose, to show you my power and my glory, and that my name may be proclaimed throughout the earth. Yet until now you still hold on to the people and refuse to let them go. Tomorrow at this time I will send down a very great and severe hail, the like of which has not been in Egypt from the day it was founded until now. (In a version of the Septuagint: "which has not been like it in Egypt from the day I founded it until this day of people.") Now send and gather your livestock and all that you have in the field, for every beast or man found in the field and not brought into the house will be struck by the hail and die. Whoever among the servants of Pharaoh feared the word of God moved his servants and his livestock into the houses, but whoever did not regard the word of the Lord left his livestock and servants in the field. The Lord said to Moses:

Stretch out your hand toward the sky, so that hail will fall upon all the land of Egypt, upon men, beasts and all the plants of the field. (In a version of the Septuagint: "upon men, livestock and all the vegetation of the wilderness.") Moses stretched out his staff toward the sky, and the Lord sent thunder and hail, and fire ran down upon the earth. The Lord sent hail down, and fire blazed within the hail, and it was very severe and great. There had never been anything like it in all the land of Egypt since the day the children of men settled there. The hail struck all the land of Egypt, everything and everyone in the field, both men and beasts (p-57), and the Lord destroyed all the herbs of the field and shattered all the trees of the groves. Only in the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel dwelt, did no hail fall. Pharaoh sent and summoned Moses and Aaron and said to them:

I have sinned this time also. The Lord is righteous, and I and my people are wicked. (In a version of the Septuagint: "I have sinned, the Lord is righteous, and I and my people are wicked.") Pray before the Lord, for it is enough that there be thunder and hail, and I will let you go, and you will not stay any longer. (In a version of the Septuagint: "and I will let you go, and I will not delay you any longer.") Moses said to Pharaoh:

When I leave the city, I will spread out my hands to the Lord, and the thunder will cease and the hail will no longer fall, so that you may know that the earth and all that is in it belong to the Lord. But I know that you and your servants have not yet feared the Lord God nor dreaded his punishment. The flax and the barley were destroyed (in a version of the Septuagint: "the hail struck the barley and the flax"), for the barley was in the ear and the flax was in bloom. But the wheat and the spelt were not destroyed, for they ripen later. When Moses left the city from before Pharaoh, he spread out (in a version of the Septuagint: "but the wheat and the millet were not harmed, for they were late, and Moses went out from Pharaoh outside the city and spread out") his hands before God toward the sky, and he turned away the thunder and hail, and the rain ceased from the earth. Pharaoh saw that the rain, hail and thunder had ceased and stopped, so he went back to sin, and his heart and the hearts of his servants were hardened (in a version of the Septuagint: "his heart and the heart of his servants hardened and became stubborn"), and he did not send the children of Israel as the word of the Lord had spoken through Moses. (In a version of the Septuagint: "as the Lord had spoken through Moses.")

The Lord said to Moses:

Go to Pharaoh, for I am the one who hardens his heart and the hearts of his servants, so that I may show these signs of mine, that you may tell your sons and your sons' sons of what I did to the Egyptians and of my many signs which I displayed, so that they may know that I am the Lord. Moses and Aaron came to Pharaoh and said to him:

Thus says the Lord, God of the Hebrews:

How long will you refuse to fear me and to be in awe of me? Let my people go that they may serve me. But if you refuse to let my people go, behold, tomorrow I will bring locusts upon all your borders, and they will cover the surface of the earth so that no one can see the ground. Whatever hail has left for you, they will eat, and they will eat every tree that grows for you in the field. They will fill your houses, the houses of your servants and the houses of all the Egyptians, as your fathers and forefathers have never seen since the day I founded the earth until this day. (In a version of the Septuagint: "Tomorrow at this time I will bring upon you a great swarm of locusts upon all your borders.") They turned and left Pharaoh. Pharaoh said to his servants:

How long shall this be a snare to us? Let the people go and serve the Lord their God. Do you not know that Egypt is ruined? (In a version of the Septuagint: "Pharaoh's servants said to Pharaoh: How long shall this trouble be to us? Let the men go and serve the Lord their God. Do you not know that Egypt is ruined?") They brought Moses and Aaron back to Pharaoh, and he said to them:

Go and serve the Lord your God. But who among you will go?

Moses said to him:

We will go with our young and old, our sons and daughters, our flocks and our herds, for it is a feast to us to the Lord. He said to them:

So be it, as you have said, and may the Lord be with you when I let you and your company go. Beware, for some misfortune may befall you on the road. But it shall not be so. Go now, you men, and serve the Lord, for that is what you seek. And they drove them from before Pharaoh. The Lord said to Moses:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 137 (part 3 of 4):

Raise your hand over the land of Egypt, and the locusts will come and settle upon the land of Egypt and eat the grass of the field and all that the hail has left. So Moses raised his staff over the land of Egypt, and the Lord brought an east wind upon the land all that day, and that night. When morning came, the east wind had brought the locusts, and the locusts went up over all the land of Egypt and settled on all the borders of the Egyptians' land. They were very numerous and very great. There had never been locusts like them before, nor will there be such locusts after them. They covered the whole face of the earth, so that the earth was darkened, and they ate all the grass of the field and all the trees that the hail had spared. No branch, leaf or green thing remained on the trees or in the fields throughout the land of Egypt. (p-60) Pharaoh hastened and called Moses and Aaron and said to them: "I have sinned before the LORD your God, and now forgive my sin and my folly this once, and pray to the LORD your God that He may take this plague and death away from me." So Moses went out from before Pharaoh and prayed before the LORD. The LORD turned the wind into a strong west wind, which carried the locusts away and cast them into the Sea of Suph. (In the Septuagint version: the Lord changed that wind into a very strong wind from the sea, which took the locusts and threw them into the Red Sea.) Not one locust remained in all the borders of the Egyptians. But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he did not let the children of Israel go. Then the LORD said to Moses: "Raise your hand toward heaven, so that darkness and gloom will be over all the land of Egypt, and the darkness will humble them." So Moses raised his hand toward heaven, and there was darkness and gloom over all the land of Egypt. (In the Septuagint version: it became darkness and a whirlwind over all the land of Egypt.) No one could see his neighbour for three days, but all the children of Israel had light and illumination in their dwellings. Pharaoh called Moses and said to him: "Go, serve the LORD your God. But leave your flocks and herds here, and take your children with you." Moses said to Pharaoh: "You must also give us sacrifices, so that we may slaughter them to the LORD our God. Our cattle must also go with us; not a hoof shall be left behind, for we must take from our property to sacrifice before the LORD our God, and we do not know with what we shall worship God until we arrive there." But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he refused to let them go. (p-61) Pharaoh said to Moses: "Get out from before me, and beware of appearing before me again, for on the day you appear before me you shall die." Moses said to him: "You have spoken well! I will not see your face again." The LORD said to Moses: "I will bring one more plague upon Pharaoh and the Egyptians; after that he will let you go from here, and when he lets you go, you shall all leave." He commanded the people and said to them: "Let every man ask from his neighbour, and every woman from her neighbour, for articles of gold and silver." (In the Septuagint version: vessels of silver and vessels of gold, and clothing.) The LORD gave the people favour and mercy in the hearts of the Egyptians, and Moses was held in great honour and dignity throughout the land of Egypt. (In the Septuagint version: in the sight of the Egyptians, in the sight of Pharaoh and in the sight of all his servants.) Moses said: "Thus says the LORD: 'I am going out at midnight, and I will pass through the land of Egypt, and I will strike down all the firstborn of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sits on his throne, to the firstborn of the maidservant who is behind the mill, and all the firstborn of the cattle will die. There will be a great wailing, a loud cry and a terrible groaning, the like of which has never been heard before.' (In the Septuagint version: and it shall not return to be like it.) But against the children of Israel no harm will be done, neither to man, nor beast, nor even a dog shall bark with its tongue. (In the Septuagint version: and not a dog among all the children of Israel shall growl with its tongue.) So that they may know that the LORD distinguishes between the Egyptians and the family of Israel. Then all these servants of yours will come down to me and bow to me and say: 'Go out, you and all the people who follow you.' After that I will go out." Moses went out from Pharaoh's presence in great anger. (p-62) The LORD said to Moses: "Pharaoh will not obey you, so that My signs and wonders may be multiplied in the land of Egypt." Moses and Aaron had been struck with these wounds, and they showed all these signs before Pharaoh. The LORD hardened (in the Septuagint version: and the LORD made hard) the heart of Pharaoh, so that he did not let the children of Israel leave his land. The LORD said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt: "This month shall be for you the first of the months, and it shall be the first month of the year. Speak to the whole assembly of the children of Israel: on the tenth day of this month each man shall take a lamb for his household, and a lamb for his father's family. If the household is too small for a lamb, then he and his nearest neighbour shall share one according to the number of people, and you shall estimate each person's share according to how much he eats of the lamb. The lamb shall be without blemish, a male, a year old, of the sheep or the goats, and you shall take it. It shall be kept for you until the fourteenth day of this month, and the whole congregation of the assembly of the children of Israel shall slaughter it in the evening. They shall take some of its blood and put it on the two doorposts and on the lintel of the houses in which they eat it. That is, as a sign for the angels who are commanded to kill the firstborn of the Egyptians. You shall eat the flesh that night, roasted with unleavened bread, and you shall not eat it raw or boiled in water, (p-63) and you shall leave none of it until morning, and you shall not break any of its bones. Whatever remains of it until morning, burn it with fire. Eat it with your loins girded, your sandals on your feet and your staffs in your hands, and eat it in haste, for it is the Passover of the LORD. I will pass through the land of Egypt that night and strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt, both of men and of beasts, and I will execute judgment against all the gods of the Egyptians: I am the LORD! This day shall be a memorial for you, and you shall keep it as a feast to the LORD for your generations forever; you shall keep it as a feast for seven days. You shall eat unleavened bread, and you shall remove leaven from your houses from the first day. Whoever eats leavened bread, that soul shall be cut off from Israel from the first day to the seventh day. You shall do no work on these days. Keep this commandment, for on this very day your armies went out from Egypt. So make this day a statute for your generations. From the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month, you shall eat unleavened bread until the evening of the twenty-first day of the month. No leaven shall be found in your houses for seven days. Whoever eats what is leavened, that soul shall be cut off from the congregation of the children of Israel, whether a stranger or a native of the land. You shall eat nothing leavened; in all your dwellings you shall eat unleavened bread." Moses summoned all the elders of the children of Israel and said to them: "Hurry, take lambs for your families and slaughter the Passover (p-64) and take a bunch of hyssop, dip it in the blood of the lamb, and sprinkle it on the lintel and the doorposts of your doors. (In the Septuagint version: on the threshold and both doorposts, from the blood that is in the basin.) None of you shall go out of the door of his house until morning. (In the Septuagint version: until dawn.) You shall keep this statute and this commandment, you and your children, forever. When you enter the land that the LORD will give you, as He promised, you shall keep this rite. When your children ask you, 'What is this rite?' you shall say to them: 'This is the sacrifice of the Passover of the LORD, who passed over the houses of the children of Israel in Egypt when He struck the Egyptians and delivered our houses.'" The whole people bowed down and worshipped God, and the children of Israel went and did as the LORD commanded Moses and Aaron. In the houses of the children of Israel, when it was midnight, the LORD struck down all the firstborn in the land of Egypt. (In the Septuagint version: every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sits on his throne.) (In the Septuagint version: on his seat.) Even the firstborn of the captive in the prison, and all the firstborn of the cattle. Pharaoh rose up that night, he and all his servants and all the Egyptians. (In the Septuagint version: and all the Egyptians.) There was a great wailing throughout the land of Egypt, for there was no house in which there was not a dead person. Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron that night and said to them: "Rise up, go out from among my people, you and the children of Israel also, and go and serve the LORD as you have said. Take your flocks and your herds also, as you have said, and go, and bless me too, and pray for me." The Egyptians pressed the people to send them out of the land quickly, for they said: "We are all going to die." (p-65) So the people took their dough before it had risen, with their kneading troughs wrapped in their garments and laid on their shoulders. The children of Israel did as Moses had commanded. They asked the Egyptians for articles of gold and silver and clothing. (In the Septuagint version: vessels of silver and gold and clothing.) The LORD gave the people favour in the eyes of the Egyptians, so they lent them what they asked, and they despoiled the Egyptians. The children of Israel set out from Ramesses (in the margin of the Septuagint version: it is 'Ain Shams), toward Sakkoth, six hundred thousand men on foot, besides the children and the women. A great mixed multitude also went up with them, and very many flocks and herds and livestock. They baked the dough they had brought out of Egypt into unleavened cakes. (In the Septuagint version: "Farrani," unleavened, which they did not let rise.) This was because the Egyptians drove them out and they could not delay, and they had not prepared any provisions for the journey. The dwelling of the children of Israel in the land of Egypt was four hundred and thirty years. On that very day all the hosts of the LORD went out from the land of Egypt. (In the Septuagint version: by night.) The LORD had appointed in His foreknowledge the keeping of that night in which they went out of Egypt, and that night was kept and known before the LORD, for the destruction of the firstborn of Egypt and for the bringing out of all the children of Israel, so that the remembrance of it would be in all their generations and their descendants. The LORD said to Moses and Aaron: "This is the statute of the Passover: no foreigner shall eat of it. Every slave bought with money, when you have circumcised him, then he may eat of it. A hired servant and a sojourner shall not eat of it. (p-66) It shall be eaten in one house; you shall not carry any of the flesh outside the house, nor break any bone of it. When a stranger sojourns with you and wants to keep the Passover to the LORD, let all his males be circumcised, and then he may come near and keep it, and he shall be as a native of the land. But no uncircumcised person shall eat of it. There shall be one law for the native and for the stranger who sojourns among you." (In the Septuagint version: every male slave bought for silver, let him be circumcised, and then he shall eat of it. The settler and the hired servant shall not eat of it. And it shall be eaten in one house.) All the children of Israel did as the LORD commanded Moses and Aaron. On that very day the LORD brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt, with all their hosts. The LORD said to Moses: "Consecrate to Me every firstborn male, every firstborn that opens the womb among the children of Israel, both of men and of beasts; they shall be Mine." Moses said to the people:

Remember this day on which you went forth from Egypt, from servitude and bondage, for the Lord brought you out from here with a mighty hand. [This continues what has passed in Surat al-Baqarah.] Then in the fifth [book] he mentioned the reason for the Passover (fisḥ), and said:

"Observe the month of Abib, and make the Passover to the Lord your God, for in the month of Abib He brought you out of the land of Egypt by night. You shall sacrifice the Passover to the Lord your God, of the flock and the herd, in the place which the Lord your God will choose. You shall not eat leavened bread with it; seven days you shall eat unleavened bread with it, the bread of affliction, for you came out of the land of Egypt in haste, that you may remember the day when you came out of the land of Egypt all the days of your life. No leaven shall be seen among you in all your territory for seven days. Nor shall any of the flesh which you sacrifice on the first day in the evening remain overnight until the morning. You may not sacrifice the Passover within any of your gates which the Lord your God gives you; but at the place where the Lord your God chooses, to make His name dwell there, there you shall sacrifice the Passover at twilight, at the going down of the sun, at the season that you came out of Egypt."

Then he said:

"And you shall count seven weeks from the time you begin to put the sickle to the standing grain. Then you shall keep the Feast of Weeks to the Lord your God with the tribute of a freewill offering from your hand, which you shall give as the Lord your God blesses you. You shall rejoice before the Lord your God, you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, the Levite who is within your gates, the stranger, the fatherless, and the widow who are among you, at the place where the Lord your God chooses to make His name dwell. And you shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt; so you shall be careful to observe these statutes. You shall observe the Feast of Tabernacles seven days after you have gathered from your threshing floor and your winepress. You shall rejoice in your feast... and you shall be altogether joyful. Three times a year all your males shall appear before the Lord your God in the place which He chooses: at the Feast of Unleavened Bread, at the Feast of Weeks, and at the Feast of Tabernacles."

End quote.

In it is what may not be said in our law: the attribution of "son" in His words "My firstborn son" (Israel), which is interpreted to mean that He honors him with the honor due to a child; and the application of "God" (ilah) to other than God, the Most High, is meant in the sense of a ruler. This usage is not permissible according to us.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 138:

When He, glory be to Him, had finished showing them the awesome acts by which He rescued them from that tyrant, he began to mention what they returned to Him of ignorance, and what He returned to them of forbearance, and then what He brought upon them after a long respite of humiliation and transformation into the shape of apes. He said, linking it to His saying ﴿So We drowned them in the sea﴾ [al-A'raf: 136], or to His saying ﴿Then after them We sent Moses﴾ [al-A'raf: 103], ﴿and We brought across﴾, that is, We caused to cross, by Our majesty, and He phrased it in the form of mufa'alah (the verbal pattern denoting reciprocal or intensive action) to magnify it. It is narrated that their crossing took place on the day of 'Ashura', and that Moses, peace be upon him, fasted it in thanksgiving to God, the Exalted, for their deliverance and the destruction of their enemy. ﴿with the Children of Israel﴾, after the signs they had witnessed, ﴿the sea﴾. I made it linked to the beginning of the story because all these narratives are an explanation that among people there is one of evil essence, whom signs do not benefit, as has passed at His saying ﴿And the good land﴾ [al-A'raf: 58], and an explanation of His saying ﴿We seized its people with misfortune and adversity﴾ [al-A'raf: 94] to its end. This is indicated, along with how the narratives began, by His concluding them with His saying ﴿That is the example of the people who denied Our signs﴾ [al-A'raf: 176], and His saying ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell﴾ [al-A'raf: 179]. Its placement after His saying ﴿And the word of your Lord was fulfilled, the best [promise]﴾ [al-A'raf: 137] is fitting, because when it was said ﴿for what they endured patiently﴾ [al-A'raf: 137], the soul longed to know their conduct in times of ease: did they give thanks? So He made clear that many of them disbelieved, confirming His saying ﴿And We found most of them not upholding a covenant﴾ [al-A'raf: 102] and what resembles it. How excellent is the sequence of this with His saying ﴿Then they came upon﴾, that is, they passed by, with the fa' of sequence, ﴿a people﴾, that is, people of strength. It was said they were from Lakhm, ﴿devoted to﴾, that is, circling and gathering around, persistently and constantly, ﴿their idols﴾, that is, in which there is no power and no benefit. Thus their devotion to them is an example of foolishness. It was also said that they were images of a cow, and that this was the first beginning of the calf.

When He, glory be to Him, had informed of this, the listener knew that they were between two states: either gratitude or disbelief. So he longed to know what they did, and He, glory be to Him, answered his question with His saying ﴿They said﴾, that is, their remembrance did not last, after what God, glory be to Him, had shown them of His greatness, and their gratitude for the blessings He had poured upon them, except for a brief moment, once they were safe from their enemy by crossing the sea and their drowning in it, until they sought a god other than Him, by saying ﴿O Moses﴾. They called him by his name, as you see, out of rudeness and harshness, relying on the kindness and forbearance that had encompassed them, not showing courtesy in light of the greatness of his portion from God and his station with Him, which had overwhelmed them. ﴿Make for us a god﴾, that is, something we can see and circle around, bound by imagination, ﴿as they have gods﴾. This is the speech of one who does not regard the God who did these deeds with them as anything, and does not call Him to mind in any way.

Since this from them was grave, He resumed the answer to one who longed to hear what Moses, peace be upon him, said to them, with His saying ﴿He said: Indeed you are a people﴾, that is, those who persist in the desires of the souls, ﴿who are ignorant﴾. He used the present tense, ﴿taj-halūn﴾, to indicate that this is in them like a nature and an instinct, from which they do not move, in past or future. Know that there is no repetition in these narratives, for each context of them is for a matter that has not preceded [its like]. The purpose of the story of Moses, peace be upon him, and Pharaoh, upon whom be the curse and blame, is this existential argument for His saying ﴿And indeed We found most of them to be defiant﴾ [al-A'raf: 102]. From here you know that the context of the story of the Children of Israel after their deliverance from their enemy is to explain their haste in disbelief and their breaking of covenants. God, glory be to Him, continued in this argument until the end of the surah. How appropriate is His saying ﴿And when your Lord took from the children of Adam﴾ [al-A'raf: 172] and its verse, in response to His saying ﴿And We found most of them not upholding a covenant﴾ [al-A'raf: 102]. In the beginning of the surah that follows, He mentioned their disputing over the spoils, as a warning to them not to be among the most blameworthy in this respect. This differs from the purpose of the context of the narratives of the Children of Israel in al-Baqarah, for there it is to draw them to faith by reminding them of blessings, because that is in the context of His address to all people with His saying ﴿Worship your Lord who created you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21], ﴿How can you disbelieve in God when you were dead and He gave you life﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28], and what resembles it, by appealing through enumerating blessings and repelling punishments. And God knows best.

(p-71) When the extent of his denunciation toward them was inferred from his words, he gave the reason for this denunciation by saying: ﴿Indeed, these people — what they are engaged in is doomed﴾, i.e., the people; ﴿mutabbar﴾ means broken, shattered, destroyed, used in an emphatic sense. When the vessel is corrupt, what it contains is corrupt too. This is alluded to by making "these people" the subject of *inna* (indeed), and by placing the predicate of the sentence, which is itself the predicate of the preceding clause, before its subject.

Since a thing may be destroyed in this world [or in the Hereafter], and this is true, He informed them that this destruction is [the destruction] in the sight of God, the Most Knowing, regardless of whether it occurs in this world or in the Hereafter, because what they are engaged in is false. So He said, using the nominal form to indicate that it is so now, even if it appears otherwise: ﴿and vain is what they used to do﴾, i.e., perishing and passing away, ﴿what they used to do﴾, i.e., by nature and disposition, ﴿they were persisting in it﴾, namely the idols, the devotion (*al-ukuf*) and all their actions performed for their sake, none of which has any weight or consideration at all. [And] in this there is an indication that worship is fitting only for the Everlasting who is not subject to change; and when that is so, the action directed to Him is likewise enduring and lasting, not subject to nullification. In its being followed by the mention of the destruction of the family of Pharaoh there is an indication of the reason for this, and that everyone who is in the same condition as they, worshipping other than God, will have destruction as his end.

Since this (argument) was a proof that idols such as those they passed by are not fit to be worshipped, that was not sufficient for them, given their ignorance, which has been established; perhaps they thought that other things besides God might be worthy of worship. So it is as if it were said: "This is not enough as an answer for such people; did He say anything else to them?" It was said: "Yes!" ﴿He said﴾, disapproving and marveling (p-72): ﴿"Should I seek for you a god other than God"﴾, that is, the One who possesses all greatness, so He alone deserves worship, ﴿"while He"﴾, that is, while the state is that He alone ﴿"has favored you"﴾ over others, not those of your time or before it, ﴿"above all peoples"﴾. That is: even if there were no reason requiring that they be devoted to Him in worship except His singling them out for distinction over the rest of His servants, those whose knowledge reached them, among those who were stronger than them in condition and greater in number and wealth, it would have been sufficient.

When he had established that divinity is not fit for anyone other than Him, and that no other could bestow favor upon them, and since the context called for [a display of] majesty, it was as if it were said, signaling the hardness of their hearts, the scarcity of their understanding, and the badness of their response to the Benefactor: "Remember that," i.e., His favor to you in choosing your forefathers Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and the blessings that preceded for them and for their descendants, especially Joseph, peace be upon him, whom He made ruler over the whole land whose people had subjugated you. He then turned, by way of an iltifat (a shift in grammatical person) toward the manifestation of majesty, to remind [them] of the greatness of what follows, saying: ﴿And [remember] when﴾, i.e., remember when, ﴿We saved you﴾, i.e., by what We are of majesty, which you recognize, and which you witness at every time in those signs. ﴿from the people of Pharaoh﴾, and what We bestowed upon you after the deliverance of great blessings and showed you of mighty signs, so that you would know that We preferred you (p-73) over all of mankind. Then he resumed explaining what saved them from it, saying: ﴿who inflicted upon you﴾, i.e., they constantly brought upon you, ﴿the worst torment﴾.

Since the context, as has passed, was to explain their haste in disbelief and the severity of their arrogance in their strength and coarseness, and since the purpose of the surah is to warn those who turn away and to caution them against the calamities that He brought upon those before them, He explained the worst torment, moving away in his explanation from التَّذْبِيحِ (al-tadhbih, slaughtering), because it does not occur at the time of cutting the throat, whereas in origin it means simply cutting, to the expression بِالقَتْلِ (killing), because it is more indicative of causing death and more striking. It may also take a severe and hideous form, such as cutting into pieces, impaling, and beating, and other such things, while killing necessarily involves ending life. So he said: ﴿they slaughter﴾, i.e., they kill in great numbers, ﴿your sons﴾, and he indicated the reality of killing by his saying: ﴿and spare﴾ [your women].

Since the meaning is that they did not spare females, young or old, and since what is denied is the preservation of women without men, because of the fear of loss and shame, and since the place of shame is greater, he referred to them by saying: ﴿your women﴾. And as a reminder that the killing of sons was only out of fear of their becoming men, lest one of them strip them of their kingdom, as their soothsayers had informed their king of him, he indicated the severity of that by saying: ﴿And in that﴾, i.e., in that matter, which is difficult and terrifying, there was ﴿a trial﴾, i.e., a test for you and for them, ﴿from your Lord﴾, i.e., the One who does good to you in both states of hardship and ease, for He concealed from them the one for whose sake they intended to kill, and delivered you through him after He had raised him in the house of the one who was striving to slaughter him. ﴿Mighty﴾.

[p. 74] When He reminded them of the blessing of rescuing their bodies, He followed it with a reminder of something greater: that blessing was for the preservation of their religions and the safeguarding of the jewel of faith, through the law He established for them in the Torah. He said, marvelling at their state, given that He had bestowed upon them the establishment of a law to guide them out of error and had singled out their Prophet for special closeness through intimate conversation, while they took for themselves another god, one with no benefit whatsoever, which no heart or intellect would accept as an object of worship. This is connected, by conjunction, to what He had already marvelled at concerning them in His words: ﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across﴾ (Al-A'raf: 138) ﴿And We appointed for Musa thirty﴾, that is, by Our manifest majesty, ﴿nights﴾, that is, the intimate conversation of thirty nights, ﴿and We completed them﴾, that is, the appointment, ﴿with ten﴾, that is, nights. This was because, when thirty nights had passed, which was the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah according to what was said, Musa, peace be upon him, had fasted them by night and day. He noticed a change in his mouth, so he used the miswak. God informed him that he had spoiled the scent of his mouth, and commanded him to fast ten more days, which were the ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, so that what he had removed would be restored. This was because Musa, peace be upon him, had promised the Children of Israel, while they were in Egypt, that when God, may He be exalted, destroyed their enemy, he would bring them a Book from Him containing an explanation of what they should do and what they should avoid. When God destroyed their enemy, Musa, peace be upon him, asked for the Book, so He commanded him to fast thirty days and then commanded him with the ten.

Since it was possible that the thirty would be the end point, and that it was divided into twenty and then ten, He removed this possibility by His words: ﴿So the appointed time of his Lord was completed﴾ (p. 75), that is, the appointed time He had decreed from eternity for Him to converse with him after that, ﴿forty﴾, by the particle fa' (so/then). And since the ten were not explicit about nights, He said ﴿nights﴾, thereby excluding the possibility that they were hours, for example. He expressed it as "appointed time" (mi'qat) because no action was prescribed within it, whereas waqt (time) is the duration of a thing, whether it is appointed or not. He expressed it with "Lord" to indicate kindness toward him, compassion for him and mercy upon him. The mi'qat is the forty, as al-Farisi said in al-Hujjah. He took the accusative of "forty" to be governed by "counted as this number," just as you say, "The people completed twenty," meaning, "counted as this number." God, may He be exalted, left the forty unspecified in al-Baqarah, because the purpose of that context is to remind them of great blessings and to bring them near with kindness and honour, so that this would more readily lead them back to faith and more effectively turn them away from disbelief. This is evident from what preceded their story: His words ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 21) and ﴿How can you disbelieve in God?﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 28), and what surrounded it at the beginning and end, namely His words, "O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you," the two verses that open with it and close with it. Here, however, He detailed the forty into thirty and ten, because the purpose of this context, as previously explained, is to show their disbelief and rebellion despite their disgrace and their deceit, and that asking for miracles did not benefit them, nor did the continual succession of blessings and signs avail them anything, just as was the case in the stories of the earlier nations and the past generations mentioned in this sura, as evidence, as previously explained, that the corrupter is more numerous than the reformer, and for other purposes summarised in His words, exalted is He: ﴿We did not send a prophet to any town without seizing its people﴾ (Al-A'raf: 94), to the end of the verse, and as consolation for this noble Prophet and as a warning to his people, given what befell them of painful punishment. The distinction between the two contexts is subtle and is grasped only by people of insight, and God knows best. Thus, the purpose of detailing the forty here is to show that Musa's, peace be upon him, delay beyond what they had known of the appointed promise was only ten days, and in those days they committed this crime, which is the greatest of crimes. God, may He be exalted, pointed to the magnitude of their audacity and their deep-rootedness in foolishness in His words, connected by conjunction to ﴿We appointed﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 51): ﴿And Musa said﴾, that is, when We had made the appointment with him, ﴿to his brother﴾, then He clarified this by naming him explicitly, saying: ﴿Harun, take my place﴾, that is, be my successor among them, doing what I used to do. He emphasised the appointment of him with what he would find for him in the words ﴿among my people﴾, and He indicated urging him to strive by His words ﴿and set things right﴾, that is, continue in the state you are in of bringing about reform.

Since he knew that the Prophet, peace be upon him, was free from evil, but that there was gentleness in him, He said: ﴿And do not follow﴾, that is, do not burden yourself with what you were not created to do, by following ﴿the way of the corrupters﴾, that is, seeking to reform them and fearing to drive them away. They deviated from the path, as Musa, peace be upon him, had perceived about them, and they did not consider the consequence. They did not fear the vengeance of the one who had inflicted vengeance on those who had been subjecting them to the worst torment, nor did they listen to their brother's counsel toward righteousness, nor did they wait ten days. So none were more feeble in judgement, nor more audacious in disobedience.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 143:

(p-77) When He, glory be to Him, mentioned His appointment with Moses and Moses' care in setting right his people, He explained his condition during the appointment and their condition after his absence, saying: ﴿And when Moses came at Our appointed time﴾, that is, at the first part of the time We had set for the private conversation. Since the station of majesty is awesome and no one can bear to hear speech in its presence, He turned to the station of honour and said: ﴿and his Lord spoke to him﴾, that is, without an intermediary, ﴿his Lord﴾, that is, the One who did good to him in all kinds of goodness and who bestowed favours upon his people in all kinds of blessings. According to the Ash'aris, who are among the Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunni community), what Moses, peace be upon him, heard is the eternal attribute (of speech), without sound or letters. There is no difficulty in this, just as there is no difficulty in seeing the Essence of God, glory be to Him, while He is neither a body nor an accident nor a substance, and "there is nothing like Him" (Qur'an 42:11). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that He, glory be to Him, spoke to him throughout the appointment and wrote the Tablets for him. It was also said that He spoke to him only at the beginning of the forty days, but the first view is more preferable.

When He spoke to him with the attribute of lordship, which looks upon him with tenderness and kindness, and seeing was possible, Moses longed to see Him with a longing he could not control, because of the sweetness of the address he had tasted. So he asked for it, knowing that it was possible. ﴿He said﴾ [dropping the particle of address, as is the custom of those close to God]: ﴿My Lord, show me﴾, that is, Your most holy Essence, by lifting the veil from me so that I may be enabled to look. This is the meaning of the words of the scholar Ibn 'Abbas: "Give me." [And it is confirmed that this is seeing with the eye, by His words in answer to the command] ﴿Look﴾ [that is, direct the gaze of the eye]. He indicated His greatness, glory be to Him, and the loftiness of His rank (p-78) [the loftiness of majesty, not of distance], by using the verb with the particle of limit [after he had indicated, by dropping the particle of address, the ultimate nearness through His favour], saying: ﴿at You﴾, that is, so that I may see You.

Since He, glory be to Him, had decreed that he, peace be upon him, would not see Him in this world, He said, negating the aim, which is the seeing itself and not its prerequisite, namely looking, which is staring with the eye: ﴿You will not see Me﴾. By this expression God indicated that His being seen is possible, since He did not say "I shall not be seen" or "no one shall see Me." Then He increased this clarification by making it conditional on something possible, saying: ﴿But look at the mountain﴾, pointing to a mountain that was known to them, which was the greatest mountain there. [He also added to the indication of seeing by expressing it with the particle of doubt and following it with a possible command, saying]: ﴿If it remains firm in its place﴾, that is, if it finds its stability in complete existence. He also indicated the remoteness of the seeing and the sublimity of what is sought from it by His words: ﴿then you will see Me﴾, that is, by a promise that admits no failure. ﴿But when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain﴾, that is, the One who did good to him with every gift and every withholding [and He made clear by His use of the preposition "li" (to) that this was a manifestation of nearness and special favour; had He used "ʿalā" (upon), for example, it would have been something else], He said: ﴿to the mountain﴾, that is, by unveiling to the mountain some of the veils of His majesty. ﴿He made it crumble﴾, that is, reduced it to dust; "dakk" and "daqq" are two related words. ﴿And Moses fell down unconscious﴾, that is, he fell in a swoon, ﴿with a terrifying sound﴾. Thus it is known that the sense of the exception is: you will not be able to bear My seeing in this abode, and you do not know this now; but you will know it through an example that I shall show you, which is the mountain. [For the one who is passing away, as is reported from Imam Malik, should not look upon (p-79) the One who remains.] When he recovered from his swoon, ﴿he said: Glory be to You﴾, that is, exalting You above my asking of You what You have not permitted. ﴿I repent to You﴾, that is, from that. ﴿And I am the first of the believers﴾, that is, the one who most hastens to believe in everything You have informed of, everything these verses contain. [His expression "belief" is most fitting to the absence of seeing, because the condition of belief is that it be in the unseen. In our Prophet ﷺ there are two verses: one of them may indicate seeing by the expression "Muslims" rather than "believers" in His words: "And I am the first of the Muslims" (Qur'an 6:163); and the second points to its absence, which is: "The Messenger believes..." (Qur'an 2:285) up to His words: "Each believes in Allah" (Qur'an 2:285). And Allah knows best.] All this is a rebuke to his people and a reproach to them for worshipping the calf, a deterrent from that, and an admonition to them that divinity is linked with greatness and majesty and is far removed from things that have bodies, since God, glory be to Him, knew that they would repeatedly worship idols. Thus He attributed to the true God speech, and the impossibility of seeing Him because of the veil of pride and majesty, and the crumbling of the mountain at His manifestation, and the establishment of the law that guides to the straightest path, as an allusion to the calf. To this guides His, exalted be He, words: "Did they not see that it does not speak to them?" (Qur'an 7:148), and so on.

Al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 144:

When He withheld from him the vision after he had asked for it, and balanced that with the excellence of deeds and words, the listener became eager to learn what honour he had been met with. So Glorified is He resumed by informing of what He bestowed upon him, as consolation for what He had withheld and as a command to thank Him, by His saying: ﴿"O Moses"﴾ (p-80), reminding him of His favours in a context that indicates their great worth and the obligation to give thanks for them, dropping for him the manifestation of majesty, for intimacy and gentleness [towards him]: ﴿"I have chosen you"﴾, that is: I have chosen you with a complete choosing, just as the pure part of a thing is chosen, purified from every stain. ﴿"Above the people"﴾, that is: those who are in your time. ﴿"With My messages"﴾, that is: the numerous signs which I manifested and manifest through your hands [from the books of the Torah and others]. ﴿"And with My speech"﴾, that is: without an intermediary. It seems that He repeated the preposition (ḥarf al-jarr) to draw attention to this, just as He chose Muhammad (ﷺ) above people in general, in every age, through his universal message, through his miraculous speech, and through his being addressed without an intermediary in the heaven which has always been sanctified and kept free from being defiled by disobedience.

Since that required the utmost of readiness and energy, He made His saying a consequence of it: ﴿"So take what I have given you"﴾, that is: singling you out with it, ﴿"and be among the thankful"﴾, that is: among those who are firmly rooted in the quality of thankfulness and disposed to it.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 145:

When the matters with which He, glory be to Him, comforted him had ended, He shifted the speech (*iltifat*, a shift in grammatical person or address) in His report to us about the magnitude of what He had given him, to the manifestation of majesty (*mazhar al-'azamah*). So He said, detailing that message and clarifying some of what it contained: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets﴾, meaning by Our majesty. He made the word "the tablets" definite (*'arrafaha*) to honour them, as an indication that because of the greatness of what they were specially given, they are as if they alone bore this name. Greater than this, He made the heart of the Unlettered Prophet a tablet, receptive to what is cast into it and comprehensive of the knowledge of the earlier and later generations. ﴿Of everything﴾, meaning everything the Children of Israel needed. That was the Ten Commandments, whose relation to the Torah is like the relation of al-Fatihah to the Qur'an. In them are (p-81) the foundations of religion, the foundations of the rulings, reminders of blessings, the command to asceticism and scrupulousness, adherence to good deeds, and distance from their evils. For this reason He said, as a substitution (*mubdilan*): ﴿as an admonition and a detailed explanation﴾, meaning, despite their brevity, they were the cause of ﴿everything﴾, because they, along with being foundational principles and comprehensive summaries, are detailed, such that the seas of knowledge return to them and its springs gush forth from them.

Since this was so, His saying, may He be exalted, followed from it necessarily, with a shift (*iltifat*) to addressing Moses, peace be upon him, in the tone of reassurance, indicating that undertaking the obligations is difficult: ﴿So take them﴾, meaning the tablets, ﴿with strength﴾, meaning with earnestness and resolve in knowledge and action. ﴿And command your people﴾, meaning the strong among them, to attempt what is intended, ﴿they will take the best of it﴾. It is as if He, glory be to Him, permitted Moses, peace be upon him, to take everything in them, because of the faculty he possessed that restrains him from any transgression. For this reason He said to him: ﴿with strength﴾, and He restricted them to ﴿the best﴾, so that the very good would prevent them from reaching the evil, such as retaliation, pardon, self-defence, and patience.

Since it was as if it were said: "Does anyone leave the best?" The answer was: "Yes, the defiantly disobedient (*al-fasiq*) leaves it, and indeed transgresses from the good to the evil, and even to the worst of evils. And whoever leaves it, I will destroy him, however great his household and however mighty his armies and wealth." He said, as a kind of justification for that: ﴿I will show you the abode of the defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning those who go out from My commands to what I have forbidden them. I will give you victory over them and enable you, through their disobedience, over their necks and wealth, from (p-82) the Canaanites, the Hittites, and others among the inhabitants of the sacred lands, so that you may know that whoever opposes Me and abandons My command, I will empower you against him. He mentioned "the abode" only so that its strong defences would not deceive them, so that once they settled in it they would not think that no one could overcome them, given the roughness of its land, the towering of its mountains, and the firmness of its walls. If you reflect on what will come in the explanation of these verses from the Torah, this meaning will become clear to you. The same applies to what is mentioned from the Torah at His saying in al-Ma'idah: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something worse than that as a recompense from God?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 60]. In this concise sentence there is good news of the fulfilment of the promise to give them victory over those people if they obey, and a warning should they disobey. It is as if it were said: If they take the best, I will show them the abode of the defiantly disobedient, and I will complete My blessing upon them as long as they are thankful; and if they do not take it, I will destroy them as I destroyed the defiantly disobedient before them. Thus He warned them, lest they do as those people did once the abode had settled them and their troubles had departed from them. The reading of whoever recited ﴿I will make you inherit﴾ (*sa-'uwarrithukum*), from inheritance, supports that the intended land is the Holy Land (al-Quds) and not Egypt (Misr), for it is the land intended by bringing them out of Egypt and sending Moses, peace be upon him. This does not exclude the possibility that Egypt is also intended. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 146:

When that had ended, it was as if it were said: "How could a rational person choose that? How much more so one who has seen the signs and witnessed the miracles?" So He said: ﴿I will turn away from My signs﴾, that is, those that are heard and those that are seen, despite their greatness, by what the idafa (possessive construction) indicates, [He will turn them away] from understanding them, from following them, and from the ability to find fault with them in a way that affects their invalidation, ﴿those who are arrogant﴾, that is, who seek arrogance through what is not theirs and exert their strength in it, ﴿in the earth﴾, that is, its kind, in which I commanded humility.

When a person whom Allah has elevated through a virtuous quality places himself in the position of that quality and does not debase himself, out of regard for the blessing and gift Allah has bestowed upon him, that is often called arrogance, and his pursuit of those noble traits which bring about his elevation is often called pride. [This is not so, even though it resembles it in outward form, because it differs from it in meaning. For it is the preservation of the self from humiliation, while lowering oneself below one's rank is a deliberate act and not humility. Arrogance is the rejection of truth and the belittling of people. So in this restriction there is a subtle indication of affirming dignity through truth and standing at the limit of humility without deviating into affectation, standing firm upon the condition of resolve laid down over the edge of the fire of arrogance. Imam al-Suhrawardi said: "None is strengthened in this and remains steadfast upon it except the feet of the firmly rooted scholars."] He, exalted is He, said, guarding against it and including every arrogance [that is devoid] of complete truth: ﴿without right﴾, that is, only one who chooses what is not best chooses it by My decree, which cannot be averted, and My command, which is higher than the command of every earnest person. So I make attractive to those whose base origin and wretched essence I know what I wish, until they commit every ugly deed and abandon every beautiful one, and thus they turn away from the signs and become blind to the clear proofs.

When He had informed of their arrogance in the present, He followed it with their conduct in the outcome, so He said: ﴿And if they see every sign﴾, that is, seen or heard, ﴿they will not believe in it﴾, that is, because of their arrogance toward the truth. ﴿And if they see the way of right guidance﴾, that is, the path of righteousness and correctness which is fit to be followed, ﴿they will not take it as a way﴾, that is, they will not follow it with intent, reflection, and deliberate purpose; rather, if they follow it at all, it is without intention. ﴿And if they see the way of error﴾, that is, deviation, ﴿they will take it as a way﴾, that is, with utmost desire, deliberate purpose, and eagerness to follow it.

Since this is a matter of wonder, He answered the one who asks about it with His words: ﴿That﴾, that is, this great turning away, which exceeds mere turning away by blindness to faith and to adopting right guidance, ﴿is because they﴾, that is, because of the fact that they ﴿denied Our signs﴾, that is, despite their greatness, ﴿and were heedless of them﴾, [that is, specifically] by natural disposition and inclination, ﴿heedless﴾, that is, their habit and way was to treat them with aversion, to the point that they were as if forgotten, so they persist in what they do.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 7, verse 147:

When he had mentioned the conditions of the arrogant ones whose arrogance led them to denial in this world, he mentioned their condition in the Hereafter, saying: ﴿And those who﴾, i.e., denied these, while the state is that those who ﴿denied Our signs﴾, i.e., did not heed their greatness, ﴿and the meeting of the Hereafter﴾, i.e., their meeting with it, or their meeting with what they were promised therein, which necessarily follows from denying the signs, which carries belief in them toward the lofty (ma'ali) qualities of character, ﴿their deeds have become worthless﴾, i.e., they have been corrupted and have fallen away, ﴿their deeds﴾ [This verse is of the type called ihtibak (a balanced omission): mentioning heedlessness first indicates that its counterpart is intended second, and mentioning meeting second indicates that its counterpart is intended first.]

(p-85) When it was as though it were said: Why did they become void? It was said: ﴿Will they be recompensed except for what﴾, i.e., the recompense of what ﴿they used to do﴾, i.e., by the voiding of their deeds, even if they did every good deed other than faith, because they voided the signs and the Hereafter by denying them, i.e., by regarding them as false. Recompense is of the same kind as the deed. The outcome is that when they were blind to the signs, because they did not reflect upon them nor submitted to what their intellects indicated about their matter, but rather closed the door of thought regarding them, God increased them in blindness and sealed over their faculties, so that they were no longer benefited by them, and they became ones who do not comprehend. These verses are the greatest deterrent from arrogance, for they make clear that it necessitates disbelief, persistence in it, and weakness in all affairs.

Now when all of this is among the things that the one granted success finds astonishing in its commission, God, exalted is He, followed it up, making clear, depicting, confirming the occurrence of it, and establishing His saying, by way of conjunction with: ﴿Then they came upon a people devoting themselves to idols﴾ [al-A'raf: 138], making clear their haste in disbelief: ﴿And the people of Musa took﴾, i.e., with the utmost eagerness, ﴿after him﴾, i.e., by the making and approval of the Samiri, and they did not take heed of anything of what had come to them with those signs, the like of which had never been seen. ﴿After him﴾, i.e., after his delay away from them by the ten days with which We completed the forty. ﴿Of their ornaments﴾, i.e., which were with them from their own wealth and from what they had borrowed from the Copts. ﴿A calf﴾. And since "calf" was a name for the young of a cow, He made clear that it only resembled its form, so He said, substituting for it: ﴿a body﴾.

And since the report that it was a body conveyed that it was devoid of anything resembling that which arises from a spirit, He said: ﴿That lowed﴾, i.e., a sound like the lowing of a cow. The meaning is that there is no one more astray or more blind than a people who had with them ornaments that they had taken from those who used to enslave and harm them, and who were, despite that, the most disbelieving of disbelievers. It was therefore deserving of hatred, being one of the traces of the oppressing enemies. They believed that by its fashioning it had become a god, and they exaggerated in loving it and in worship of it, though it was a body they could see and touch, while their prophet, whom God guided by him and chose for His speech, asks to see God and does not reach it.

Since there was no explicit text in the speech about their taking it as a god, He indicated that by rebuking them in His saying: ﴿Did they not see﴾, i.e., those who took a god, ﴿that it does not speak to them﴾, i.e., as God spoke to Musa, peace be upon him, ﴿nor guide them to a way﴾, as God, exalted is He, guided them to the way of salvation, among it their traversing the sea, which was a cause of the destruction of their enemy just as it was a cause of their own deliverance.
